docs.title: California 1A Auditor's Field Guide
docs.text:
Working research preview. This is the reading layer for the California handbook while the legal research is still under active development.

The guide is designed around a practical question: what legal rule actually applies to this place, this activity, and this government response? It avoids shortcuts such as "public property means anything goes" or "an employee told you to leave, so remaining is automatically trespass."

docs.title: Start with the situation
docs.text: Before using a scenario, read the Standing scenario. It defines the factual baseline so a peaceful encounter is not silently turned into an obstruction, disturbance, trespass, or disorderly-conduct hypothetical.

docs.title: Recording government activity
docs.text: Begin with Recording public officials, then use Public-forum doctrine when the dispute turns on the character of the place.

docs.title: An employee or officer orders you to leave
docs.text: Use Trespass and removal. It separates public access, facility policy, forum classification, removal authority, and the actual elements of California trespass statutes.

docs.title: Police begin questioning, detaining, frisking, or arresting you
docs.text: Use Police encounters for the Fourth Amendment, identification, probable cause, Fifth Amendment, Miranda, and device-search layers.

docs.title: The encounter happens at a public meeting
docs.text: Use Public meetings for the Brown Act and Bagley-Keene rules, plus the limited-public-forum overlay.

docs.title: You need the agency's video, records, or evidence preserved
docs.text: Use Public records and evidence preservation.

docs.title: You are researching a facility before a field visit
docs.text: Use Facility research and field verification. It traces controlling law, written policy, signage, prior incidents, exclusion/removal authority, police enforcement, and post-visit records without treating policy as law.

docs.title: One distinction that runs through the entire guide
docs.text:
Public ownership, public access, and public-forum status are different questions.

A government property can contain several legally different areas. An exterior public sidewalk, lobby, service counter, meeting room, employee corridor, and secured area should not be assigned one blanket constitutional label merely because they share an address.

The guide therefore analyzes specific areas and specific activities, and it uses UNRESOLVED when the available authority does not justify a confident classification.

docs.title: Current California core
docs.text:
The current handbook has substantive chapters for:

  • the standing factual scenario;
  • facility research and field verification methodology;
  • constitutional foundations;
  • recording public officials;
  • public-forum doctrine;
  • police encounters and identification;
  • trespass and public-agency removal;
  • disorderly conduct;
  • assemblies, dispersal orders, and emergency scenes;
  • Brown Act and Bagley-Keene meetings; and
  • public records and evidence preservation.

Facility-specific work—such as police lobbies, DMV offices, libraries, courthouses, campuses, and other recurring locations—is intentionally being built on top of that statewide doctrinal spine rather than guessed in advance.

docs.title: Research standard
docs.text:
Every substantive rule should be traceable to authority a reader can independently verify. The project distinguishes controlling authority from persuasive cases, agency policy, secondary commentary, and incident evidence.

The California authority index shows the working authority map. Detailed sweep ledgers remain available through the research links in the handbook.

docs.title: Working-draft notice
docs.text: This guide is not legal advice. Statutes, regulations, policies, and case law change, and real encounters can turn on facts that are not present in a simplified field scenario. Check the verification date and source before relying on a rule.

docs.title: California 1A Auditor's Field Guide
docs.text:
Research baseline: September 21, 2026

This directory is the California handbook. The goal is to build a rigorous statewide legal spine first, then add facility-specific chapters and case studies.

docs.title: Standing scenario
docs.text:
The canonical baseline is maintained in standing-scenario.md.

Unless a chapter says otherwise, assume the auditor begins lawfully present in the specific public area, peacefully gathers information, and does not independently fight, threaten, create unreasonable noise, block access, physically interfere, obstruct or intimidate public-agency business, resist/delay/obstruct an officer, participate in the kinds of violent/unlawful gatherings or post-warning non-dispersal excluded by the standing scenario, or engage in other unstated misconduct.

The fact that an employee, contractor, visitor, security guard, or private individual dislikes the activity or becomes upset does not itself change those assumptions.

The detailed standing-scenario page explains how this baseline interacts with Penal Code §§ 403, 407-409, 415, 416, 602/602.1, 647, § 148, public-meeting disruption, and later removal orders.

The handbook does not depend on professional status or credentials. The same baseline is intended to apply to an ordinary member of the public carrying only a phone. Identification demands are treated as a separate legal question: a police request, a call for service, and an actual legal duty or authority concerning identification are not interchangeable.

A chapter being drafted does not mean its entire code family or case-law layer has been exhaustively completed.

docs.title: Federal premises in California
docs.text:
Federal premises are maintained separately under docs/federal/.

For a federal facility located in California, the project does not assume that the California Penal Code, CPRA, or other California facility rules automatically govern merely because the building is physically in California. Federal-premises research begins with federal constitutional law, the applicable federal statute/regulation, agency/facility rules, and federal cases. California law is checked only when a specific jurisdictional or incorporation doctrine makes it relevant.

This separation prevents the California state/local handbook from being accidentally treated as the governing conduct or records code for USPS property, federal courthouses, GSA-controlled buildings, or other federal premises.

docs.title: Field-rule philosophy
docs.text:
A field rule should be short enough to remember but narrow enough to be defensible.

Bad field rule:

If the public can walk into the lobby, it is a public forum.

Better field rule:

Public access and public-forum status are different questions. Classify the specific area and activity. A public-facing government interior can be a nonpublic or limited forum, while an adjacent ordinary public sidewalk can have a different classification. See public-forum-doctrine.md.

Bad field rule:

There is a "No Recording" sign, so recording here is illegal.

Better field rule:

A sign is evidence that a restriction is being asserted; it is not proof of the restriction's legal validity or criminal enforceability. Identify the written policy, who adopted it, the authority supporting it, the specific area/activity it governs, and any independent removal or criminal statute. See facility-investigation-methodology.md.

Bad field rule:

Public property means they cannot trespass you.

Better field rule:

Identify the actual trespass provision. For a public agency open to the public, Penal Code § 602.1(b) requires intentional interference by obstruction or intimidation plus refusal after the qualifying request; § 602(o) instead concerns property not open to the general public; § 602(q) concerns a public building when it is regularly closed. Other law or a lawful facility restriction may independently matter.

Bad field rule:

The employee used a personal phone, so the recording is private.

Better field rule:

Under City of San Jose, a work-related writing does not lose potential public-record status merely because it is created or stored on a personal account/device. Analyze content, context, purpose, scope of employment, disclosure exemptions, and the agency's search duty separately.

Bad field rule:

I requested the video, so deleting it automatically violates the CPRA.

Better field rule:

City of Gilroy holds that the CPRA itself is not a general retention statute. Give a preservation notice, promptly request the record and applicable retention schedule, and distinguish lawful routine disposition from other retention law, litigation-preservation duties, or deliberate destruction.

Bad field rule:

Recording police is always legal.

Better field rule:

Penal Code § 148(g) expressly says recording a public/peace officer in public, or from a place the recorder has a right to be, does not by itself establish § 148 obstruction, reasonable suspicion, or probable cause.

Bad field rule:

If I am detained, police have to read me Miranda rights.

Better field rule:

A Terry detention is a Fourth Amendment seizure but is not automatically Miranda custody. Analyze the justification for the detention separately from whether custodial interrogation rules have attached.

Bad field rule:

Hiibel says I have to identify whenever police detain me.

Better field rule:

Hiibel upheld Nevada's specific stop-and-identify statute during a valid Terry stop. In California, identify the particular statute, context, and applicable case law before treating an ID request as compulsory, and never provide a false identity.

The guide should teach the actual elements, not magic phrases.

docs.title: California Authority Index
docs.text:
Purpose: Track every statewide/federal authority that may materially affect a peaceful First Amendment audit in a publicly accessible government area in California.

This is a completeness ledger, not a claim that every listed authority creates a field rule.

docs.title: Status meanings
docs.text:
• DOCTRINE-REVIEWED — controlling doctrine/material cases reviewed for the narrow proposition stated.
  • DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART — narrow proposition reviewed; broader family/application incomplete.
  • PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED — current primary text checked; case layer may remain incomplete.
  • PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED-IN-PART — part of broader family checked.
  • SOURCE-CHECKED — primary text/source checked but handbook treatment incomplete.
  • RESEARCH — identified; not yet fully reviewed.
  • SPECIALIZED — distinct facility/event/context.
  • FACILITY-SPECIFIC — depends on particular agency/facility/local rule.
  • N/A-STANDING-SCOPE — reviewed but ordinarily outside the standing peaceful-audit facts.

docs.title: Completeness rule
docs.text: Do not claim the handbook contains every relevant California law until this index and the sweep ledgers have systematically addressed remaining RESEARCH entries or affirmatively documented them as outside scope.

docs.title: Assemblies, Dispersal Orders, and Emergency Scenes
docs.text:
Research status: Core California Penal Code text verified; controlling-case layer still in progress. Last verified: September 17, 2026.

This chapter covers California statutes that are commonly relevant when peaceful First Amendment activity occurs near protests, demonstrations, public meetings, emergency scenes, police lines, or disaster closures. It does not assume that a peaceful observer becomes part of an unlawful assembly merely by being present nearby.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text: Peaceful presence near a protest or emergency does not by itself answer whether a dispersal order or closure is lawful. Identify the exact authority being invoked, whether its statutory predicates exist, whether notice was actually given, whether the person is inside the area covered by the order, and whether a statutory exception applies.

docs.title: Penal Code § 403 — disturbing or breaking up a lawful meeting
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=403.

Section 403 makes it a misdemeanor, without authority of law, to willfully disturb or break up a lawful assembly or meeting, subject to the section's stated exceptions.

Field rule: Mere attendance, observation, recording, disagreement, or criticism is not the statutory text. The section requires willful disturbance or breaking up of the meeting.

Limit: What conduct legally amounts to disturbs or breaks up requires case-law analysis. Do not reduce the statute to a subjective complaint that someone was uncomfortable.

docs.title: Penal Code § 407 — unlawful assembly
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=407.

Section 407 defines an unlawful assembly as two or more persons assembled either:

  • to do an unlawful act; or
  • to do a lawful act in a violent, boisterous, or tumultuous manner.

Field rule: A gathering is not an unlawful assembly merely because it is a protest, contentious, unpopular, or being recorded. The statutory definition must be satisfied, together with controlling constitutional case law.

docs.title: Penal Code § 408 — participation in a rout or unlawful assembly
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=408.

Section 408 makes participation in a rout or unlawful assembly a misdemeanor.

Field rule: The statute targets participation in the prohibited assembly; it should not be treated as establishing that every observer, journalist, passerby, or person recording nearby is necessarily a participant. Case law is required to define the participation element and constitutional limits.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409 — remaining after lawful warning to disperse
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.

Section 409 applies to a person who remains at the place of a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly after it has been lawfully warned to disperse, subject to the statute's exceptions for public officers and persons assisting them.

Field rule: Failure to disperse under § 409 is not simply refusal to obey any request to leave. The statutory text ties the offense to a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly and a lawful warning to disperse.

Research queue: Controlling cases are needed on adequacy of warning, opportunity to comply, geographic scope, knowledge, protected observers, and First Amendment limitations.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.5 — calamity and emergency command-post closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.5.

Section 409.5 authorizes specified public officers and employees to close an area when a calamity creates a menace to public health or safety and separately permits specified officers to close the immediate area surrounding an emergency field command post or other command post activated to abate a listed calamity, riot, or civil disturbance.

Subdivision (c) states that an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters an area closed under subdivision (a) or (b) and willfully remains after receiving notice to evacuate or leave commits a misdemeanor.

Subdivision (d) provides a statutory access rule for duly authorized representatives of a news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, subject to the section's terms.

Field rule: Before treating ordinary police tape as a § 409.5 criminal closure, identify whether the statutory closure authority and factual predicates actually apply. Conversely, a qualifying calamity or command-post closure is a materially different situation from an ordinary public sidewalk or government lobby.

docs.title: Important § 409.5 / § 409.6 text difference
docs.text:
The misdemeanor language of § 409.5(c) is not worded the same way as the avalanche statute in § 409.6(c).

  • § 409.5(c) is written in terms of an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters the closed area and then willfully remains after notice to leave.
  • § 409.6(c) separately reaches both an unauthorized person who enters and remains and an unauthorized person who willfully remains in the closed area after receiving notice to leave.

Why it matters: The Field Guide should preserve the elements the Legislature actually wrote rather than paraphrasing both statutes as though they were identical.

Limit: This textual distinction does not itself establish that a person who was already inside a § 409.5 closure may always remain. Other statutes, lawful orders, emergency authority, or constitutional doctrine may independently affect the situation. The case-law layer remains necessary.

docs.title: § 409.5 press limitation
docs.text:
Section 409.5(d) uses specific statutory language concerning duly authorized representatives of a news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network.

The project should not rewrite that special statutory access rule into a universal citizen exemption. It also should not treat the statute's category as a universal definition of who possesses First Amendment newsgathering rights. Whether an independent journalist or self-publisher qualifies under this particular provision is a separate question requiring statutory and case-law analysis.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.6 — avalanche-area closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.6.

Section 409.6 is a specialized avalanche-area closure statute. Its subdivision (c) expressly reaches an unauthorized person who willfully and knowingly enters and remains after notice or an unauthorized person who willfully remains within a closed area after receiving notice to leave.

Classification: Specialized. It is retained because it demonstrates that California's emergency-closure statutes are not textually interchangeable and may matter in a location/event-specific audit.

docs.title: Penal Code § 409.7 — special news-representative protections at demonstrations and related closures
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.7.

Section 409.7 applies when peace officers close specified command-post areas or establish police lines or rolling closures at demonstrations, marches, protests, or rallies involving activity protected by the First Amendment or Article I of the California Constitution.

For a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, the section provides specified access and protection from intentional assault, interference, or obstruction while gathering information, and specified protection from citation for failure to disperse, curfew, or Penal Code § 148(a)(1) when gathering, receiving, or processing information. The statute also provides a mechanism to contact a supervisory officer after detention, subject to circumstances, and states that other applicable laws may still be enforced against unlawful activity.

docs.title: Do not equate § 409.7 with the entire First Amendment right to gather news
docs.text:
Section 409.7 supplies a special California statutory protection package in the circumstances it describes. It is not the source of every constitutional right to observe or record public officials.

The statute does not, in its text, define duly authorized representative or online news service. Therefore the Field Guide should not categorically declare that an independent journalist, self-publisher, auditor, blogger, or citizen journalist either qualifies or does not qualify without supporting authority.

Similarly, a person who does not qualify for § 409.7's special statutory protections may still possess independent First Amendment protections for lawful recording, observation, speech, or newsgathering. Those constitutional questions require their own doctrine and cannot be answered solely by § 409.7.

Field rule: Treat § 409.7 as an additional statutory protection for people who fall within its terms—not as a licensing system for constitutional journalism and not as a declaration that everyone carrying a camera receives the same special access.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415 — disturbing the peace
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.

Section 415 covers three distinct categories:

  1. unlawfully fighting in public or challenging another person in public to fight;
  2. maliciously and willfully disturbing another person by loud and unreasonable noise; and
  3. using offensive words in public that are inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction.

A fuller treatment belongs in disorderly-conduct.md.

Field rule for this chapter: Do not use disturbing the peace as a generic label for peaceful recording, criticism, or mere public discomfort. Analyze the actual statutory category being asserted.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415.5 — school and campus variant
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.5.

Section 415.5 contains a school/community-college/university variant of fighting, loud-and-unreasonable-noise, and provocative-offensive-words offenses and includes its own scope and exceptions.

Classification: Specialized. Handle the details in the future school/campus chapter rather than applying § 415.5 as a general public-property rule.

docs.title: Penal Code § 416 — assembly for disturbing the peace or committing an unlawful act
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=416.

Section 416(a) applies when two or more persons assemble for the purpose of disturbing the public peace or committing an unlawful act and do not disperse after being directed or commanded to do so by a public officer.

Field rule: Purpose is written into the statute. Peaceful people gathered for lawful observation, recording, criticism, or petitioning should not be analytically collapsed into § 416 merely because an officer says disperse; the actual statutory predicates and constitutional limits still matter.

docs.title: What this chapter does not establish
docs.text:
These statutes do not, by themselves, establish:

  • that every police line or piece of tape is a criminal exclusion zone;
  • that every gathering ordered to disperse was legally an unlawful assembly;
  • that an observer automatically becomes a participant in unlawful conduct committed by others;
  • that every dispersal order is constitutionally sufficient;
  • that press status under §§ 409.5 or 409.7 is identical to the constitutional freedom of the press;
  • that a person outside a special statutory press category therefore lacks constitutional recording/newsgathering protection;
  • that an independent journalist necessarily qualifies or necessarily fails to qualify under § 409.7;
  • that a person may ignore a legally valid emergency closure or dispersal order.

docs.title: Case-law research queue
docs.text:
The next case-law pass for this chapter should identify controlling authority on:

  • constitutional narrowing of unlawful assembly and related statutes;
  • required notice and opportunity to comply with dispersal orders;
  • observers versus participants;
  • independent journalists, self-publishers, and the meaning of statutory news-service terminology;
  • constitutional newsgathering rights distinct from special statutory access rights;
  • police lines and emergency closures;
  • protest recording and retaliation;
  • § 415 loud-noise and fighting-words limitations;
  • interaction between §§ 407-409, 409.5, 409.6, 409.7, 415, 416, and Penal Code § 148.

Until that case layer is complete, this chapter is a primary-text-verified statutory foundation rather than a complete statement of protest/emergency-scene doctrine.

docs.title: Constitutional Foundations
docs.text:
Research status: Primary constitutional text verified; controlling-case layer still in progress. Last verified: September 17, 2026.

This chapter identifies the constitutional provisions that form the legal foundation for peaceful First Amendment auditing in California. It does not by itself answer every facility-access or recording question. Forum doctrine, statutes, regulations, court rules, and facility-specific law can materially change the analysis.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text: A California audit may implicate several distinct constitutional interests at once: speech/press, petition/assembly, access to government information, privacy, due process, freedom from unreasonable searches/seizures, and protection against compelled self-incrimination. Do not collapse those into a single slogan such as First Amendment means I can record anywhere.

docs.title: California Constitution
docs.text: Primary source for Article I: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I

docs.title: Article I, § 1 — privacy
docs.text:
California expressly identifies privacy as an inalienable right.

Why it matters: Government transparency and recording questions can intersect with privacy interests. Article I, § 3(b) itself expressly preserves the privacy right in § 1, so the access-to-information provision is not a command to disregard privacy law.

Limit: The existence of a privacy interest does not automatically establish that a particular restriction on observation or recording is lawful. The actual statute, regulation, case law, forum, and facts still matter.

docs.title: Article I, § 2(a) — speech and press
docs.text:
California provides that every person may freely speak, write, and publish sentiments on all subjects, subject to responsibility for abuse of the right, and that law may not restrain or abridge liberty of speech or press.

Why it matters: This is an independent state constitutional speech/press foundation in addition to the federal First Amendment.

Research note: The extent to which California's speech clause provides broader protection in a particular government-property setting is a case-law question and should not be assumed from the text alone.

docs.title: Article I, § 2(b) — source and unpublished-material shield text
docs.text:
Section 2(b) contains California's constitutional shield language for specified publishers, editors, reporters, and other persons connected with or employed by newspapers, magazines, periodicals, press associations, wire services, radio stations, or television stations. Within the terms of the provision, it protects against contempt for refusing to disclose certain sources or unpublished newsgathering information.

The text defines unpublished information broadly enough to include material such as notes, outtakes, photographs, tapes, and other data not itself disseminated to the public.

Why it matters: Auditors and independent journalists may preserve unpublished recordings, notes, and source material. This provision therefore belongs in the Field Guide's research universe even though its application is specialized and doctrine-heavy.

Important limit: Do not use § 2(b) as a universal definition of who counts as press, journalist, or news media for every other California or federal law. Different statutes use different language. Penal Code § 409.7, for example, expressly refers to a duly authorized representative of a news service, online news service, newspaper, or radio or television station or network, which is not identical to the language of § 2(b).

The project should not assume that an independent journalist or self-publisher either qualifies or fails to qualify under a separate statute merely by comparing labels. That requires analysis of the particular statutory text and relevant case law.

docs.title: Article I, § 3(a) — petition and assembly
docs.text:
California protects the rights to instruct representatives, petition government for redress, and assemble freely to consult for the common good.

Why it matters: Public comment, demonstrations, petitioning, and other direct engagement with government can implicate this provision as well as the federal First Amendment.

docs.title: Article I, § 3(b) — access to government information
docs.text:
California expressly gives the people a right of access to information concerning the conduct of the people's business and states that meetings of public bodies and writings of public officials and agencies shall be open to public scrutiny.

Section 3(b)(2) directs that authorities furthering access be broadly construed and authorities limiting access be narrowly construed. Section 3(b) also preserves existing privacy and confidentiality protections and expressly references public-records/open-meeting law.

Field rule: This is a powerful transparency provision, but it is not a standalone rule that every government room, record, computer screen, conversation, or physical area must be open to observation or recording.

docs.title: Article I, § 7 — due process and equal protection
docs.text:
California prohibits deprivation of life, liberty, or property without due process and denial of equal protection.

Why it matters: Removal, exclusion, government-imposed restrictions, and selective enforcement can raise due-process or equal-protection questions depending on the facts and governing law.

docs.title: Article I, § 13 — searches and seizures
docs.text:
California protects persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures and imposes warrant requirements.

Why it matters: A detention is a seizure for Fourth Amendment purposes under federal doctrine, and searches/seizures of phones, cameras, bags, recordings, or other property may raise both federal and California constitutional issues.

Important California construction rule: Article I, § 24 states that specified California criminal-procedure rights—including the right to be free from unreasonable searches and seizures—are construed consistently with the U.S. Constitution in criminal cases.

docs.title: Article I, § 15 — self-incrimination and due process in criminal causes
docs.text:
Section 15 provides, among other protections, that a person may not be compelled in a criminal cause to be a witness against themselves and may not be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process.

Why it matters: This is the California constitutional counterpart relevant to compelled self-incrimination. It should be analyzed separately from whether a person must identify themselves or comply with a lawful detention/order under a specific statute or case.

docs.title: Article I, § 24 — relationship to federal constitutional rights
docs.text:
Section 24 first states that rights guaranteed by the California Constitution are not dependent on rights guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution. It then imposes an important criminal-case construction rule for specified rights, including equal protection, due process, search/seizure, privacy, self-incrimination, double jeopardy, and others.

Field rule: Do not assume every California constitutional provision necessarily tracks federal law in every context; also do not ignore § 24's express consistency rule for the criminal-procedure rights it lists.

docs.title: First Amendment
docs.text:
Official text: https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-1/

Protects freedom of speech and press and the rights of peaceable assembly and petition.

Why it matters: This is the principal federal constitutional foundation for recording/observing government activity, speaking, petitioning, public comment, and forum doctrine. The actual scope depends heavily on place, government purpose, forum classification, and applicable restrictions.

Press/newsgathering note: The existence of a special statutory protection for certain news representatives does not mean everyone outside that statutory category lacks First Amendment protection. Constitutional recording/newsgathering analysis and a statute such as Penal Code § 409.7 are separate layers and must not be collapsed into each other.

docs.title: Fourth Amendment
docs.text:
Official Constitution Annotated resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-4/

Protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and governs warrants.

Why it matters: Police encounters can move from consensual contact to detention or arrest; searches and seizures of devices/property require separate Fourth Amendment analysis.

docs.title: Fifth Amendment
docs.text:
Official text/resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/amendment-5/

Protects against compelled self-incrimination and includes federal due-process protections.

Jurisdiction note: The Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause restrains the federal government. State and local government due-process analysis ordinarily runs through the Fourteenth Amendment and applicable state constitutional provisions.

docs.title: Fourteenth Amendment, § 1
docs.text:
Official Constitution Annotated resource: https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-14/

Prohibits states from depriving persons of life, liberty, or property without due process and from denying equal protection.

Why it matters: Most California state/local First Amendment and Fourth Amendment claims operate against state/local actors through federal constitutional doctrine applied to the states, together with any independent California constitutional protections.

docs.title: What these provisions do not establish by themselves
docs.text:
None of these provisions, standing alone, establishes all of the following:

  • that every government-owned property is a public forum;
  • that every area open to the public may be recorded without restriction;
  • that a person may enter staff-only, secured, closed, or otherwise restricted areas;
  • that privacy/confidentiality statutes cease to apply in government buildings;
  • that an order from an official is necessarily lawful or necessarily unlawful;
  • that a detention, search, seizure, exclusion, or arrest is valid merely because an official asserts authority;
  • that a person must be institutionally credentialed media before constitutional newsgathering protections can exist.

Those questions require the next layers of the Field Guide: forum doctrine, facility-specific law, statutory elements, and controlling cases.

docs.title: Case-law research queue
docs.text:
This chapter still needs controlling cases addressing at least:

  • incorporation of First/Fourth Amendment protections against state/local actors;
  • California's independent speech-clause doctrine;
  • scope and limits of Article I, § 2(b), including its application to modern and independent newsgathering;
  • public-forum classifications and government-property restrictions;
  • recording matters of public interest and public officials;
  • retaliation for protected recording/speech;
  • consensual encounters, detention, arrest, searches, and seizure of digital devices;
  • relationship between California constitutional protections and Article I, § 24.

Until that work is complete, this chapter should be treated as a primary-text-verified constitutional foundation rather than a complete doctrinal chapter.

docs.title: Disturbing the Peace and Disorderly Conduct
docs.text: California does not have one generic offense that means "someone was uncomfortable with your behavior." Two provisions especially worth separating are Penal Code §§ 415 and 647.

docs.title: Penal Code § 415 — disturbing the peace
docs.text:
Section 415 criminalizes three categories of conduct:

  1. unlawfully fighting in public or challenging another person in public to fight;
  2. maliciously and willfully disturbing another person by loud and unreasonable noise; or
  3. using offensive words in public that are inherently likely to provoke an immediate violent reaction.

Primary source: California Penal Code § 415

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Under the project's standing scenario, the assumed auditor is not fighting, challenging anyone to fight, creating loud and unreasonable noise, or using words assumed to satisfy § 415(3).

A government employee, contractor, visitor, security guard, or private individual becoming angry, offended, uncomfortable, or confrontational does not by itself supply one of § 415's statutory categories. The analysis remains focused on the auditor's own conduct. Another person's reaction may still be relevant context when § 415(3) is actually at issue, but the reaction alone does not substitute for the statute's elements.

Therefore, if § 415 is asserted against a peaceful auditor, identify which subsection and which conduct is alleged to satisfy it rather than accepting "you are causing a disturbance" as though that were the statutory text.

The third subsection requires separate case-law treatment because constitutional "fighting words" doctrine and context matter. That case-law section remains to be researched and added.

docs.title: Penal Code § 647 — disorderly conduct
docs.text:
Section 647 is a list of specifically defined offenses. It is not a free-floating power to arrest a person merely for behaving unusually or making another person uncomfortable.

Primary source: California Penal Code § 647

docs.title: Loitering provisions relevant to common audit claims
docs.text:
Section 647(d) concerns loitering in or around a public toilet for the purpose of engaging in or soliciting a lewd, lascivious, or unlawful act.

Section 647(h) concerns a person who loiters, prowls, or wanders on the private property of another without visible or lawful business with the owner/occupant. The statute defines "loiter" there as delaying or lingering without a lawful purpose on the property and for the purpose of committing a crime as opportunity may be discovered.

Under the standing scenario, § 647(h) will ordinarily fall outside scope because the auditor is not silently assumed to be on another's private property without lawful purpose and for the purpose of committing a crime as opportunity may be discovered. Do not rely on public ownership alone: a government office can occupy leased or privately owned property, so analyze the actual property/access facts when they matter.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
"Loitering" should never be treated as a generic synonym for "standing around longer than an employee wants."

When a public employee or officer uses the word, identify the exact statute, ordinance, regulation, or facility rule being invoked and compare its actual elements with the conduct observed.

docs.title: Useful factual questions
docs.text:
• Which statute are you referring to?
  • Which subsection?
  • What specific conduct are you saying satisfies that subsection?
  • Are you saying the issue is noise, fighting, threatening words, obstruction, or something else?

docs.title: Research still required
docs.text:
This chapter still needs controlling case law on:

  • fighting words;
  • offensive speech directed at police;
  • heckler's-veto doctrine;
  • unreasonable-noise standards;
  • protected criticism versus actual threats;
  • local disorderly-conduct ordinances that may appear in facility encounters.

docs.title: Source records
docs.text:
authority: "California Penal Code § 415"
source_url: "https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415"
last_verified: "2026-09-21"
status: "verified"

authority: "California Penal Code § 647"
source_url: "https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=647"
