docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Research the facility before testing the policy.

The project-methodology status describes this page's workflow function. Legal propositions referenced here remain subject to the verification status in the substantive chapters, authority index, and sweep ledgers.

A strong facility investigation should establish what the law says, what the agency says its policy is, how the policy was adopted, how employees and police have applied it, and what actually happens during a peaceful field visit.

The goal is not to manufacture a confrontation. It is to document and test a defined legal or policy question under the project's standing scenario.

docs.title: 1. Start with a research question
docs.text:
Do not begin with "let's see whether they kick us out." Begin with a proposition that can be tested.

Examples:

  • Does this facility actually have a written no-recording policy?
  • What area does the policy cover?
  • What statute, regulation, order, or other authority does the agency claim supports it?
  • Is a visitor sign-in or identification rule written down?
  • Has the agency previously instructed staff to call police when a person records from a place they may lawfully be?
  • What offense have officers previously relied on when enforcing the policy?
  • Are favorable and unfavorable expressive reactions treated differently at a public meeting?
  • Has a policy changed after a complaint, claim, lawsuit, or earlier audit?

The research question belongs in the facility file before the visit.

docs.title: 2. Build the authority chain
docs.text:
A sign or employee instruction is not the end of the analysis. Trace the claimed authority through each layer.

Layer Research question Constitution / controlling cases What federal and California constitutional rules govern the specific area and activity? Statute / regulation / court rule / ordinance What enacted law actually authorizes or limits the conduct? Agency policy What does the agency's written rule say, who issued it, and when was it adopted or revised? Facility implementation What signs, screening procedures, visitor instructions, or employee practices implement the policy? Enforcement practice What have security staff, supervisors, or police actually done when the rule was invoked? Exclusion / removal authority Who is authorized to restrict access or order departure from this specific area, and what law, policy, property-management authority, or other rule supports that action? Police / criminal authority If police intervention occurs, what particular offense or detention/arrest basis is asserted, and what facts support that basis or satisfy the offense elements? Remedy / follow-up What administrative, records, complaint, civil, or judicial process applies if the policy or enforcement appears unlawful?

The project should never collapse these into one proposition such as "there is a sign, therefore it is illegal to record" or "the employee wants the person gone, therefore police have arrest authority."

docs.title: 3. Build a pre-visit facility research packet
docs.text: Before field verification, gather what is reasonably available.

docs.title: Facility and access facts
docs.text:
Record:

  • agency and facility name;
  • ownership or controlling agency where relevant;
  • exact areas open to the public;
  • public hours;
  • entrances and security checkpoints;
  • appointment, badge, sign-in, or identification conditions;
  • public counters, waiting rooms, meeting rooms, hallways, secured doors, employee workspaces, and exterior areas;
  • posted signs and their exact wording;
  • available floor plans, public maps, meeting-room diagrams, or visitor instructions.

Do not assign one forum label to the entire address merely because the building has a public lobby.

docs.title: Policy and authority records
docs.text:
Look for or request:

  • photography, video, audio, media, visitor-conduct, security, and public-access policies;
  • administrative regulations, general orders, manuals, directives, bulletins, FAQs, and staff instructions;
  • the ordinance, statute, regulation, resolution, order, or other authority cited for the policy;
  • adoption records, revision history, effective dates, and superseded versions;
  • training materials addressing cameras, auditors, media, disruptive visitors, removal, trespass, public comment, or records requests;
  • signage specifications or records showing who authorized a posted restriction;
  • security contracts and post orders where public and disclosable;
  • retention policies for surveillance, body-camera, dispatch, or incident records.

The fact that a record is requested does not guarantee disclosure. Exemptions, privileges, privacy rules, and specialized statutes must still be analyzed.

docs.title: Prior-incident records
docs.text:
Where relevant and lawfully obtainable, collect:

  • prior complaints about the same policy;
  • incident reports;
  • calls for service and CAD/dispatch records;
  • body-camera or other official recordings;
  • written trespass notices or exclusion orders;
  • citations or arrest records identifying the offense relied upon;
  • claims, lawsuits, settlements, published judicial decisions, or administrative rulings;
  • correspondence showing how the agency interpreted the policy;
  • later policy revisions following an incident.

Preserve chronology. A policy adopted after an incident cannot be silently treated as the policy that governed the earlier event.

docs.title: 4. Use CPRA as a research tool, not as a slogan
docs.text:
California Constitution article I, section 3(b) recognizes a right of access to information concerning the conduct of the people's business and provides that the writings of public officials and agencies shall be open to public scrutiny, subject to lawful limitations.

Government Code § 7922.525 states that public records are open to inspection during agency office hours and that every person has a right to inspect public records except as otherwise provided. The existing CPRA chapter contains the project's detailed rules on requests, searches, exemptions, personal devices, retention, and preservation.

Useful pre-visit requests can seek the actual policy and its provenance, not merely ask the agency whether recording is "allowed."

See Public Records and Evidence Preservation.

Primary sources:

  • California Constitution art. I, § 3(b): https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I&sectionNum=SEC.+3.
  • Government Code § 7922.525: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.525

docs.title: 5. Classify policy questions before the visit
docs.text:
Facility files should use research flags rather than prematurely declaring an agency unlawful.

Suggested flags:

  • SUPPORTED-BY-IDENTIFIED-AUTHORITY — a current source has been identified that appears to support the rule;
  • AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED — the policy exists, but the project has not yet identified adequate authority for or against it;
  • POTENTIAL-FACIAL-CONFLICT — the written rule itself appears to conflict with controlling law and requires final legal review;
  • POTENTIAL-AS-APPLIED-CONFLICT — the rule may be lawful in some applications but prior enforcement raises a constitutional/statutory issue;
  • POTENTIAL-VIEWPOINT-COMPARATOR — comparable favorable and unfavorable expression appears to have been treated differently;
  • POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP — a policy violation appears to have been treated as sufficient basis for detention, citation, arrest, or criminal trespass without the required offense elements or legal bridge being identified;
  • SUPERSEDED-OR-REVISED — the policy has changed and historical versions must not be treated as current.

These are research flags, not court holdings.

docs.title: 6. Plan a peaceful field verification
docs.text:
The visit should test the defined question while preserving the standing scenario.

Before entering, decide:

  • what specific area is being observed;
  • what activity is being tested;
  • what policy is expected to be invoked;
  • what conduct is deliberately being avoided;
  • what factual questions would distinguish a lawful restriction from an unsupported one;
  • whether the visit will include a records request, observation only, consensual conversation, public comment, or some combination;
  • what evidence should be preserved if police are called.

A useful investigation is reproducible. Another researcher should be able to understand what was tested and why.

docs.title: 7. Consensual conversation can state the investigative purpose
docs.text:
This methodology applies to an ordinary member of the public. It does not depend on profession, organizational affiliation, or carrying any project or role credential.

If an official voluntarily asks what the person is doing, a truthful response can be as simple as:

I am gathering information about this facility's recording and public-access policies and how they are enforced.

Where prior research has identified a concrete issue:

I am investigating whether this facility's policy or enforcement practice conflicts with California or federal law.

Those statements explain the purpose of the activity. They do not claim special access or create a new legal privilege.

docs.title: 8. Document policy enforcement as evidence
docs.text:
During the visit, preserve:

  • the exact area and time;
  • normal public hours;
  • signs and where they are posted;
  • the identity/role of the official when reasonably available;
  • the exact rule or policy cited;
  • whether a written copy is offered or refused;
  • the legal authority the official says supports the rule;
  • the specific conduct the official says is prohibited;
  • whether similarly situated people are treated differently;
  • warnings and opportunities to comply;
  • whether the government describes the issue as policy, trespass, obstruction, disturbance, safety, privacy, security, or something else;
  • whether the reason changes after police arrive.

Statements are evidence of what an official said. They are not, by themselves, proof that the official's legal interpretation is correct.

docs.title: 9. If police arrive, document the policy-to-law transition
docs.text:
A central research question is whether law enforcement identifies an independent legal basis for intervention or simply treats the employee's preference as sufficient.

Useful factual questions include:

  • Am I free to leave?
  • Am I being detained?
  • What is the reason for the stop?
  • What specific offense do you reasonably suspect?
  • Which statute, ordinance, regulation, or other legal authority are you relying on?
  • What conduct are you saying satisfies its elements?
  • Is the issue a facility policy violation, or are you saying the policy violation itself constitutes a crime?
  • Who has authority to order removal from this particular area?
  • Is the order limited to this area or the entire property?

The guide does not assume that every policy is invalid or that officers may never assist with a lawful facility restriction. It requires the authority chain to be identified.

California has a separate stop-notice rule relevant to pedestrian detentions at facilities. Vehicle Code § 2806.5 requires a peace officer making a traffic or pedestrian stop, before questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation, to state the reason for the stop, unless the officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from an imminent threat. The Field Guide retains the pedestrian-stop application here; traffic-stop doctrine is outside the current facility-audit focus. The statutory notice requirement is not the same as a requirement to disclose every fact underlying reasonable suspicion.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=2806.5

docs.title: 10. Post-visit investigation
docs.text:
The field visit usually creates a second records phase.

Depending on the event, request or preserve:

  • CAD/dispatch logs;
  • body-camera and other official recordings;
  • incident reports;
  • employee emails or messages concerning the encounter where potentially public and disclosable;
  • supervisor instructions;
  • the policy/version actually relied upon;
  • records showing policy changes after the encounter;
  • retention schedules;
  • complaints, use-of-force records, citations, or exclusion records where applicable and lawfully available.

Compare the contemporaneous records with what officials said on scene. Preserve contradictions without overstating what they prove.

docs.title: 11. Member-of-public baseline
docs.text:
The Field Guide does not depend on professional status or credentials.

A person using this methodology is analyzed as a member of the public unless a genuinely role-specific law applies. The baseline is intended to work for a person carrying only a phone. The legal analysis starts with the rights, duties, and restrictions that apply to the person in the specific place and activity.

No project ID or other self-created credential is required by this methodology. Likewise, the existence or absence of such a credential does not determine whether the person's activity is protected.

Identification demands during police encounters are analyzed separately in police-encounters.md. The project does not treat an officer's desire to investigate, the fact that someone "called the police," or a request for identification as interchangeable with an actual legal duty or authority concerning identification.

docs.title: 12. Facility-registry integration
docs.text:
Every mature facility entry should eventually contain both legal classification and evidence history.

Minimum fields:

  • facility and controlling agency;
  • specific area;
  • access status and public hours;
  • federal forum classification;
  • California Speech Clause classification;
  • activity analyzed;
  • current written policy;
  • policy source/provenance;
  • claimed legal authority;
  • signage/implementation;
  • prior incidents;
  • prior police/security enforcement;
  • exclusion/removal authority previously invoked;
  • offense/detention/arrest authority previously invoked;
  • comparator evidence;
  • current research flag(s);
  • field-verification date/result;
  • post-visit records obtained;
  • unresolved questions;
  • last verified.

The resulting record should let a reader trace:

controlling law → enacted authority → written policy → implementation → prior enforcement → field verification → post-incident records.

That chain is the core investigative product.

docs.title: Quality rule
docs.text:
The project should seek facilities with documented legal or policy questions, not invent misconduct to create a test.

A strong investigation is one where the standing scenario remains intact and the disputed government action can therefore be evaluated without guessing whether unrelated obstruction, threats, noise, restricted-area entry, or other misconduct occurred.

docs.title: Police Encounters — Detention, Identification, Questioning, Arrest, and Devices
docs.text:
Research status: This chapter reviews the core federal constitutional and California authorities governing the recurring transition from peaceful First Amendment activity to police contact. The principal encounter sequence is covered at the doctrine level: consensual contact, Fourth Amendment seizure/detention, reasonable suspicion, identification demands, protective frisks, probable-cause arrest, Fifth Amendment/Miranda questioning, and the basic warrant rule for digital searches of a seized phone. Important edge questions remain separately queued, including when force converts a Terry stop into an arrest, compelled phone unlocking, anonymous-tip doctrine, detailed prolonged-stop rules, and remedies/qualified immunity.

A First Amendment audit can quickly implicate several constitutional layers:

  • First Amendment: what expressive/recording activity is protected and what restrictions may government impose?
  • Fourth Amendment: when may government seize the person, frisk, arrest, seize property, or search it?
  • Fifth Amendment: when may government compel testimonial self-incrimination and what rules govern custodial interrogation?
  • Fourteenth Amendment: the incorporation bridge through which relevant federal Fourth/Fifth Amendment protections apply to California state and local actors, plus its own due-process/equal-protection protections.

California Constitution article I, sections 13 and 15 supply parallel state search/seizure and self-incrimination protections. Their complete independent state-doctrine layer remains separately queued.

docs.title: Encounter map
docs.text:
Analyze each stage separately:

  1. Consensual contact — may the person decline questions or terminate the encounter?
  2. Seizure/detention — has police conduct restrained liberty under the Fourth Amendment?
  3. Reason for stop / reasonable suspicion — for a California pedestrian stop within this project's current scope, what reason was stated before covered questioning, and what specific, articulable facts actually justified the detention when it began?
  4. Scope/duration — is the investigation reasonably related to its basis and pursued diligently?
  5. Identification — is identification merely requested, or does a specific law require it here?
  6. Frisk — is there a separate reasonable basis to believe the person is armed and dangerous?
  7. Arrest — did facts known to police establish probable cause?
  8. Questioning/self-incrimination — is the person merely detained, or in Miranda custody and being interrogated?
  9. Phone/camera — is police asking for consent, physically seizing the device, or searching digital contents?
  10. Afterward — release, property return, records preservation, and remedies are distinct questions.

The legal threshold can change during the encounter. Do not collapse the entire interaction into one label.

docs.title: 1. Consensual encounter versus Fourth Amendment seizure
docs.text:
Police do not need reasonable suspicion merely to approach a person in a public place, identify themselves, ask questions, or request identification so long as the circumstances would communicate to a reasonable person that the person may decline the requests or otherwise terminate the encounter.

A Fourth Amendment seizure occurs when physical force or a show of authority restrains liberty under the governing doctrine. A show-of-authority seizure generally requires submission to that authority.

A useful field question is:

Am I free to leave?

This helps clarify the officer's asserted posture. It is not a magic constitutional test; courts examine the totality of circumstances.

docs.title: People v. Tacardon, 14 Cal.5th 235 (2022)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court rejected a bright-line rule that use of a spotlight necessarily detains a person. On the facts before it, the deputy approached a parked vehicle with a spotlight but without emergency lights, blocking the vehicle, drawing a weapon, or initially issuing a command. The court required a totality-of-circumstances analysis.

Official sources:

  • https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s264219-people-v-tacardon
  • https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/S264219.PDF

Field rule: police attention is not automatically a detention. Commands, physical restraint, blocking movement, threatening displays, emergency lights, weapons, multiple officers, tone, and other circumstances can matter.

docs.title: 2. Terry detention — reasonable suspicion
docs.text:
Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968) recognizes a limited investigative seizure short of arrest. Police may briefly detain a person when reasonable suspicion is supported by specific and articulable facts that criminal activity is afoot. Reasonable suspicion is less than probable cause, but more than a hunch.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-392_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: People v. Flores, 15 Cal.5th 1032 (2024)
docs.text:
The California Supreme Court held the facts there insufficient for reasonable suspicion. The opinion reinforces that a high-crime-area label is contextual rather than individualized suspicion and that unusual/evasive conduct must be assessed in the whole factual picture. It does not hold that evasive behavior can never matter.

Official sources:

  • https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s267522-people-v-flores
  • https://courts.ca.gov/opinion/citings-archive/2024-05-02/s267522

docs.title: Penal Code § 148(g) — recording bridge
docs.text:
California Penal Code § 148(g) provides that photographing or recording a public/peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place the recorder has a right to be, does not in and of itself:

  • violate § 148(a);
  • create reasonable suspicion to detain; or
  • create probable cause to arrest.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148

docs.title: California pedestrian-stop notice rule — Vehicle Code § 2806.5
docs.text:
For this project's present facility-audit scope, the relevant part of Vehicle Code § 2806.5 is its pedestrian-stop rule. Effective January 1, 2024, the statute requires a peace officer making a traffic or pedestrian stop, before engaging in questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation, to state the reason for the stop. The traffic-stop branch exists but is not developed further in this Field Guide at this stage. The officer must also document the reason on any resulting citation or police report.

The statute has an exception when the officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from an imminent threat.

Section 2806.5 is a stop-notice rule. It does not convert a consensual police approach into a detention; first determine whether a traffic or pedestrian stop has actually occurred.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=2806.5

In People v. Valle, A169080 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 18, 2024), the published First District Court of Appeal described § 2806.5 as requiring notice to the detainee of the objective reason for a stop before the covered questioning. Valle arose from a traffic stop; the Field Guide retains it only for the statute's interpretation and does not use it to expand the project's traffic-stop scope. The court also explained that the statute does not alter the federal Fourth Amendment analysis governing whether the stop itself is objectively justified. Valle notes that proposed language making a failure to state the reason grounds for a suppression motion was removed before enactment.

Official California Judicial Branch source:

https://courts.ca.gov/opinion/published-extended-post/2024-09-18/a169080

docs.title: Reason for the stop is not the same as the full reasonable-suspicion record
docs.text:
Section 2806.5 creates a California notice requirement. It does not say that the officer must recite every observation, caller statement, inference, or item of evidence that may later be used to establish reasonable suspicion.

The Fourth Amendment question remains whether sufficient specific and articulable facts actually existed when the seizure began.

Useful questions are therefore:

Am I free to leave?

Am I being detained?

What is the reason for the stop?

What crime do you reasonably suspect me of committing?

What specific facts are you relying on?

These questions help preserve the encounter timeline and the officer's contemporaneous explanation. Absent the statutory exception, failure to state the reason before questioning covered by § 2806.5 violates the stop-notice requirement. That does not by itself establish that the detention lacked Fourth Amendment reasonable suspicion; remedies are a separate layer. Refusal to provide every underlying fact on scene likewise does not, by itself, establish that reasonable suspicion was absent.

docs.title: 3. Reasonable suspicion must exist when the seizure begins
docs.text:
A Terry stop must be justified at inception. Facts learned during a lawful stop may expand the investigation or eventually supply probable cause, but later discoveries do not retroactively create reasonable suspicion for an earlier unlawful seizure.

Existence and disclosure are separate questions. For a California pedestrian stop within this project's current scope, Vehicle Code § 2806.5 may require the officer to state the reason before covered questioning, but stating a reason cannot manufacture reasonable suspicion that did not already exist when the seizure began.

A useful timeline is:

T1: what facts were known when the seizure began? T2: what new facts lawfully developed? T3: did probable cause later arise?

Do not project everything eventually learned backward to the beginning of the encounter.

docs.title: 4. Scope and duration
docs.text:
Under United States v. Sharpe, 470 U.S. 675 (1985), there is no universal stopwatch for Terry detentions. The inquiry includes whether police diligently pursued investigative means likely to confirm or dispel suspicion reasonably quickly under the circumstances.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-470_PDFA.pdf

For traffic stops, Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015) holds that police may not prolong the traffic mission to pursue unrelated investigation absent an independent legal basis.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/575bv.pdf

Field rule: a stop lawful at inception can become unlawful if its scope or continued duration is no longer justified.

docs.title: 5. Identification — request, statutory duty, silence, booking, and false information are different questions
docs.text:
Avoid both slogans:

You never have to identify in California.

and

If you're detained, you have to show ID.

The correct sequence is:

  1. Is the encounter consensual, a lawful detention, or an arrest?
  2. Is the officer merely asking for identification?
  3. Is there a current California statute requiring specified identifying information in this context?
  4. Is this a driver, citation, booking, specialized-facility, probation/parole, or other special setting?
  5. Is the issue silence/refusal, or false information? Those are not equivalent.

docs.title: Hiibel does not itself create a California duty
docs.text:
Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court, 542 U.S. 177 (2004) upheld application of Nevada's own stop-and-identify statute during a valid Terry stop. As authoritatively construed, Nevada required Hiibel to state his name. The Court found that requirement constitutional on those facts and rejected the Fifth Amendment claim because stating his name did not present a reasonable danger of incrimination there.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/542bv.pdf

Hiibel establishes that a state may enact a qualifying stop-and-identify requirement. It does not legislate one for California and does not hold that identity can never have Fifth Amendment implications.

docs.title: Historical California context — Kolender v. Lawson
docs.text:
In Kolender v. Lawson, 461 U.S. 352 (1983), the Supreme Court invalidated California's former requirement that a stopped person provide credible and reliable identification because the scheme was unconstitutionally vague and gave excessive enforcement discretion. Hiibel itself discusses that history.

This historical case does not mean all modern California identification requirements are invalid. Current specialized statutes still control their own settings.

docs.title: United States v. Landeros, 913 F.3d 862 (9th Cir. 2019)
docs.text:
Published Ninth Circuit authority held that a passenger's refusal to identify himself, where officers lacked reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offense, did not itself create reasonable suspicion and did not justify prolonging the traffic stop to investigate him.

Official Ninth Circuit opinion:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/01/11/17-10217.pdf

The important distinction is request versus compulsion. An officer may ask without necessarily having authority to impose criminal consequences for refusal.

docs.title: California published cases — § 148 is not a generic silence offense
People v. Quiroga, 16 Cal.App.4th 961 (1993)
docs.text:
The published Court of Appeal decision drew several important lines under Penal Code § 148:

  • slow compliance and verbal argument did not automatically amount to § 148 obstruction;
  • refusing to give a name after arrest while being transported did not itself violate § 148 because the arrest had already been effected and booking had not begun;
  • refusing identity during a felony booking interview could violate § 148 because it actually delayed the booking process;
  • the court distinguished misdemeanor/infraction identification contexts, for which California statutes separately address identification and release/custody procedures.

The current Judicial Council CALCRIM No. 2656 cites Quiroga under Verbal Resistance or Obstruction and specifically describes the nondisclosure proposition as identity following arrest for a felony, not misdemeanor.

Official Judicial Council source:

https://courts.ca.gov/advisory-body/criminal-jury-instructions-advisory-committee

Full published opinion text (reporter reproduction):

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/961.html

docs.title: In re Chase C., 243 Cal.App.4th 107 (2015)
docs.text:
This published Court of Appeal decision applied Quiroga in a police-investigation setting. The court held that, on the facts before it, the minor's refusal to identify himself while detained/postarrest but before booking did not constitute § 148 obstruction; the opinion described that refusal as protected Fifth Amendment silence. It distinguished the booking stage and false identification.

The case is also important more generally because it emphasized that refusal to cooperate becomes criminal under § 148 only when it actually obstructs lawful police activity; verbal protest, slow compliance, or refusal cannot simply be relabeled obstruction without the statute's elements.

Published opinion text:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2015/d067787.html

docs.title: Limits of Quiroga / Chase C.
docs.text:
Do not turn these cases into:

The Fifth Amendment always lets every California detainee refuse every identification demand.

That would conflict with the context-specific structure of Hiibel and California statutes. The narrower California proposition is:

Silence or refusal to identify is not automatically Penal Code § 148 obstruction. Identify the actual statutory duty and stage of the encounter. Booking and specialized statutory contexts can be different.

docs.title: Penal Code § 148.9 — false identity is separate
docs.text:
Penal Code § 148.9 makes it a misdemeanor, under its stated elements, to falsely represent or identify oneself as another or fictitious person to specified officers upon lawful detention or arrest for the purpose of evading process or proper identification.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.9

Section 148.9 tells a detainee what not to do. Its text does not itself say every lawfully detained pedestrian must affirmatively produce ID.

docs.title: Carrying physical identification is a separate question
docs.text:
The current California sweep has not identified a general statute requiring an ordinary pedestrian merely existing in public to carry a physical identification card.

That question is separate from whether an officer may ask for a name, whether a specific statute requires identifying information in a specialized context, or whether a person is subject to an arrest/booking/citation procedure.

A call for service, an officer's desire to "investigate," or an officer's request for identification does not itself create a general carry-ID statute. Facts reported in a call can still matter to reasonable-suspicion analysis, and a specific statutory context can create a real identification duty.

The project therefore distinguishes:

carry ID → produce a document → state identifying information → do not provide false identity

Those are different legal questions.

Scope of this conclusion: the present field rule concerns the absence of a general carry-ID statute and a general statutory stop-and-identify rule. It does not yet resolve every California case-law question about whether, during an otherwise lawful detention, an officer may direct a person to produce proof of identity that the person actually possesses. Older published California cases addressing identification production and identification searches are queued for reconciliation before the guide states a broader categorical rule.

docs.title: Drivers — Vehicle Code § 12951
docs.text:
Driving is different. Vehicle Code § 12951 requires a driver to possess the valid license when driving on a highway and present it on demand to a peace officer enforcing the Vehicle Code.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=12951

docs.title: Infraction-arrest citation — Penal Code § 853.5
docs.text:
Section 853.5 supplies identification/fingerprint procedures when an officer is issuing a written promise to appear after an infraction arrest. It is not a general pre-arrest pedestrian stop-and-identify statute.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=853.5

docs.title: Vehicle Code § 40302
docs.text:
Section 40302 supplies additional identity/custody rules after arrest for specified nonfelony Vehicle Code violations.

Primary source:

https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=40302

docs.title: Current California field rule
docs.text:
This sweep has not identified a current general California pedestrian stop-and-identify statute equivalent to Nevada's statute in Hiibel. That is not the same as saying identification can never be required. Determine the specific current authority and context. Silence/refusal is not automatically § 148 obstruction, but false identity can independently violate § 148.9.

Useful question:

What law requires me to provide identification under these circumstances?

And regardless of whether a duty exists:

Do not give a false identity.

docs.title: 6. Stop does not automatically authorize a frisk
docs.text:
A Terry detention and Terry frisk are analytically distinct. A protective frisk requires a reasonable basis to believe the detained person is armed and dangerous. Its purpose/scope is protective rather than a general evidence search.

Useful question:

Are you frisking me because you believe I am armed and dangerous? What facts support that?

Do not physically resist. Plain-feel/container doctrine remains queued.

docs.title: 7. Arrest — probable cause is a different threshold
docs.text:
An arrest ordinarily requires probable cause to believe the person committed or is committing an offense.

  • reasonable suspicion: supports a limited investigative detention;
  • probable cause: ordinarily supports arrest.

docs.title: Devenpeck v. Alford, 543 U.S. 146 (2004)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court held that warrantless-arrest legality is an objective probable-cause inquiry. The offense objectively supported by known facts need not be the same offense the officer announced.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/543bv.pdf

Thus:

Asking What offense? is excellent record-building, but an officer's verbal answer is not necessarily the complete later probable-cause analysis.

docs.title: 8. Fourth Amendment detention is not the same as Miranda custody
docs.text:
A Terry detainee is not free to leave for Fourth Amendment purposes but is not automatically in custody for Miranda purposes.

In Berkemer v. McCarty, 468 U.S. 420 (1984), the Supreme Court explained that ordinary traffic stops resemble Terry stops and generally are noncustodial for Miranda even though they significantly restrict movement. Miranda applies when the treatment reaches the degree associated with formal arrest.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-468_PDFA.pdf

Field distinction:

4A: Am I seized, and what justifies that seizure?

5A/Miranda: Am I in Miranda custody and being interrogated?

A person may answer yes to the first and no to the second.

docs.title: 9. Fifth Amendment privilege and Miranda
docs.text:
The Fifth Amendment protects against compelled testimonial self-incrimination. Malloy v. Hogan, 378 U.S. 1 (1964) applies that privilege against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. California Constitution article I, section 15 provides a parallel state privilege.

Miranda is a procedural doctrine protecting the privilege during custodial interrogation. Failure to give Miranda warnings does not automatically make the underlying detention or arrest unlawful.

docs.title: Clear invocation is the safer rule
docs.text:
In Berghuis v. Thompkins, 560 U.S. 370 (2010), the Court held in the Miranda context that invocation of the right to remain silent must be unambiguous; prolonged silence did not itself invoke the right on those facts.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/560bv.pdf

In Salinas v. Texas, 570 U.S. 178 (2013), a plurality concluded that a person in a voluntary, noncustodial interview could not rely on silence alone on the facts there because he had not expressly invoked the privilege.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/570bv.pdf

Because Salinas is plurality-limited and invocation doctrine is context-dependent, the Field Guide should not say silence never invokes the Fifth Amendment. The safer operational advice is:

If you intend to invoke, say so clearly rather than expecting silence alone to communicate the invocation.

Useful language:

I invoke my right to remain silent. I do not want to answer investigative questions.

No exact incantation is required; clarity is the point.

Invocation does not automatically terminate a lawful detention or erase a specific identification duty that is otherwise constitutionally enforceable.

docs.title: 10. Hiibel's Fifth Amendment holding is narrow
docs.text:
Hiibel rejected the Fifth Amendment challenge because on those facts stating the detainee's name did not create a reasonable danger of incrimination. The opinion did not hold that identity can never be testimonial/incriminating.

For California, ask in order:

  1. Is there a lawful detention?
  2. Is there a current law requiring the particular information?
  3. What exactly is demanded — name, document, address, DOB, fingerprint, etc.?
  4. Does the Fifth Amendment create an additional issue on these facts?

docs.title: 11. Phones and cameras — seizure is not digital search
docs.text:
Keep separate:

  1. consent to hand over the device;
  2. physical seizure;
  3. legal basis for seizure;
  4. search of digital contents;
  5. warrant/consent/exception;
  6. compelled unlocking.

docs.title: Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014)
docs.text:
The Supreme Court held that search incident to arrest does not ordinarily authorize police to search digital information on a cellphone merely because the phone was seized from a lawfully arrested person. Police generally need a warrant to search digital contents, subject to recognized case-specific exceptions such as exigency.

Official source:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/573BV.pdf

Critical distinction: Riley does not mean police can never physically seize a phone. Seizure/retention and digital-content search require separate analysis.

Useful language:

I do not consent to seizure or search of my phone. If you are ordering me to hand it over, I am complying under protest and not consenting.

Do you have a warrant to search its digital contents?

Do not physically fight over the device.

docs.title: Compelled unlocking — still RESEARCH
docs.text: Passcodes, biometrics, encryption, the testimonial-act doctrine, warrants/orders, and the foregone-conclusion doctrine require a dedicated California/Ninth Circuit review. Do not use slogans such as passcode = Fifth Amendment or biometrics are always unprotected.

docs.title: 12. Practical encounter script — evidence-preserving, not magic words
Initial contact
docs.text: Am I free to leave?

docs.title: If no
docs.text:
Am I being detained?

What is the reason for the stop?

What offense do you reasonably suspect me of committing?

What specific facts are you relying on?

docs.title: If ID is demanded
docs.text:
What legal authority requires me to provide identification under these circumstances?

Never provide false/fictitious identity.

docs.title: If a frisk/search begins
docs.text:
I do not consent to any search.

Are you frisking me because you believe I am armed and dangerous?

docs.title: If substantive questioning begins
docs.text: I invoke my right to remain silent. I do not want to answer investigative questions.

docs.title: If a device is demanded
docs.text:
I do not consent to seizure or search of my device. If you are ordering me to hand it over, I am complying under protest and not consenting.

Physical nonresistance and legal consent are different things.

docs.title: 13. Common bad field rules
docs.text: Bad slogan Better rule If I'm not under arrest, I can leave. A Terry detainee may be temporarily not free to leave without being under formal arrest. If I'm detained, they have to Mirandize me. Fourth Amendment detention and Miranda custody are different thresholds. Hiibel says I have to identify whenever detained. Hiibel upheld Nevada's statute; identify California authority for the actual context. The officer has to tell me all of the RAS immediately. For a pedestrian stop within the guide's current scope, California § 2806.5 requires the reason for the stop before covered questioning, subject to its exception. That is different from requiring an on-scene recital of every fact underlying reasonable suspicion. California has no stop-and-ID law, so I can lie. Whether affirmative ID is required is separate from § 148.9's false-ID offense. Refusing my name is automatically obstruction. California published cases distinguish silence/refusal from actual § 148 obstruction and distinguish booking from earlier stages. A legal stop automatically allows a frisk. A frisk requires a separate armed-and-dangerous basis. No Miranda warning means the arrest is illegal. Arrest legality is primarily a 4A probable-cause question; Miranda concerns custodial interrogation/statement use. Arrest means police can search my phone. Riley generally requires a warrant for digital contents; seizure and search are separate.

docs.title: Public-Forum Doctrine
docs.text: Research status: Core federal forum architecture, Ninth Circuit government-building doctrine, and the principal California Speech Clause overlay have been reviewed. This chapter does not classify every California facility. Contra Costa public libraries now have an initial system-level Sweep 006, but branch-specific library classifications remain unresolved; police/sheriff lobbies, DMV offices, courthouses, campuses, transit facilities, and other recurring locations still require facility- and area-specific research.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text:
Public ownership is not the same thing as a public forum, and public access is not the same thing as a public forum.

Classify the specific place or channel of communication actually at issue. A single government property can contain areas with different forum classifications and different rules.

Under the federal First Amendment:

  • traditional public forums, such as ordinary public streets, parks, and sidewalks, receive the strongest forum protection;
  • government may intentionally create a designated public forum and then is generally held to the same forum standard while it remains open;
  • a limited public forum is opened only for specified speakers or subjects; restrictions within the forum must fit the forum's purpose and be reasonable and viewpoint neutral;
  • nonpublic government property is not opened by tradition or designation for general expressive activity; restrictions still must be reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral.

California's Speech Clause can be broader than the First Amendment in some settings. Do not assume the federal classification automatically resolves the California constitutional question.

docs.title: 1. Define the forum before classifying it
docs.text:
The first question is not merely, What building am I in? It is:

What exact property, room, walkway, meeting period, bulletin board, display space, or other channel is the speaker seeking to use for what expressive activity?

In Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, the Supreme Court instructed courts to identify the forum by looking to the access sought. Where only limited access is sought, the forum can be narrower than the whole government property.

The Ninth Circuit applied the same area-specific approach in Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair. The court separately analyzed the exterior unticketed area and the enclosed ticketed event area because they were physically separated and governed by different policies.

Field consequence: Do not say the courthouse is a public forum or the DMV is a nonpublic forum without identifying the area and activity. The front public sidewalk, exterior plaza, lobby, service counter, employee corridor, hearing room, and meeting-comment period can present different questions.

Authorities:

  • Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund, Inc., 473 U.S. 788 (1985).
  • Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023).

docs.title: Traditional public forum
docs.text:
Traditional public forums are places that historically have been devoted to assembly, debate, and public communication. The canonical examples are ordinary public streets, sidewalks, and parks.

A government generally may impose content-neutral time/place/manner rules in such a forum if the rules are narrowly tailored to serve a significant governmental interest and leave open ample alternative channels of communication. Content-based exclusions ordinarily face strict scrutiny, and viewpoint discrimination is forbidden.

Authorities:

  • Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association, 460 U.S. 37, 45-46 (1983).
  • United States v. Grace, 461 U.S. 171 (1983).
  • Ward v. Rock Against Racism, 491 U.S. 781, 791 (1989).

docs.title: Government-building boundary warning
docs.text:
The public sidewalk outside or around a government building can be a traditional public forum even though the building interior is not. In Grace, the sidewalks forming the perimeter of the Supreme Court grounds were treated differently from the Court grounds/building. Physical proximity to a sensitive government facility does not automatically erase the forum character of an ordinary public sidewalk.

At the same time, a walkway that merely resembles a sidewalk is not automatically a traditional public forum. United States v. Kokinda illustrates that the purpose, location, physical characteristics, and use of the particular walkway matter.

docs.title: Designated public forum
docs.text:
Government can intentionally open property that is not a traditional public forum for public expressive activity. While the government maintains that designation, restrictions are generally analyzed under the same standards that govern a traditional public forum.

Intent matters. Government does not create a designated public forum merely by allowing some speech, by tolerating occasional expressive activity, or by opening property for ordinary government business.

Authorities:

  • Perry, 460 U.S. at 45-46.
  • Cornelius, 473 U.S. at 802.
  • Pleasant Grove City v. Summum, 555 U.S. 460, 469-70 (2009).

docs.title: Limited public forum
docs.text:
A limited public forum is opened only for certain groups or for discussion of certain subjects. In the Ninth Circuit, restrictions must be reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral.

This classification frequently matters for public meetings, school or university channels, government-created message spaces, and other contexts in which government invites some private speech without opening the forum for every speaker and every topic.

In Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc), the Ninth Circuit held that a city-council meeting opened to public participation is a limited public forum. The court rejected the claim that all First Amendment protection disappears after public comment ends and emphasized viewpoint neutrality and actual disruption in the meeting-removal context.

The category can be confusing because Supreme Court and circuit opinions have not always used identical terminology. The Field Guide therefore records both the label and the actual governing rule instead of relying on the label alone.

Authorities:

  • Christian Legal Society Chapter of the University of California, Hastings College of the Law v. Martinez, 561 U.S. 661 (2010).
  • Wright v. Incline Village General Improvement District, 665 F.3d 1128 (9th Cir. 2011).
  • Hopper v. City of Pasco, 241 F.3d 1067 (9th Cir. 2001).
  • Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc).

docs.title: Nonpublic forum
docs.text:
Government property does not become a public forum simply because members of the public may enter it.

In a nonpublic forum, government may reserve property for its intended use and may draw distinctions based on subject matter or speaker identity when the distinctions are reasonable in light of the forum's purpose and viewpoint neutral.

That is a lower level of scrutiny than applies in a traditional/designated public forum, but it is not no First Amendment protection.

Authorities:

  • Perry, 460 U.S. at 46.
  • Cornelius, 473 U.S. at 806.
  • Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky, 585 U.S. 1 (2018).
  • Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002).

docs.title: Reasonableness still has content
docs.text:
In Sammartano, the Ninth Circuit agreed that a judicial/municipal complex was a nonpublic forum. It nevertheless held, at the preliminary-injunction stage, that challenged expressive-clothing restrictions were likely invalid because the record did not adequately connect the restrictions to the asserted safety/order interests and at least one restriction was viewpoint discriminatory.

Field rule: Nonpublic forum does not mean officials may prohibit expression for any reason they choose. Ask how the restriction relates to the purpose of the area and whether comparable viewpoints are treated alike.

Mansky likewise shows that a nonpublic-forum rule must supply an objective, workable standard rather than leaving officials without a sensible basis for distinguishing permitted from prohibited expression.

docs.title: 3. A government building can be open to the public and still be a nonpublic forum
docs.text:
This is the distinction most likely to matter in an ordinary audit.

In Sammartano, the Ninth Circuit agreed that a complex used for county and judicial business was a nonpublic forum. Its function was conducting governmental/court business, not serving as a place traditionally or intentionally opened for assembly and debate.

That proposition must be used carefully:

  • Sammartano does not hold that every government lobby in California is categorically a nonpublic forum;
  • it does not mean a nonpublic forum is exempt from the First Amendment;
  • it does not mean any employee can order any visitor out for any reason;
  • it does not convert a policy violation automatically into criminal trespass;
  • it does show why the lobby is open to the public is not enough, standing alone, to prove traditional/designated-public-forum status.

This directly complements the trespass chapter's distinction between access status, forum status, facility policy, and criminal authority.

Authority:

  • Sammartano, 303 F.3d 959.

docs.title: 4. Viewpoint discrimination is a separate red flag
docs.text:
Forum classification determines how much subject-matter control government has. It does not generally authorize viewpoint discrimination against private speakers within an otherwise permitted subject.

A rule or enforcement decision can be viewpoint discriminatory when government allows discussion of a subject but disfavors one side, perspective, affiliation, or opinion on that subject.

In a nonpublic or limited forum, government may often limit the forum to its intended subjects or classes of speakers. But once a subject is within the forum's permissible scope, excluding a speaker merely because officials oppose the speaker's viewpoint is constitutionally suspect.

Authorities:

  • Cornelius, 473 U.S. at 806, 812.
  • Rosenberger v. Rector & Visitors of the University of Virginia, 515 U.S. 819, 828-30 (1995).
  • Sammartano, 303 F.3d at 970-72.

Evidence-preservation consequence: If an official says a rule applies because the recorder is anti-police, an auditor, critical of the agency, supportive of the agency, or otherwise because of the message being expressed, preserve that statement. It can matter independently of the ultimate forum classification.

docs.title: 5. Content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions
docs.text:
In a traditional or designated public forum, government may impose reasonable content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions. Under Ward, the familiar test asks whether the restriction:

  1. is justified without reference to the content of the regulated speech;
  2. is narrowly tailored to serve a significant governmental interest; and
  3. leaves open ample alternative channels for communication.

Narrowly tailored in this context does not mean the government must always choose the least restrictive conceivable alternative. But the restriction may not burden substantially more speech than necessary to further the interest.

This doctrine can validate genuine safety, pedestrian-flow, congestion, noise, or operational rules while still requiring a real fit between the asserted interest and the restriction.

Authorities:

  • Ward, 491 U.S. 781.
  • Camenzind, 84 F.4th 1102.
  • Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012).

docs.title: 6. California Constitution: analyze separately
docs.text:
California Constitution article I, section 2(a) states an independent liberty-of-speech guarantee.

California doctrine is not simply a copy of the federal public-forum test. California courts have recognized speech rights in some privately controlled properties that would not be public forums under the federal First Amendment, most famously certain shopping-center settings.

For the Field Guide's government-property focus, two cautions are especially important.

docs.title: California's government-property forum test is not perfectly settled
docs.text:
In International Society for Krishna Consciousness of California, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles, 48 Cal.4th 446 (2010), the California Supreme Court expressly declined to decide whether LAX was a public forum under the California Speech Clause because the solicitation restriction at issue was valid even if the relevant public areas were assumed to be public forums.

In Camenzind, the Ninth Circuit therefore noted that California's forum standard differs from the federal test and that the state-law test has generated uncertainty. The panel held that the exterior, unticketed area at Cal Expo was a public forum under the California Speech Clause and that the enclosed, ticketed portion during a privately organized festival was nonpublic. The panel also expressly acknowledged that, absent controlling California Supreme Court authority on the point, it was predicting how that court would decide the state-law question. Judge VanDyke dissented from part of that state-law analysis.

Project status consequence: Treat Camenzind as binding published Ninth Circuit authority for federal courts within the circuit, while separately identifying its California-law classification as a federal appellate prediction of unsettled state constitutional law rather than pretending the California Supreme Court itself announced that exact test.

docs.title: Do not use the old basic incompatibility test as the classification rule
docs.text:
An older California Court of Appeal decision, U.C. Nuclear Weapons Labs Conversion Project v. Lawrence Livermore Laboratory, described government property on a continuum and asked whether proposed expressive activity was basically incompatible with the normal activity of the place. Older Ninth Circuit decisions, including Carreras and Kuba, adopted that formulation when predicting California law.

That is now a research trap. In San Leandro Teachers Association v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009), the California Supreme Court observed that the basic incompatibility formulation had not appeared in California appellate cases since U.C. Weapons Labs and noted that Grayned used incompatibility to evaluate a restriction after forum status had been determined, not to classify the forum itself. Camenzind later described the California Supreme Court as having declined to adopt that classification test and warned that the older Ninth Circuit cases applying it rest on a doubtful foundation.

Field Guide rule: Do not classify a California property as a public forum merely because the proposed speech seems compatible with the property's normal activity. Use current controlling California authority and the more recent guideposts identified here; where the state-law classification remains unsettled, mark it UNRESOLVED.

San Leandro is also useful for a narrower point. The California Supreme Court treated internal school mailboxes as nonpublic under federal forum doctrine and then separately rejected the claim that the California Speech Clause required a different result on those facts. California's broader speech clause therefore does not automatically convert every restricted government communication channel into a public forum.

Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012), later declined to apply the old basic incompatibility formulation and instead analyzed the outdoor grounds of the Redding Municipal Library using the federal forum framework. On its property-specific record, the court treated the public open space at the entrance, the entry/exit-door area, and the adjacent parking lot as a traditional public forum. That holding is useful California authority for library exteriors, but it does not classify every library exterior—or the library interior—the same way. See public-libraries.md.

Authorities:

  • San Leandro Teachers Ass'n v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009).
  • U.C. Nuclear Weapons Labs Conversion Project v. Lawrence Livermore Laboratory, 154 Cal.App.3d 1157 (1984) — historical context; do not use its basic incompatibility formulation as the current classification rule.
  • Camenzind, 84 F.4th 1102.

docs.title: California can protect more speech without making every public-facing place a public forum
docs.text:
Cases such as Robins v. Pruneyard Shopping Center, Ralphs Grocery Co. v. UFCW Local 8, and Park Management Corp. v. In Defense of Animals show that California's Speech Clause uses a broader and fact-sensitive concept in some private-property settings. Those cases are important context, but they should not be converted into the slogan California says every place open to the public is a public forum.

Authorities:

  • Cal. Const. art. I, § 2(a).
  • International Society for Krishna Consciousness of California, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles, 48 Cal.4th 446 (2010).
  • Robins v. Pruneyard Shopping Center, 23 Cal.3d 899 (1979), aff'd, 447 U.S. 74 (1980).
  • San Leandro Teachers Ass'n v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009).
  • Ralphs Grocery Co. v. United Food & Commercial Workers Union Local 8, 55 Cal.4th 1083 (2012).
  • Park Management Corp. v. In Defense of Animals, 36 Cal.App.5th 649 (2019).
  • Camenzind, 84 F.4th 1102.

docs.title: 7. Forum doctrine does not by itself answer the right-to-record question
docs.text:
Forum doctrine regulates expressive use of government property, but a recording dispute can involve additional doctrines:

  • whether recording the particular subject is protected First Amendment activity;
  • whether a facility rule is directed at speech/press activity, conduct, privacy, security, court administration, or another interest;
  • whether the recorder is in a place they have a right to be;
  • whether a statute independently protects recording, such as Penal Code § 148(g) in its scope or open-meeting statutes;
  • whether the location is governed by a specialized statute, court rule, school rule, security regulation, or agency policy;
  • whether the person is actually interfering with operations;
  • whether exclusion/removal has an independent lawful basis.

Accordingly:

Forum classification is an important layer, not a universal recording permission slip or prohibition.

The recording, public-meeting, trespass/removal, police-encounter, and facility-specific chapters must still be consulted.

docs.title: 8. Forum doctrine does not itself create criminal trespass
docs.text:
A First Amendment conclusion and a criminal-trespass conclusion are different questions.

For example:

  1. an area may be a nonpublic forum;
  2. a viewpoint-neutral facility restriction may be constitutionally permissible there;
  3. a visitor may violate the restriction;
  4. but the state must still identify the actual legal authority supporting exclusion, detention, citation, or arrest.

Conversely, a person's conduct can satisfy an independently valid trespass statute even if the person is engaged in some expressive activity. The constitutional and statutory questions have to be analyzed together rather than collapsed into either slogan.

See trespass-removal.md for Penal Code §§ 602 and 602.1.

docs.title: 9. Facility-registry classification protocol
docs.text:
For every future registry entry, classify areas, not merely facilities.

Minimum forum fields:

Field What to record Facility Agency/building name Specific area Public sidewalk, plaza, parking lot, lobby, counter queue, hearing room, corridor, secured area, etc. Access status Open to general public, appointment-only, screened, ticketed, employee-only, closed hours, etc. Federal forum classification TPF / designated / limited / nonpublic / unresolved California Speech Clause classification Public / nonpublic / unresolved; do not assume federal result controls Authority Controlling case/statute/rule/policy supporting classification Expressive activity analyzed Filming, leafletting, signs, public comment, solicitation, conversation, etc. Restrictions Actual rule and source Confidence HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW / UNRESOLVED Last verified Date

A registry entry should use UNRESOLVED rather than infer a forum classification merely from a building's ownership or the presence of a public service counter.

docs.title: 10. Field questions during a forum/access dispute
docs.text:
These questions are primarily for preserving the factual record:

  • What exact area are you saying has a restriction?
  • Is this area open to members of the public for agency business?
  • What rule or policy are you enforcing?
  • May I see or obtain a copy of that rule?
  • Does the rule prohibit recording, all expressive activity, or only particular conduct?
  • Is the same rule applied regardless of the speaker's viewpoint?
  • What conduct are you saying is disrupting or interfering with operations?
  • Are you ordering me to leave this specific area or the entire property?
  • What legal authority supports that removal order?

These are not magic phrases and do not require officials to litigate constitutional doctrine on scene. Their value is factual clarity for later review.

docs.title: 11. Doctrine-reviewed propositions from Sweep 005
docs.text:
The following narrow propositions have reached DOCTRINE-REVIEWED or DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART status:

  1. Specific forum first: forum analysis can be area/channel-specific rather than building-wide.
  2. Public access ≠ public forum: public entry for government business does not itself establish a traditional/designated public forum.
  3. Traditional forum baseline: ordinary public streets, parks, and sidewalks are canonical traditional public forums, subject to context-specific boundary analysis.
  4. Designated forum requires intentional opening: government does not create one merely by permitting isolated speech.
  5. Limited forum: restrictions must be reasonable in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutral.
  6. Nonpublic forum: restrictions must be reasonable in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutral; nonpublic does not mean no First Amendment protection.
  7. Government-building example: Sammartano treated the judicial/municipal complex before it as nonpublic but, at the preliminary-injunction stage, found the challengers likely to succeed against restrictions that lacked adequate reasonableness support and included viewpoint discrimination.
  8. California separate analysis: California's Speech Clause can differ from the federal test; ISKCON left LAX classification unresolved, and Camenzind contains a published Ninth Circuit prediction/application of California law with a partial dissent.
  9. Forum ≠ trespass: forum classification does not itself establish criminal trespass or removal authority.
  10. Forum ≠ recording doctrine: recording disputes may require additional constitutional, statutory, privacy, security, and facility-specific analysis.

docs.title: 12. Still unresolved
docs.text:
Sweep 005 does not yet establish categorical forum answers for:

  • ordinary city/county administrative lobbies;
  • police and sheriff lobbies;
  • DMV and other state-agency service centers;
  • public-library branches and particular library areas beyond the initial Contra Costa system sweep;
  • courthouse interiors, courtrooms, clerk windows, and exterior courthouse plazas beyond authorities already identified;
  • public college/university grounds and building interiors;
  • K-12 grounds;
  • transit stations and platforms;
  • public hospital/clinic spaces;
  • parking lots as a general category;
  • government social-media pages or other digital forums;
  • government employee workspaces;
  • temporary/private events on public property beyond the facts and holdings of reviewed cases.

Those belong in facility-specific sweeps. The registry should mark them UNRESOLVED until supported by adequate authority.

docs.title: Source record
docs.text:
Primary and authoritative sources used for this sweep include:

  • First Amendment text and doctrine: https://constitution.congress.gov/
  • California Constitution art. I: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&article=I
  • Ninth Circuit Sammartano: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2002/08/26/0116685.pdf
  • Ninth Circuit Camenzind: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2023/10/31/22-15931.pdf
  • California Supreme Court San Leandro Teachers Ass'n (California Supreme Court archive reproduction; official citation 46 Cal.4th 822): https://scocal.stanford.edu/opinion/san-leandro-teachers-assn-v-governing-bd-33007/
  • California Supreme Court ISKCON (opinion reproduction; official citation 48 Cal.4th 446): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2010/s164272/

See ../research/SWEEP-005-PUBLIC-FORUM-DOCTRINE.md for the detailed authority ledger.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
A public library is not one constitutional forum. Identify the exact area, access condition, activity, and rule before drawing a First Amendment or trespass conclusion.

A library may contain an ordinary public entrance, reading and collection areas, service counters, children's or teen areas, study rooms, intentionally opened meeting rooms, display/distribution channels, restrooms, staff workspaces, and exterior sidewalks or plazas. Those areas can have different purposes, controllers, access conditions, and constitutional classifications.

Contra Costa County Library is the first system-level library sweep for this chapter. The resulting rules are useful statewide, but local library systems still require their own policy and facility research.

See also:

  • Standing Scenario
  • Public-Forum Doctrine
  • Trespass and Removal
  • Facility Research and Field Verification

docs.title: 1. Start with the specific library area
docs.text:
Do not begin with:

This is a public library, so it is a public forum.

Begin with:

What exact area am I asking to use, for what activity, under what access rule?

For library investigations, useful area categories include:

Area/channel Typical access question Current doctrinal posture Exterior ordinary public sidewalk Is it municipal/public right-of-way or library-specific property? Traditional-forum analysis may apply; verify boundary Entrance/lobby Open for ordinary library access or subject to screening/check-in? Public access does not itself determine forum status Stacks/reading/service areas Open for reading, research, borrowing, staff assistance, and related use Exact Ninth Circuit classification for all expressive activity remains unresolved Children's/teen area Age/purpose restrictions? Area-specific access conditions can lawfully matter; analyze actual rule Study room Reservation, occupancy, purpose, and time conditions? Room/channel-specific analysis Meeting/community room Intentionally opened to outside groups or speakers? May be limited/designated forum depending policy/practice; Faith Center is controlling for historical Antioch room Exhibit/display/distribution channel Open to outside groups/materials? Separate intentionally opened communication channel; restrictions need forum analysis Restroom Publicly accessible ancillary space? Access status does not itself create general expressive rights Staff/restricted area Actually closed to public? Restricted access; do not enter under standing scenario Special self-service period Card/PIN/orientation agreement required? Different access condition from ordinary staffed hours

The same building can contain several of these at once.

docs.title: 2. Controlling Ninth Circuit library case: Faith Center
Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover
docs.text:
Citation: 480 F.3d 891 (9th Cir. 2007), amended published opinion.

Official opinion:

https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2007/03/09/0516132.pdf

The case involved the meeting room at the Antioch branch of the Contra Costa County Library.

The Ninth Circuit held that the Antioch Library meeting room on the record before it was a limited public forum. The court considered the County's policy, the kinds of speakers and activities admitted, the application process, fees, exclusions, actual practice, and the relationship between meeting-room activity and the library's primary function.

Most important for this project, the court rejected reliance on other library meeting rooms because the relevant forum is defined by the access sought by the speaker. In that case, the forum was the Antioch meeting room.

docs.title: What to carry into the field guide
docs.text:
Retained rule: classify the specific library area or communication channel, not the library building as a whole.

Faith Center does not establish that:

  • every Contra Costa branch interior is a limited public forum;
  • every California public library is a limited public forum;
  • every meeting or study room has the same classification;
  • filming is automatically permitted or prohibited;
  • a violation of a room rule automatically creates criminal trespass.

The decision is a strong library-specific application of the broader forum rule already retained from Cornelius and Sweep 005.

docs.title: 3. California library-exterior anchor: Prigmore v. City of Redding
docs.text:
Citation: Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322, 150 Cal.Rptr.3d 647 (2012), Third District Court of Appeal.

Published opinion:

https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2012/c068866.html

Prigmore involved leafleting on the outdoor grounds of the Redding Municipal Library, not expressive activity inside the building.

The court approved defining the forum by the access actually sought and treated three outdoor components together on the record before it:

  1. the public open space on the entry side of the library;
  2. the entry/exit-door area; and
  3. the adjacent parking lot.

It held those outdoor areas to be a traditional public forum on the particular facts, emphasizing unrestricted public access, physical characteristics encouraging congregation, the entrance area's benches and newspaper rack, adjacency to parks and other public buildings, and the library's information-dissemination function.

docs.title: What Prigmore adds
docs.text:
This is published California appellate authority and is especially useful because it applies the same area-specific principle used throughout this project:

the forum is defined by the access sought, not automatically by the outer boundary of the government property.

It also distinguished the outdoor forum from the building interior and declined to use the older California "basic incompatibility" formulation as the forum-classification test.

docs.title: What Prigmore does not establish
docs.text:
Do not convert Prigmore into:

Every sidewalk, entrance, plaza, or parking lot around every California library is automatically a traditional public forum.

The holding depended on the physical and functional characteristics of the Redding property. A branch investigation should still establish ownership/control, public-thoroughfare function, access, boundaries, customary use, seating/congregation features, and the exact expressive activity.

The court's footnote 11 broadly observed that federal courts had treated a library interior as a limited public forum, citing Faith Center and Kreimer. For this project, that footnote is not treated as a categorical holding about all library interiors: Faith Center actually defined the forum before it as the Antioch meeting room. Ordinary reading, stacks, circulation, and service areas still require their own analysis.

docs.title: Restrictions reviewed in Prigmore
docs.text:
At the preliminary-injunction stage, the Court of Appeal largely sustained relief against Redding's outdoor policy. Among other things, the case addressed:

  • confinement of leafleting to a small designated "free speech area";
  • a 72-hour advance-reservation requirement;
  • restrictions on solicitation;
  • a prohibition on offensively coarse speech/gestures; and
  • leafleting of vehicles in the parking lot.

The court treated most challenged restrictions as likely invalid on the record, but upheld the parking-lot vehicle-leafleting ban based on the safety rationale before it.

Field-use rule: Prigmore is strong authority for scrutinizing artificial speech zones and advance-permission systems in a library's established outdoor public forum. It is not authority for ignoring reasonable, content-neutral safety rules or for assuming the same forum status indoors.

docs.title: 4. Faith Center's old religious-services dispute is historical, not current County policy
docs.text:
The 2007 Faith Center opinion involved a County meeting-room policy that barred religious worship services.

The current Contra Costa meeting-room policy document now shows that restriction struck through, with an effective date of July 6, 2009:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/LP-RMS-MeetingRoomRules_2025E_ADA.pdf

On remand after the Ninth Circuit appeal, a federal district court held the religious-services restriction unconstitutional under the then-prevailing Establishment Clause framework. That 2009 district-court reasoning relied on doctrine later displaced by the Supreme Court's modern Establishment Clause approach.

In Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022), the Supreme Court stated that it had abandoned the Lemon test and its endorsement-test offshoot.

Official opinion:

https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/21pdf/21-418diff_k4l8.pdf

Current-use rule: retain Faith Center's forum analysis where it remains applicable, but do not describe the old religious-services ban as current Contra Costa policy or carry the 2009 Lemon analysis forward as the current general Establishment Clause test.

docs.title: 5. Ordinary library floors: public access and forum status remain distinct
docs.text:
The ordinary library floor presents a different question from a meeting room intentionally opened for community use.

No published controlling Ninth Circuit or California appellate decision located in Sweep 006 categorically classifies all ordinary reading, stacks, service, and circulation areas of California public libraries for every kind of expressive activity.

That means the handbook should resist two shortcuts:

The doors are open to everyone, therefore the entire interior is a public forum.

and:

Libraries are quiet-use facilities, therefore no First Amendment activity is protected inside.

Neither proposition follows automatically.

docs.title: Persuasive authority: Kreimer
docs.text:
In Kreimer v. Bureau of Police for Town of Morristown, 958 F.2d 1242 (3d Cir. 1992), the Third Circuit treated the library before it as a limited public forum for activity compatible with the purposes for which it had been opened.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/958/1242/371694/

Kreimer emphasized library purposes involving receipt of information, reading, writing, and quiet contemplation. It upheld a rule requiring patrons to be engaged in activities associated with public-library use.

Kreimer is persuasive, not controlling, in California.

Other persuasive courts have used different forum terminology. Doe v. City of Albuquerque, 667 F.3d 1111 (10th Cir. 2012), for example, used designated-public-forum language when reviewing a broad exclusion from city libraries.

A newer Tenth Circuit decision, Spiehs v. Morgan, No. 25-3174 (10th Cir. Sept. 8, 2026), addressed restrictions on displaying signs inside a public library. The court assumed the library's designated-public-forum classification for the appeal and upheld content-neutral restrictions aimed at preserving reading and study from disruption. The decision is persuasive only in California and concerns signs, not filming, but it reinforces the need to analyze the specific activity and the library-purpose rationale rather than treating "public library" as a universal forum label.

Source:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca10/25-3174/25-3174-2026-09-08.html

The practical lesson is not to choose a label by analogy alone. Determine the local policy, purpose, practice, area, and activity first.

docs.title: 6. Contra Costa's current "library activity" requirement
docs.text:
