The Contra Costa County Board of Supervisors approved an amended Patron Conduct Policy on February 10, 2026.

Current policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/Patron-Conduct-Policy_ADA.pdf

Board adoption record:

https://contra-costa.legistar.com/LegislationDetail.aspx?GUID=FE18DC5D-D8D2-4476-A6C2-C7215C123DC5&ID=7870598&Options=&Search=

The policy requires patrons in the building to be engaged in activities associated with use of a public library. It provides examples including reading, studying, quiet conversation, working, use of library materials/equipment, and participation in a library program/activity.

docs.title: Recording and observation remain unresolved
docs.text:
The current policy does not expressly answer whether peaceful:

  • observing public library operations;
  • photographing or videorecording;
  • documenting public officials performing public duties;
  • asking questions; or
  • gathering information for later speech

is itself an activity associated with use of the library.

Sweep 006 did not locate a dedicated current public-facing Contra Costa policy specifically governing ordinary patron photography/videography inside library facilities.

Do not write: "Contra Costa has no photography policy."

Write: "No dedicated public-facing photography/videography policy was located in the sources reviewed as of September 21, 2026."

That distinction matters because an internal, branch-specific, newly adopted, or posted rule may exist even when it has not been located online.

Current status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: 7. A camera objection is not automatically disruption
docs.text:
Contra Costa's Patron Conduct Policy protects other patrons' use of the library and staff members' ability to perform their duties. It also contains rules concerning threats, harassment, blocking, noise, disruptive behavior, restricted areas, and misuse of designated spaces.

Those are legitimate factual predicates to investigate.

Under the project's standing scenario, however, none of them is silently established merely because:

  • an employee dislikes being recorded;
  • a patron notices the camera;
  • someone becomes uncomfortable;
  • an employee approaches the recorder;
  • someone calls security or police.

The investigator should document:

  • where the recorder was standing;
  • what was being recorded;
  • distance from other people;
  • volume;
  • whether a doorway, aisle, desk, queue, or computer was obstructed;
  • whether the recorder followed or crowded anyone;
  • whether staff work actually stopped or was materially impeded;
  • what exact policy provision was invoked.

The policy may matter. The government's characterization of the conduct does not substitute for the underlying facts.

docs.title: 8. Children's and teen areas are a separate access problem
docs.text:
Contra Costa has a specific Children/Teen Areas policy:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/LP-Children-Teen-Area-Policy_ADA.pdf

The policy reserves children's areas primarily for children age 11 and under, their parents/guardians, and patrons using the children's collection at staff discretion. Teen areas are primarily for patrons age 12-18, persons accompanying them, and patrons using the teen collection at staff discretion.

An unaccompanied adult can therefore encounter a legitimate area/purpose restriction even though the broader library is open to the public.

This is why the standing scenario requires lawful presence in the specific area, not merely lawful entry into the building.

The presence of minors can also make privacy and safety interests especially important, but the children/teen policy itself is not a categorical public-camera statute. Any recording rule still needs its own source and analysis.

docs.title: 9. Meeting rooms: system policy, branch implementation, sometimes different controllers
docs.text:
Contra Costa's room directory is unusually useful:

https://ccclib.org/rooms/

The system makes meeting and study rooms available under varying rules. Some are controlled or booked by the County Library; some community rooms are booked through a city or town.

Examples currently include rooms associated with:

  • City of Brentwood;
  • City of Clayton;
  • Town of Danville;
  • City of San Pablo; and
  • other local entities.

A room inside a library building therefore does not automatically mean the County Library controls every condition of its use.

For each room, record:

  1. physical location;
  2. owner/controller;
  3. booking authority;
  4. applicable County and local rules;
  5. classes of eligible users;
  6. permitted subjects/purposes;
  7. access hours;
  8. whether the room is open to the general public during a reservation;
  9. branch-specific restrictions;
  10. forum classification for the particular requested use.

Faith Center is controlling authority for the historical Antioch meeting-room record. It is not a template that automatically classifies every listed room today.

docs.title: 10. Displays and distribution are their own communication channel
docs.text:
Contra Costa maintains rules for non-library displays and distribution:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2024/10/LP-rulesforexhibitsdisplay-October2024E.pdf

The Library permits qualifying non-library materials in designated display/distribution areas, subject to authorization, available space, priority rules, and subject/use restrictions.

Because the government has intentionally opened a communication channel to outside materials, that channel requires its own forum analysis.

The current rules include restrictions involving religious use and instructions on how to vote for a candidate or political party, while allowing announcements of political meetings.

Sweep 006 does not reach a constitutional conclusion about those restrictions.

Questions reserved for deeper review include:

  • what exact forum the County has created;
  • which subject restrictions define the forum versus discriminate within it;
  • whether standards are reasonable in light of the channel's purpose;
  • whether they are viewpoint neutral;
  • whether branch-specific rules add materially different restrictions.

Current status: AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED.

docs.title: 11. Patron privacy records are not a visitor-camera prohibition
docs.text:
Contra Costa's privacy materials identify California Government Code section 7927.105 as protecting qualifying library patron registration and use records.

Library privacy page:

https://ccclib.org/privacy/

California State Library law compilation:

https://www.library.ca.gov/uploads/2025/01/California-Library-Laws-2025.pdf

A confidentiality statute governing records maintained by the library is not the same thing as a statute prohibiting a visitor from using a camera.

Do not reason:

Patron borrowing records are confidential, therefore filming anywhere in the library is illegal.

Separate issues may still create lawful restrictions, including constitutional privacy, confidential communications, harassment, children's areas, particular programs, copyrighted performances, disruption, and a valid facility policy. Each requires its own authority and factual predicates.

docs.title: 12. Suspension and exclusion
docs.text:
Contra Costa's current Suspension Policy was approved by the Board of Supervisors on February 10, 2026:

https://ccclib.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/72/2026/03/Suspension-Policy_ADA.pdf

The policy establishes escalating suspension periods and can impose systemwide exclusions from all Contra Costa County Library facilities for qualifying misconduct.

For longer suspensions, the published policy provides formal appeal or review procedures. The published policy does not state the same formal appeal procedure for suspensions of one week or less.

docs.title: Due process is duration- and context-sensitive
docs.text:
Persuasive authority includes Neinast v. Board of Trustees of Columbus Metropolitan Library, 346 F.3d 585 (6th Cir. 2003):

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/346/585/510700/

On the facts of a one-day eviction, the Sixth Circuit found adequate process where the patron was told the charge and had an opportunity to give his side. It did not announce one procedure for every library suspension.

A nonbinding Eastern District of California screening decision, Van Den Heuvel v. Dorothy, treated a weeks-to-month countywide library exclusion as plausibly implicating a liberty interest at the pleading stage:

https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/caedce/2%3A2021cv02176/403475/24/

Current California/Ninth Circuit library-specific rule: unresolved in this sweep.

For an actual exclusion, record:

  • immediate removal versus prospective suspension;
  • duration;
  • one branch versus systemwide scope;
  • stated conduct;
  • written notice;
  • opportunity to respond;
  • appeal/review mechanism;
  • emergency/safety rationale;
  • whether later access is conditioned on reentry procedures.

docs.title: 13. A suspension policy does not finish the trespass analysis
docs.text:
Contra Costa's Suspension Policy states that a suspended person who returns before the return date will be asked to leave, police will be contacted if the person refuses, and the person is subject to arrest for trespass under California Penal Code section 602.

The policy does not identify a particular section 602 subdivision or walk through its elements.

That creates an important research issue:

POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP

The flag does not mean an arrest would necessarily be unlawful. It means the public-facing policy statement is not the complete criminal-law analysis.

For an actual event:

  1. identify the administrative suspension and its scope;
  2. identify the authority to order removal;
  3. identify the specific Penal Code subdivision;
  4. test every statutory element against the actual area and access facts;
  5. separately analyze any detention or arrest under the Fourth Amendment.

See Trespass and Removal.

docs.title: 14. Special-access periods can change the access analysis
docs.text:
Contra Costa currently operates Self-Service Sundays at Concord and San Pablo, with Pittsburg listed as coming soon. Access requires advance enrollment, a library card in good standing, orientation, a signed user agreement, and card/PIN entry. Library staff are not present during the self-service period.

Current program page:

https://ccclib.org/self-service-sundays/

That is not the same access condition as ordinary staffed public hours.

A branch Registry entry should distinguish:

  • ordinary staffed hours;
  • special card/enrollment-controlled access;
  • room-only after-hours access;
  • closed hours;
  • temporary closures;
  • emergency restrictions.

The legal question begins with the access condition that actually existed at the time.

docs.title: 15. Contra Costa branch research protocol
docs.text:
After the system-level sweep, a branch investigation should answer these facts before any field test:

Field Branch question Building/property control County-owned, city-owned, leased, shared, or mixed? Exterior Ordinary public sidewalk/plaza or library-controlled approach? Hours Normal staffed hours and any special-access periods Entrance Open entry, card access, security, check-in, or other condition? Main floor Reading/stacks/service layout and ordinary public circulation Designated areas Children's, teen, computer, quiet, maker, or other purpose-limited spaces Rooms Study/meeting/community rooms; controller and booking authority Display channels What public materials may be posted/distributed and where? Restrooms Publicly accessible or conditioned? Restricted areas Staff doors, workrooms, secured spaces Recording rule Posted sign, written policy, staff instruction, or none located? Removal authority Who may order a person from the area and under what rule? Criminal bridge Exact statute/subdivision if law enforcement is invoked Prior enforcement Complaints, exclusions, police calls, bodycam/CAD/incident records Current flags Supported, unresolved, facial/as-applied issue, comparator, criminal-authority gap

The first branch should be selected for research value and reproducibility, not because it appears likely to create a confrontation.

docs.title: 16. Contra Costa system findings to carry forward
docs.text:
As of September 21, 2026:

  • the Board of Supervisors has adopted current Patron Conduct and Suspension policies;
  • the system requires patrons to engage in activities associated with use of a public library;
  • no dedicated public-facing ordinary-patron photography/videography policy was located in the sources reviewed;
  • children's and teen areas have explicit purpose/age access conditions;
  • meeting and study rooms vary materially by branch and controller;
  • Faith Center supplies controlling Ninth Circuit authority for the historical Antioch meeting room and supports area-specific forum analysis;
  • current meeting-room policy shows the old religious-services prohibition struck effective July 6, 2009;
  • display/distribution channels contain separate subject restrictions requiring further forum review;
  • systemwide suspensions can extend beyond a single branch and have duration-dependent review procedures;
  • the Suspension Policy cites Penal Code section 602 generically, leaving the exact criminal-law bridge unresolved.

These are system-level findings. They are not a Registry status for every Contra Costa library branch.

docs.title: 17. What remains unresolved
docs.text:
The next research layer should address:

  • California/Ninth Circuit law governing peaceful photography/videography in ordinary public-library interiors;
  • the status of peaceful governmental observation and information gathering under a "library activity" rule;
  • California Speech Clause treatment of library interiors and opened library channels;
  • First Amendment retaliation in a library-recording context;
  • procedural due process for short, intermediate, and long systemwide exclusions;
  • exact California trespass theories after a valid or disputed library suspension;
  • the constitutional status of current Contra Costa display/distribution restrictions;
  • branch-specific property and room control;
  • privacy issues tied to minors, computers, records transactions, and sensitive patron activity;
  • seizure/search of a camera or phone if an encounter escalates.

Until those questions are resolved, use UNRESOLVED rather than fill gaps with assumptions.

docs.title: Public Meetings: Brown Act and Bagley-Keene
docs.text:
Research status: Core attendance, recording, comment, and removal statutes source-checked; controlling-case layer and full chapter-range sweep still in progress. Last verified: September 21, 2026.

California has separate open-meeting statutes for local legislative bodies and many state bodies. Do not treat the Brown Act and Bagley-Keene as interchangeable.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text: At a covered open meeting, California law may protect more than the ability to sit in the room. The Brown Act and Bagley-Keene contain provisions addressing attendance conditions, recording, public comment, criticism, and disruption/removal. For covered meetings, a person ordinarily cannot be required to give a name or complete a sign-in form merely as a condition of attendance, and recording is expressly protected subject to the statutes' disruption standards.

docs.title: Government Code § 54950 — purpose
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54950.

The Brown Act declares that local public bodies exist to conduct the people's business and that their actions and deliberations are to occur openly.

Use in the guide: § 54950 states legislative purpose. It is not by itself the operative attendance, recording, comment, or removal rule.

docs.title: Government Code § 54953.3 — no mandatory sign-in or identification prerequisite
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54953.3

Section 54953.3 states that a member of the public may not be required, as a condition of attendance at a meeting of a local legislative body, to register a name, provide other information, complete a questionnaire, or otherwise satisfy a condition precedent to attendance.

If a sign-in sheet, register, questionnaire, or similar document is posted or circulated, it must clearly state that completion is voluntary and that attendance is permitted regardless of whether a person signs or registers.

Field rule: At a covered Brown Act meeting, you must sign in before you can attend is not the statutory rule. A voluntary attendance sheet is different from a mandatory condition of entry.

Limit: This section concerns attendance at covered meetings. It is not a general rule that a government facility may never lawfully request identifying information for some other purpose.

docs.title: Government Code § 54953.5 — recording an open meeting
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54953.5

Section 54953.5(a) expressly gives a person attending an open and public meeting the right to record the proceedings unless the legislative body makes a reasonable finding that the recording cannot continue without noise, illumination, or obstruction of view that constitutes or would constitute a persistent disruption.

Section 54953.5(b) separately addresses recordings made by or at the direction of the local agency and their inspection under the California Public Records Act.

Field rule: A bare statement that recording is prohibited is not the statutory standard at a Brown Act open meeting. The text specifically focuses on persistent disruption from noise, illumination, or obstruction of view.

Current-law note: The official text reflects amendments effective January 1, 2026.

docs.title: Government Code § 54954.3 — public comment and criticism
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54954.3.

Section 54954.3 requires opportunities for members of the public to address a local legislative body within the statute's terms and permits reasonable regulations including time limits.

Section 54954.3(c) states that the legislative body shall not prohibit public criticism of agency policies, procedures, programs, or services, or of acts or omissions of the legislative body. The section also states that it does not create expression privileges beyond those otherwise provided by law.

Field rule: Criticism of the agency or legislative body is not, merely because it is critical, a statutory basis for prohibiting public comment. Reasonable and lawful meeting regulations can still apply.

docs.title: Government Code § 54957.95 — removal of an individual for disruption
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54957.95.

The section authorizes the presiding member or designee to remove an individual for disrupting a meeting. Ordinarily, before removal, the person must be warned that the behavior is disrupting the meeting and that failure to cease may result in removal; the person may then be removed if the disruptive behavior does not promptly cease. The warning requirement does not apply to the statute's force/true-threat category.

The statute defines disrupting as behavior that actually disrupts, disturbs, impedes, or renders infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting. It includes failure to comply with reasonable and lawful regulations and force or a true threat of force.

Field rule: The current statute does not define disruption merely as making officials uncomfortable or expressing criticism. Apply the statutory definition and any relevant case law.

Standing-scenario consequence: A brief verbal or nonverbal audience reaction is not silently assumed to have actually disrupted, disturbed, impeded, or rendered infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting. If officials tolerate materially comparable applause, cheering, laughter, or gestures expressing approval but warn or remove someone for comparable disapproval, preserve the full sequence. The comparison may matter to viewpoint-neutrality analysis, but relevant differences in timing, duration, volume, invitation by the chair, actual effect on proceedings, and any reasonable and lawful decorum regulation must also be documented.

Current-law note: The official text reflects amendments effective January 1, 2026.

docs.title: Government Code § 54957.9 — clearing a meeting room after group disruption
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54957.9.

If a meeting is willfully interrupted by a group or groups so that orderly conduct becomes unfeasible and order cannot be restored by removing the individuals who are willfully interrupting, the legislative body may order the meeting room cleared and continue the session under the section's terms.

The statute also addresses continued attendance by representatives of the press/news media who were not participating in the disturbance and permits a procedure for readmitting individuals not responsible for the disturbance.

Field rule: § 54957.9 concerns a specific escalation—group disruption making orderly conduct unfeasible after individual-removal measures cannot restore order. Do not treat it as a general power to clear a room whenever a meeting becomes contentious.

docs.title: Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act — state bodies
Government Code § 11120 — purpose
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=11120.

Section 11120 states California's policy that public-agency proceedings be conducted openly so the public may remain informed and identifies the article as the Bagley-Keene Open Meeting Act.

docs.title: Government Code § 11124 — no mandatory sign-in or identification prerequisite
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=11124.

Section 11124(a) states that a person may not be required, as a condition of attendance at a meeting of a state body, to register a name, provide other information, complete a questionnaire, or otherwise fulfill a condition precedent to attendance.

Section 11124(b) requires any attendance list, register, questionnaire, or similar document posted or circulated at the meeting to make clear that completion is voluntary.

Section 11124(c) addresses online platforms used to attend teleconferenced meetings. A platform may require submission of information to log in, but a person required to submit information must be permitted to use a pseudonym or other anonymous information.

Field rule: For a covered Bagley-Keene meeting, in-person attendance ordinarily cannot be conditioned on identifying yourself or completing a sign-in form. For an online platform that requires login information, the statute expressly preserves the ability to use pseudonymous or anonymous information.

Limit: This is a meeting-attendance rule, not a universal prohibition on identification requirements in every state facility or transaction.

docs.title: Government Code § 11124.1 — recording and broadcasting open state-body meetings
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=11124.1.

Section 11124.1(a) gives a person attending an open and public meeting of a state body the right to record using audio/video recorders or still/motion-picture cameras unless the state body reasonably finds that the recording cannot continue without noise, illumination, or obstruction of view constituting or likely to constitute a persistent disruption.

Section 11124.1(c) also prohibits a state body from prohibiting or otherwise restricting broadcast of an open public meeting absent the specified persistent-disruption finding.

Field rule: For a covered open state-body meeting, the statute affirmatively protects recording and broadcasting subject to the persistent-disruption limitation.

docs.title: Government Code § 11125.7 — public comment and criticism
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=11125.7.

Section 11125.7 generally requires an opportunity for public comment on agenda items under its terms and permits reasonable regulations, including time limits.

Section 11125.7(d) states that the state body shall not prohibit public criticism of its policies, programs, or services, or its acts or omissions. As with the Brown Act, the statute says this does not confer expression privileges beyond those otherwise provided by law.

docs.title: Brown Act versus Bagley-Keene
docs.text:
Before relying on a meeting rule, identify which body is involved:

  • city councils, county boards, and many local legislative bodies generally implicate the Brown Act;
  • covered state boards/commissions generally implicate Bagley-Keene;
  • courts, federal bodies, school/site-specific entities, advisory groups, and other bodies may have additional or different governing rules.

Do not cite a Brown Act section to a state body or a Bagley-Keene section to a local body without first establishing coverage.

docs.title: First Amendment forum overlay
docs.text:
The open-meeting statutes above are not the entire constitutional analysis. In Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc), relying on White v. City of Norwalk, the Ninth Circuit held that a city-council meeting opened to public participation is a limited public forum. Reasonable topic, time, and decorum rules can apply, but they must remain viewpoint neutral; the court rejected the idea that all First Amendment protection disappears when the public-comment period ends. It also reiterated that removal under the constitutional meeting cases turns on actual disruption rather than simply disfavored expression.

Ninth Circuit source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2010/12/15/07-15814.pdf

This forum doctrine supplements rather than replaces the Brown Act's current statutory attendance, comment, criticism, recording, warning, and disruption rules. Norse also makes comparator evidence especially important where supportive expression is tolerated and materially comparable critical expression is punished.

See public-forum-doctrine.md and standing-scenario.md.

docs.title: Case-law and completeness queue
docs.text:
This chapter still needs:

  • a complete section-by-section sweep of Government Code §§ 54950-54963;
  • a complete section-by-section sweep of Government Code §§ 11120-11132;
  • controlling California cases interpreting attendance conditions, disruption, public comment, criticism, meeting removal, and recording;
  • additional meeting-forum cases and application beyond the core Norse/White layer;
  • local meeting rules that may be stricter, more protective, or invalid if inconsistent with controlling law;
  • treatment of virtual/teleconferenced meetings under current statutes.

Until that work is complete, this page should be treated as the primary-text-verified core statutory layer rather than the complete public-meetings doctrine.

docs.title: California Public Records and Evidence Preservation
docs.text:
Research status: The core California Public Records Act (CPRA) definition, request, search, electronic-record, enforcement, personal-account, and preservation rules have been reviewed at the primary-text and controlling-case level. The complete exemption families in Government Code Division 10, agency-specific retention schedules, specialized law-enforcement disclosure statutes, and all potential destruction/spoliation remedies remain separate research layers.

This chapter addresses a recurring audit problem: a public employee, officer, or other government worker creates evidence of an encounter—sometimes on an agency device and sometimes on a personal phone—and the auditor wants to identify, preserve, and obtain that evidence.

The analysis must keep seven questions separate:

  1. Is the item a public record?
  2. Does the agency have an obligation to search for it?
  3. Is it disclosable, or does an exemption/redaction apply?
  4. How and when must the agency respond?
  5. How long must the record be retained under law or an applicable retention schedule?
  6. Does a request or preservation notice itself stop routine destruction?
  7. What additional law may apply if destruction is deliberate or litigation is reasonably foreseeable?

A correct answer to one question does not automatically answer the others.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text:
A work-related recording does not cease to be a potential public record merely because a public employee made or stored it on a personal phone or personal account.

Under California Supreme Court authority, the key inquiry is whether the writing substantively relates to the conduct of the public's business. Device ownership and account location are not categorical exclusions.

But:

public record is not synonymous with automatically disclosable, and CPRA request is not synonymous with automatic preservation hold.

The CPRA is principally a disclosure/access statute. Other statutes, approved retention schedules, litigation-preservation rules, and destruction laws determine whether and how long a particular record must be preserved.

docs.title: 1. What counts as a public record?
Government Code § 7920.530 — public-record definition
docs.text:
Government Code § 7920.530 defines a public record to include a writing containing information relating to the conduct of the public's business that is prepared, owned, used, or retained by a state or local agency, regardless of physical form or characteristics.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7920.530

docs.title: Government Code § 7920.545 — writing includes recordings
docs.text:
The CPRA's definition of writing is deliberately broad. It includes handwriting, printing, photographing, electronic transmission, and every other means of recording upon a tangible thing, including letters, words, pictures, sounds, symbols, and combinations of them, regardless of storage method.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7920.545

Field implication: video, photographs, and audio can qualify as CPRA writings. The fact that the evidence is a phone video rather than a memorandum does not remove it from the Act's definition.

docs.title: 2. Personal devices and accounts — City of San Jose
Controlling rule
docs.text:
In City of San Jose v. Superior Court, 2 Cal.5th 608 (2017), the California Supreme Court held that a city employee's writings concerning public business are not excluded from the CPRA simply because they were sent, received, or stored using a personal account.

The Court rejected a device/location rule. A record otherwise meeting the CPRA definition does not lose its status merely because it is outside government servers or located in an employee's personal account.

Opinion: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/2017/s218066.html

California Supreme Court case page: https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s218066-san-jose-city-v-sc-smith

docs.title: What makes a personal-device item relate to public business?
docs.text:
City of San Jose cautions that not every communication involving a public employee is a public record. At minimum, the writing must relate in some substantive way to the conduct of the public's business.

The Court identified relevant considerations including:

  • the content of the writing;
  • the context or purpose for which it was written;
  • the audience;
  • whether the employee was acting or purporting to act within the scope of employment.

Primarily personal material containing only incidental references to agency business generally will not qualify merely because a public employee created it.

docs.title: Auditor-specific application — employee records the encounter on a personal phone
docs.text:
Consider these facts:

  • the employee is on duty;
  • the employee is dealing with the auditor because of the employee's public job;
  • the employee intentionally takes out a personal phone;
  • the employee records the official encounter to document the auditor, report the incident, show a supervisor, or otherwise preserve what occurred for work-related purposes.

Those facts create a strong public-record case under § 7920.530 and City of San Jose: the recording is a writing, its content concerns an official encounter, its purpose is connected to agency business, and the employee is acting or purporting to act within employment.

Do not convert that into the absolute statement every recording made by a government employee at work is a public record. A purely personal recording made for an unrelated private reason can present a different question. The legal test remains content, context, purpose, and relationship to public business.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text: A public employee's personal phone is not a CPRA safe harbor. Ask what the employee was documenting and why, not who paid for the phone.

docs.title: 3. The agency's search duty reaches qualifying personal accounts/devices
docs.text:
City of San Jose also addresses the practical search problem.

The CPRA requires reasonable efforts to locate responsive public records; the search need only be reasonably calculated to locate responsive material and need not be extraordinarily extensive or intrusive.

For records potentially located in employees' nongovernmental accounts, the California Supreme Court stated that the agency's first step should be to communicate the request to the employees in question. The agency may reasonably rely on employees to search their own personal files, accounts, and devices for responsive public records.

This does not mean a requester normally has a right to seize or personally inspect an employee's entire private phone. It means the agency cannot categorically ignore responsive public-business material merely because the employee used a private device or account.

docs.title: Useful request language
docs.text:
All video, audio, photographs, and other recordings created, received, used, or retained by agency employees relating to the interaction at [facility] on [date] at approximately [time], including responsive public records created or stored on personal devices or personal accounts used in connection with public business.

A useful additional sentence is:

Please communicate this request to employees or other custodians reasonably likely to possess responsive public records, including qualifying records in personal accounts or devices, consistent with City of San Jose v. Superior Court.

This identifies the legal search problem without demanding passwords, private-device surrender, or unrelated private content.

docs.title: 4. Public-record status is separate from disclosure
docs.text:
The CPRA begins from broad public access, but a record can be a public record and still be wholly or partly withheld under a statutory exemption or privacy/privilege rule.

Government Code § 7922.000 places the burden on the agency to justify withholding by either:

  1. an express provision of the CPRA; or
  2. facts demonstrating that the public interest served by withholding clearly outweighs the public interest served by disclosure.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.000

Government Code § 7922.525 also requires disclosure of reasonably segregable nonexempt portions after exempt material is removed.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.525

docs.title: Field Guide distinction
docs.text:
Do not argue:

It is a public record, therefore you must give me the entire unredacted file.

Use:

The item appears to be a public record. If the agency withholds or redacts any portion, identify the legal basis and release reasonably segregable nonexempt material.

docs.title: 5. Core request and response rules
docs.text: This chapter does not attempt to reproduce every CPRA exemption. These provisions form the operational core for an auditor requesting evidence.

docs.title: § 7921.300 — requester's purpose generally does not control access
docs.text:
Access cannot be limited based on the purpose for which an otherwise disclosable record is requested.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7921.300

docs.title: § 7922.500 — no delay or obstruction
docs.text:
An agency may not delay or obstruct inspection or copying of public records.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.500

docs.title: § 7922.525 — inspection
docs.text:
Public records are generally open to inspection during office hours, subject to statutory exceptions, and reasonably segregable nonexempt portions must be available.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.525

docs.title: § 7922.530 — copies and personal copying equipment
docs.text:
A request that reasonably describes an identifiable record or records triggers the agency's duty to make copies promptly available subject to applicable law and fees. The provision also allows a person inspecting a disclosable record on agency premises to use personal equipment to photograph/copy it, subject to statutory conditions and reasonable safety/order limits.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.530

docs.title: § 7922.535 — determination deadline
docs.text:
As of the 2026 text, an agency ordinarily has 10 days after receipt of a request for copies to determine whether the request, in whole or in part, seeks copies of disclosable public records in the agency's possession and to notify the requester of that determination and reasons. If records are determined disclosable, the notice must also state the estimated date and time they will be made available.

The statute permits a written extension for specified unusual circumstances, not to exceed 14 additional days.

This is a determination timeline, not a universal command that every responsive record be produced within 10 days.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.535

docs.title: § 7922.540 — written denial
docs.text:
A denial of a written request must be in writing, identify the names and titles or positions of each person responsible for the denial, and justify withholding under § 7922.000.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.540

docs.title: §§ 7922.570-7922.585 — electronic records
docs.text:
Electronic public records generally must be made available in electronic form when requested under the statutory rules. The Act addresses available formats, certain extraction/programming costs, records no longer available electronically, system security, and computer software. The fact that public-record information is stored in a computer does not remove its public-record status.

Primary sources:

  • § 7922.570: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.570
  • § 7922.575: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.575
  • § 7922.580: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.580
  • § 7922.585: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.585

docs.title: §§ 7922.600-7922.605 — duty to assist
docs.text:
Subject to statutory qualifications, an agency must reasonably assist a requester to make a focused and effective request by helping identify responsive records/information, describing information technology or physical locations in which records exist, and suggesting ways to overcome practical barriers to disclosure.

Primary sources:

  • § 7922.600: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.600
  • § 7922.605: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7922.605

docs.title: 6. Preservation is not the same thing as disclosure — City of Gilroy
The 2026 California Supreme Court rule
docs.text:
In City of Gilroy v. Superior Court, 19 Cal.5th 38 (2026), filed January 15, 2026, the California Supreme Court held that the CPRA itself does not impose a duty on agencies to preserve for three years every record responsive to a CPRA request that the agency has withheld as exempt.

Official opinion page: https://courts.ca.gov/opinion/published-extended-post/2026-01-15/s282937

The Court emphasized that the CPRA does not itself contain a general retention obligation. Government Code § 7921.010(c) expressly recognizes destruction pursuant to law, and separate statutes govern retention and evidence preservation.

docs.title: What Gilroy means in the field
docs.text:
These statements are not safe field rules:

I requested it, so the CPRA automatically freezes it.

Once I say I am going to request that recording, deletion automatically violates the CPRA.

Neither proposition follows from Gilroy.

docs.title: The deliberate-destruction limitation matters
docs.text:
The Court carefully limited what it decided. In footnote 20, it explained that its preservation holding concerned destruction connected with the normal adoption, implementation, and operation of routine records-retention practices and policies. The Court expressly stated that it had no occasion to decide intentional destruction in other contexts that might reflect deliberate misconduct.

That means Gilroy should not be converted into:

An employee is free to delete a requested recording whenever they want.

It says no such thing.

The correct analysis after a deletion is:

  1. Was the item a public record?
  2. What retention statute/schedule/policy governed it?
  3. Was the deletion routine and authorized under that law/policy?
  4. Had litigation become reasonably foreseeable, triggering separate evidence-preservation law?
  5. Was the destruction intentional and outside ordinary retention practices?
  6. Do Government Code §§ 6200-6201 or other destruction/spoliation provisions apply?

docs.title: 7. A preservation notice is still valuable — but do not describe it as magic
docs.text:
Even though a CPRA preservation notice does not automatically create a CPRA litigation hold, it remains extremely useful evidence.

If the employee records the encounter, a calm on-camera statement can establish knowledge and identify the record before it disappears:

You're recording this interaction in connection with your work here. I intend to request that recording under the California Public Records Act. Please preserve the original recording and do not delete or alter it.

This can document:

  • the existence of the recording;
  • who apparently created it;
  • when and where it was created;
  • the work-related context;
  • notice that the public sought the record;
  • an explicit preservation request;
  • what the employee or agency did afterward.

Do not tell an employee:

I gave you a preservation notice, so deleting this is automatically a felony.

The notice may later be relevant to knowledge, intent, litigation foreseeability, compliance with retention law, or credibility, but the elements of any destruction offense or spoliation remedy must still be established.

docs.title: 8. Retention rules vary by agency and record type
docs.text:
There is no single California retention period for every state/local public record.

The California State Archives explains that state executive agencies operate under the State Records Management Act and approved records-retention schedules, while local government is not governed by that same standardized state program. Local-government retention depends on agency type, specific statutes, and local schedules/policies.

California State Archives records-management source: https://www.sos.ca.gov/archives/records-management-and-appraisal/records-management-handbook

docs.title: State executive agencies
docs.text:
The State Records Management Act, Government Code §§ 12270-12279, and the State Administrative Manual establish the state executive-agency records-management system. State agencies use approved records-retention schedules. State guidance explains that unscheduled state records are not simply disposable at an employee's discretion.

California State Archives: https://www.sos.ca.gov/archives/records-management-and-appraisal

State Administrative Manual, Chapter 1600: https://www.dgs.ca.gov/Resources/SAM/TOC/1600/Chapter-View

docs.title: Cities — Government Code § 34090
docs.text:
For cities, Government Code § 34090 provides a statutory mechanism for destruction of city records after they are no longer required, subject to approval/consent requirements and enumerated exceptions. It must be read with the city's adopted retention schedule and any more specific law governing the record.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=34090

docs.title: Routine city/city-county recordings — Government Code § 34090.6
docs.text:
Government Code § 34090.6 contains specialized retention/destruction provisions for specified routine video monitoring and telephone/radio communications. Its definitions and conditions matter; it should not be generalized to an ad hoc personal-phone recording by an employee.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=34090.6

docs.title: Counties — Government Code § 26202
docs.text:
Government Code § 26202 provides county record-destruction authority under specified circumstances. County retention should be checked against that statute, other applicable laws, and the county's adopted schedule/policy.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=26202

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Do not assume two years, one year, 60 days, or any other retention period without identifying the agency type, record type, governing statute, and actual approved/adopted schedule.

When preservation matters, request the retention policy itself.

docs.title: 9. Government Code §§ 6200-6201 — deliberate destruction requires careful analysis
docs.text:
Government Code § 6200 imposes criminal liability on an officer having custody of specified records/maps/books/papers/proceedings who willfully steals/removes/secretes, destroys/mutilates/defaces, or alters/falsifies them. Section 6201 separately reaches specified acts by a person who is not the officer described in § 6200.

Primary sources:

  • § 6200: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=6200
  • § 6201: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=6201

docs.title: Published California authority — People v. Sperl
docs.text:
In People v. Sperl, 54 Cal.App.3d 640 (1976), a published Court of Appeal decision, the Los Angeles County Marshal was convicted under § 6200 based on removal/secretion/destruction of official county radio logs.

The defendant argued that the logs were not public records because no ordinance or statute expressly required that they be maintained. The court rejected that argument. It explained that an official government record need not be expressly mandated by statute to fall within the public-record concept used there; a record kept as necessary or convenient to the discharge of official duty can qualify. The court also rejected the notion that a public official may treat official government records as personal property merely because the official controls the office.

Case source: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/3d/54/640.html

Related published authority includes People v. Pearson, 111 Cal.App.2d 9 (1952), involving official vice-investigation records, and Loder v. Municipal Court, 17 Cal.3d 859 (1976), which treated an arrest record as within § 6200's protection.

  • People v. Pearson: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2d/111/9.html
  • Loder v. Municipal Court: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/17/859.html

docs.title: Why this still does not answer the personal-phone hypothetical automatically
docs.text:
Sperl is important, but it involved official county department records and a county Marshal. Section 6200 itself uses the narrower phrase officer having custody and has its own statutory object/custody/willfulness requirements. The Field Guide therefore does not equate the CPRA's broad disclosure definition with § 6200's criminal elements.

A work-related personal-phone recording may be a CPRA public record under City of San Jose without automatically establishing that:

  • the employee is an officer within § 6200;
  • the recording is within § 6200's covered record/paper categories on those facts;
  • the employee had the required custody relationship;
  • deletion was willful and unauthorized rather than lawful routine disposition;
  • § 6201 or another statute does or does not apply instead.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
If you see an employee delete a work-related recording after being told it will be requested:

  • document exactly what occurred;
  • do not announce that a felony has definitely occurred;
  • request the applicable retention/destruction policy;
  • request records concerning deletion/disposition of the recording;
  • preserve your own recording and timeline;
  • determine whether §§ 6200-6201, an agency-specific retention law, or litigation-preservation rules actually apply.

docs.title: 10. Litigation preservation is a separate layer
docs.text:
City of Gilroy expressly recognized that law outside the CPRA can create preservation duties once litigation is reasonably foreseeable.

The Court cited California spoliation/discovery authorities for the principle that destruction of evidence after litigation begins—or in anticipation of discovery when litigation is objectively probable and likely—can trigger separate legal consequences.

This does not mean an ordinary CPRA request automatically makes litigation reasonably foreseeable. That determination depends on circumstances.

docs.title: Important distinction
docs.text:
CPRA request pending

is not automatically identical to:

litigation objectively probable and likely to arise.

If an encounter escalates into an arrest, injury claim, formal government claim, attorney preservation letter, lawsuit, or similarly concrete dispute, the separate litigation-preservation analysis becomes increasingly important.

docs.title: 11. Practical workflow — public employee records you back
Step 1 — establish the recording and work context
docs.text:
Useful factual questions:

  • Are you recording this interaction?
  • Are you making that recording in connection with your work here?
  • Is that an agency device or your personal phone?

The third question can be evidentially useful, but device ownership is not dispositive under City of San Jose.

docs.title: Step 2 — give a narrow preservation notice
docs.text:
I intend to request that recording under the California Public Records Act. Please preserve the original recording and do not delete or alter it.

Do not overstate the legal effect of this statement.

docs.title: Step 3 — promptly send the CPRA request to the agency
docs.text:
Identify:

  • date;
  • approximate time;
  • facility/location;
  • employee if known;
  • subject of encounter;
  • categories of recordings sought;
  • personal-device/public-business records where applicable.

docs.title: Step 4 — ask the agency to search likely custodians
docs.text: Use City of San Jose to make clear that a responsive work-related record cannot be categorically excluded merely because it is in an employee's personal account/device.

docs.title: Step 5 — if the record is withheld
docs.text:
Ask for:

  • written legal basis for withholding;
  • release of reasonably segregable portions;
  • estimated availability date for disclosable records;
  • identification of person(s) responsible for a written denial as required by statute.

docs.title: Step 6 — if the record is missing or deleted
docs.text:
Request:

  • retention schedule governing that record category;
  • agency records-retention/destruction policy;
  • existing records documenting deletion, loss, disposition, or destruction;
  • metadata or audit logs if maintained;
  • communications concerning preservation/deletion;
  • date and manner of deletion;
  • identity/position of the person who authorized or performed disposition, to the extent maintained in public records;
  • any record showing routine automatic deletion.

Then analyze the facts under the correct retention/destruction law rather than assuming the CPRA alone prohibited deletion.

docs.title: A. Recording request
docs.text: Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, I request all video, audio, photographs, and other recordings created, received, used, or retained by agency employees relating to the interaction at [location] on [date] at approximately [time], including responsive public records created or stored on personal devices or personal accounts used in connection with public business. Please communicate this request to employees or other custodians reasonably likely to possess responsive records.

docs.title: B. Preservation language
docs.text: Please preserve responsive records while this request is being processed. This preservation request is intended to identify the records at issue and avoid preventable loss; it is not an assertion that the CPRA itself creates a universal retention period.

docs.title: C. Missing/deleted-record follow-up
docs.text:
If any responsive record existed but is no longer available, please identify any existing public records documenting its deletion, destruction, disposition, loss, retention period, or automatic-deletion process, including the applicable retention schedule/policy and responsive deletion or audit logs maintained by the agency.

These templates should be adapted to the actual agency and incident rather than used as incantations.

docs.title: 13. Enforcement
docs.text:
Government Code § 7923.000 allows a person to institute proceedings for injunctive or declaratory relief or a writ of mandate to enforce the right to inspect or receive public records.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=7923.000

docs.title: City of Gilroy — declaratory relief can remain meaningful after records are gone
docs.text:
City of Gilroy held that declaratory relief under the CPRA is available at least where a declaration would resolve an ongoing dispute about the parties' rights and obligations in a way likely to affect future records requests or future conduct.

Destroyed records cannot be recreated by a disclosure order, but a court can sometimes still resolve a recurring dispute about inadequate searches, exemption practices, or other CPRA obligations.

Do not turn this into a universal promise that every completed or historical CPRA dispute supports declaratory relief. Gilroy did not define every circumstance in which such relief is available.

docs.title: 14. What this chapter does not yet establish
docs.text:
This chapter does not yet claim completeness for:

  • every exemption in Government Code Division 10 Parts 5 and 6;
  • law-enforcement investigative-record exemptions and disclosure mandates;
  • Penal Code § 832.7 peace-officer personnel-record disclosure;

docs.title: Field rule — Penal Code § 148(g)
docs.text:
California expressly protects the act of recording public and peace officers against several common theories of police intervention.

Penal Code § 148(g) states that the fact a person takes a photograph or makes an audio/video recording of a public officer or peace officer, while the officer is in a public place or the recorder is in a place the recorder has the right to be, does not in and of itself:

  • violate § 148(a) obstruction/resistance;
  • create reasonable suspicion to detain the recorder; or
  • create probable cause to arrest the recorder.

Primary source: California Penal Code § 148

docs.title: What "in and of itself" means
docs.text:
Section 148(g) protects the recording activity itself from being treated as obstruction, reasonable suspicion, or probable cause.

It does not immunize independent conduct that separately violates the law. For example, the statute does not say that a person may physically obstruct an officer merely because the person is also recording.

The project's standing scenario deliberately removes those kinds of independent behaviors from ordinary hypotheticals so the recording itself is not silently converted into obstruction, disturbance, or some unrelated offense.

docs.title: Section 148(a)(1)
docs.text:
Section 148(a)(1) prohibits willfully resisting, delaying, or obstructing a public officer, peace officer, or specified emergency medical technician while that person is discharging or attempting to discharge an official duty.

When § 148 is asserted against a peaceful recorder, the analysis should therefore identify the conduct alleged to constitute resistance, delay, or obstruction apart from the fact of recording itself.

docs.title: Useful factual questions
docs.text:
If an officer says the recording is interfering:

  • What specific conduct, apart from my recording itself, are you saying is obstructing or delaying you?
  • Are you ordering me to move to a particular location?
  • Is that order based on a safety perimeter, access issue, evidence preservation, or another identified reason?
  • Am I being detained?

These questions preserve the factual basis for later review. They do not guarantee that an officer will agree with the legal analysis on scene.

For planned facility investigations, see Facility Research and Field Verification. That workflow separates the governing law, written policy, signage, prior incidents, and any later police enforcement before a field visit is treated as evidence.

docs.title: Forum status is a separate layer
docs.text:
A public-facing government area is not automatically a public forum merely because visitors may enter it. Conversely, calling an area a nonpublic forum does not by itself answer whether recording is protected or prohibited there.

Before turning a recording dispute into a forum slogan, separate:

  1. the specific area and its forum classification;
  2. the specific expressive activity at issue;
  3. any independent recording protection such as Penal Code § 148(g) or an open-meeting statute;
  4. privacy, security, court, school, or other specialized rules;
  5. actual interference with operations; and
  6. the independent authority for exclusion, detention, or arrest.

See public-forum-doctrine.md.

docs.title: When recording turns into a police encounter
docs.text:
Section 148(g) creates an important bridge between the recording chapter and police-encounters.md: recording by itself does not supply reasonable suspicion or probable cause within the statute's scope, but independent facts can still create lawful detention or arrest authority.

Once an officer begins controlling the recorder rather than merely speaking with them, analyze the encounter separately:

  1. is the contact still consensual, or has a Fourth Amendment seizure occurred?
  2. if detained, what specific facts supplied reasonable suspicion when the detention began?
  3. is identification merely requested, or does a particular California statute require it in this context?
  4. is a frisk supported by a separate armed-and-dangerous safety basis?
  5. if arrest occurs, what facts objectively supplied probable cause?
  6. has questioning become custodial interrogation for Fifth Amendment / Miranda purposes?
  7. if a phone/camera is taken, what authority supports physical seizure and what separate authority supports searching digital contents?

The detailed encounter doctrine and field language are maintained in police-encounters.md.

docs.title: When the public employee records you back
docs.text:
A public employee recording an auditor does not by itself establish that the auditor may record everywhere or that every facility restriction is invalid. It does, however, create a separate public-records/evidence question.

If the employee makes a work-related recording— including on a personal phone—public-records-evidence-preservation.md explains:

  • why personal-device storage does not categorically remove a work-related recording from the CPRA under City of San Jose v. Superior Court;
  • how to identify and request the recording;
  • why public-record status and disclosure are separate questions;
  • why a CPRA request or preservation notice does not itself create a universal retention period under City of Gilroy v. Superior Court;
  • how to request the applicable retention policy and deletion/disposition records if the recording later disappears.

A useful on-scene statement is narrow:

I intend to request that work-related recording under the California Public Records Act. Please preserve the original recording and do not delete or alter it.

Do not describe that statement as an automatic CPRA litigation hold or assert that deletion is automatically a crime. The applicable retention/destruction law must still be identified.

docs.title: Case-law research still required
docs.text:
This chapter is intentionally incomplete until the project verifies and adds the controlling First Amendment recording cases separately. The case index should distinguish:

  • the constitutional right to record matters of public interest;
  • recording police officers performing duties;
  • verbal criticism of officers;
  • time/place/manner restrictions;
  • safety perimeters and interference;
  • retaliation for protected recording;
  • qualified-immunity questions.

No case should be added based only on an auditor's characterization of what it supposedly held.

docs.title: Standing Scenario
docs.text:
The Field Guide uses one default factual baseline so each hypothetical can analyze the government's asserted authority without inventing unrelated misconduct.

The project-methodology status describes this page's function. Statutory and case-law propositions referenced here retain the verification status shown in the substantive chapters, authority index, and sweep ledgers.

Unless a chapter or scenario expressly changes a fact, assume the factual conditions below. The baseline does not decide whether a disputed recording restriction, expressive activity, facility rule, or later government order is lawful; those legal questions are analyzed separately.

docs.title: Baseline facts
docs.text:
At the beginning of the scenario, assume the auditor:

  1. is in a place and specific area they may lawfully be, during hours when that area is open to the public;
  2. has not entered an employee-only, secured, closed, or otherwise restricted area;
  3. is peacefully observing, photographing, filming, recording, asking questions, requesting records, or otherwise gathering information;
  4. is not blocking doors, counters, queues, sidewalks, roadways, traffic, or another person's movement;
  5. is not physically interfering with employees, officers, emergency personnel, visitors, or members of the public;
  6. is not touching, crowding, following at close range, or entering another person's personal space;
  7. is not threatening anyone, fighting, or challenging anyone to fight;
  8. is not creating loud and unreasonable noise or intentionally shouting over government business;
  9. is not intentionally obstructing or intimidating employees or people transacting business with a public agency, and is not knowingly making a material misrepresentation of law to people there to transact business with the agency;
  10. is not willfully resisting, delaying, or obstructing an officer through conduct independent of the activity being analyzed;
  11. is not gathered with others to commit an unlawful act or to carry out a lawful act in a violent, boisterous, or tumultuous manner; is not remaining at a riot, rout, or unlawful assembly after a lawful warning to disperse; and is not assembled with others for the purpose of disturbing the public peace or committing an unlawful act;
  12. has no additional misconduct silently added to the scenario; if an analysis depends on some other act, omission, intent, or circumstance, that fact must be expressly supplied;
  13. is not intentionally targeting uninvolved private individuals or their personal information; and
  14. is not assumed to carry any identification card or credential merely by virtue of being present in public.

The auditor may criticize government, decline consensual conversation, decline consent to a search, ask officials to identify legal authority, or continue recording while remaining in the same lawful physical location. Those facts are not silently converted into obstruction, intimidation, disturbance, or disorderly conduct. Whether the recording or expression itself is protected in that specific place remains a separate legal question.

An uninvolved private individual is not made a target merely by being present. If that person voluntarily engages the auditor or becomes directly relevant to the government conduct being documented, the resulting interaction may itself be documented; that does not authorize unnecessary pursuit of unrelated personal information.

The standing scenario does not create a universal rule that identification can never be required. Custody/booking, specialized facilities, and other specific legal contexts may create different duties. For ordinary pedestrian police encounters, see police-encounters.md: the current California sweep has not identified a general pedestrian carry-ID statute or general statutory stop-and-identify law equivalent to Nevada's law in Hiibel. An officer's request for identification does not itself establish a legal duty; the applicable statute, context, and case law still have to be identified.

docs.title: What the standing facts are designed to exclude
docs.text:
The standing scenario does not create immunity from any statute. It removes the common factual predicates that otherwise derail analysis of the legal issue actually presented.

Authority / label Standing-scenario consequence Penal Code § 415 — disturbing the peace No fighting or challenge to fight is assumed; no malicious/willful loud and unreasonable noise is assumed; no words satisfying § 415(3)'s immediate-violent-reaction element are assumed. Penal Code § 403 — disturbing a meeting No willful disturbance or breaking up of a lawful meeting is assumed. In a meeting scenario, a brief verbal or nonverbal reaction is not assumed to actually impede proceedings unless the facts say otherwise. Penal Code § 148(a)(1) — resisting/delaying/obstructing No independent willful resistance, delay, or obstruction is assumed. Section 148(g) separately provides that recording a public/peace officer in the statutory circumstances does not, by itself, establish § 148(a), reasonable suspicion, or probable cause. Penal Code §§ 602 / 602.1 — trespass/interference The auditor is not assumed to begin the encounter as a trespasser, to obstruct or intimidate public-agency business, or to knowingly make a material misrepresentation of law to people there to transact business with the agency. A later order to leave is a new fact that must be analyzed rather than presumed valid or invalid. Penal Code §§ 407-409 / 416 — unlawful assembly, participation, and dispersal theories No riot, rout, unlawful assembly, participation in an unlawful assembly, or gathering formed for an unlawful/disturbance purpose is assumed. Penal Code § 647 — disorderly conduct None of § 647's enumerated forms of disorderly conduct is silently assumed merely because someone calls the auditor "disorderly," "suspicious," or "annoying." Local ordinance / facility rule No unstated noise, obstruction, restricted-area entry, loitering, or similar conduct is assumed. The actual ordinance, regulation, policy, or rule must be identified and analyzed.

Primary statutory sources:

  • Penal Code § 415: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=415.
  • Penal Code § 403: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=403.
  • Penal Code § 148: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.
  • Penal Code § 602.1: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1
  • Penal Code § 407: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=407.
  • Penal Code § 408: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=408.
  • Penal Code § 409: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=409.
  • Penal Code § 416: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=416.
  • Penal Code § 647: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=647.

docs.title: Another person's reaction is not silently attributed to the auditor
docs.text:
A government employee, contractor, security guard, visitor, or private individual may become uncomfortable, angry, offended, argumentative, or confrontational because of the peaceful activity described by the standing facts.

Unless the scenario says otherwise, that reaction does not change the baseline facts about what the auditor personally did.

The guide therefore should not reason backward from:

someone became upset

to:

the auditor must have been disturbing the peace, obstructing business, intimidating someone, or causing a meeting disruption.

The relevant statute still has to be matched to the auditor's own conduct.

docs.title: Public-meeting variant
docs.text:
For a Brown Act meeting, also assume unless stated otherwise:

  • the auditor obeys otherwise lawful time limits and procedural rules governing the speaker's own comment period;
  • a brief expression such as applause, laughter, a gesture, or a short verbal reaction does not actually disrupt, disturb, impede, or render infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting;
  • the auditor does not threaten force;
  • any favorable and unfavorable audience reactions are documented separately so viewpoint-neutrality questions can be tested against comparable conduct.

Government Code § 54957.95 currently defines "disrupting" in terms of behavior that actually disrupts, disturbs, impedes, or renders infeasible the orderly conduct of the meeting and ordinarily requires a warning before removal. Section 54954.3 separately prohibits a local legislative body from prohibiting public criticism of agency policies, programs, services, or the acts or omissions of the legislative body.

The public-meeting assumption does not itself decide whether a particular reasonable and lawful decorum regulation applies. That question remains part of the statutory and First Amendment analysis.

Sources:

  • Government Code § 54957.95: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54957.95
  • Government Code § 54954.3: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=54954.3
  • Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc): https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2010/12/15/07-15814.pdf

docs.title: New facts restart the analysis
docs.text:
The standing scenario is a starting point, not a prediction of the outcome.

Examples of facts that require a fresh legal analysis include:

  • an employee or supervisor orders the auditor to leave;
  • a facility claims an area is restricted;
  • normal public hours end;
  • a security-screening condition is invoked;
  • an officer establishes a safety perimeter;
  • an officer says the auditor is detained;
  • an ordinance, regulation, court rule, or facility policy is identified;
  • the auditor changes position or conduct;
  • a meeting chair gives a warning under an applicable rule;
  • the government identifies conduct independent of filming or criticism that it claims is unlawful.

A later removal command does not retroactively make the initial lawful presence trespass, and the standing scenario does not predetermine whether refusing that later command would be lawful. That question belongs to the applicable forum, policy, removal, trespass, and police-encounter analysis.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Without a fixed baseline, a hypothetical about a camera can become a hypothetical about imaginary shouting; a hypothetical about a records request can become one about imaginary obstruction; and a hypothetical about removal can quietly assume the auditor was already trespassing.

The standing scenario prevents that drift. If a legal conclusion depends on additional misconduct, the scenario must actually supply that fact.

docs.title: Trespass and Removal from Public Agencies
docs.text:
Research status: Penal Code §§ 601-603 and the complete current § 602 / § 602.x family have been reviewed at the primary-text level. A first controlling-case pass has also been completed for § 602(m), § 602(q), and the common intentional-interference structure of § 602.1. Core public-forum doctrine is now reviewed in public-forum-doctrine.md; area-specific forum classifications, local ordinances, facility-specific rules, and several other trespass subsections still require separate research.

This chapter addresses the recurring audit problem in which a government employee or peace officer treats you were asked to leave as though it were a complete criminal-trespass rule. California's trespass statutes are more specific than that.

Under the project's standing scenario, the auditor begins lawfully present in the specific public area and is not assumed to be obstructing, intimidating, threatening, or otherwise committing an independent offense. A later order to leave is therefore treated as a new fact: the guide analyzes the authority for the order and the consequences of remaining rather than retroactively assuming the auditor was already trespassing.

docs.title: Short field rule
docs.text:
Within the California trespass statutes reviewed here, there is no general formula that reduces criminal trespass in an ordinary public-agency interior to:

A government employee asked you to leave, therefore remaining is automatically criminal trespass.

Identify the actual statute or other legal authority, then test its elements against the facts. Different provisions turn on materially different predicates: whether property is open to the general public, whether a public building is closed, whether someone is intentionally obstructing agency business, whether a person entered and occupied property without consent, whether a secured area is posted, or whether screening was intentionally avoided.

A lawful policy or facility restriction can still matter even when a particular trespass subsection does not fit. Conversely, the existence or violation of a policy does not by itself establish every element of a criminal-trespass offense.

Important separate question: open to the public is an access description, not a forum classification. A public-facing lobby may be open for agency business while still being a nonpublic or limited forum for expressive activity. Forum status must be analyzed separately, often area by area within the same facility. See public-forum-doctrine.md.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602 — complete subsection matrix
docs.text:
Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.

Section 602 lists numerous distinct ways to commit trespass. For peaceful public-facility auditing, only a subset is ordinarily central, but the entire current subsection range is accounted for below so that 602 is not treated as an undifferentiated label.

Subdivision Primary-text rule Field Guide classification § 602(a) Cutting/destroying/injuring timber on another's land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(b) Carrying away timber from another's land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(c) Maliciously injuring/severing attached property or produce N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(d) Taking earth/soil/stone from a city lot without license N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(e) Taking earth/soil/stone from land recognized as a street/alley/avenue/park without authority N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(f) Damaging specified signs/notices or placing advertisements/signage on property without permission N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(g) Shellfish-bed entry/injury/removal and boundary damage N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(h) Posted animal-raising land/building entry and related conduct SPECIALIZED § 602(i) Opening/damaging fences/gates or damaging specified no-shooting signs N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(j) Building fires on posted land without written permission N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602(k) Entering land for purpose of injuring property/property rights or intentionally interfering with, obstructing, or injuring a lawful business/occupation carried on by the possessor REVIEW-LATER;
