docs.title: § 602(m) — entering and occupying means more than transient presence
docs.text:
The statutory text uses the conjunctive phrase entering and occupying real property or a structure without consent.

This is no longer merely a textual inference. In In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (1981), the California Supreme Court explained that the predecessor subdivision requires occupation of the property, a nontransient, continuous type of possession; the subdivision was later renumbered to current § 602(m) without substantive change to this language.

The published Ninth Circuit decision Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010) applied that rule to probable cause. Officers knew that Edgerly had been on fenced property for only a matter of minutes. The Ninth Circuit held those facts did not give a reasonable officer probable cause under the entering-and-occupying subdivision. The court nevertheless found probable cause under a different trespass statute, § 602.8(a), because the property was fenced and posted. That second holding is an important warning not to turn the § 602(m) limitation into a blanket no trespass rule.

Current Judicial Council CALCRIM No. 2931 likewise instructs that the prosecution must prove that, after entering without consent, the defendant occupied some part of the property continuously until removed.

Doctrine-reviewed field rule: Mere momentary or transient presence is not enough for § 602(m)'s occupying element. Another trespass provision can independently fit the same facts.

Case sources:

  • In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (Cal. 1981): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/supreme-court/3d/29/1.html
  • Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010): https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2004/03/17/9917319.pdf
  • Judicial Council CALCRIM materials: https://courts.ca.gov/advisory-body/criminal-jury-instructions-advisory-committee

docs.title: § 602(o) — property not open to the general public
docs.text:
Section 602(o) expressly concerns land, real property, or structures not open to the general public. Its refusal-to-leave language should not be quoted as though it were a universal rule for an ordinary public counter, lobby, library floor, or other place currently open to the public.

Areas within a generally public-facing property can still be separately nonpublic. Federal cases applying California law have treated the particular area at issue—not merely the character of the larger property—as important. This proposition remains below DOCTRINE-REVIEWED for our public-agency scenario until the California case layer is completed.

docs.title: Caution: do not overstate § 602(o)'s constitutional-savings language
docs.text:
The text broadly contains a labor-activity exception. It also contains constitutional-activity language in the sentence addressing housing-authority property. Courts have not spoken with one clear published voice about whether that constitutional language operates as a general exception to all of subdivision (o) or specifically as part of the housing-authority rule.

A federal district court in Cuviello v. Cal Expo read the constitutional phrase as linked to the housing-authority clause rather than as a subdivision-wide exemption. By contrast, the 2026 Court of Appeal opinion People v. Hsiung read the phrase broadly while rejecting a First Amendment challenge—but that discussion appears in Part III, which the Court of Appeal expressly excluded from publication. It is therefore not precedential California authority.

Field Guide rule: Do not presently claim that § 602(o) contains a settled subdivision-wide constitutional exemption. Analyze the actual constitutional right independently and continue the case-law research.

docs.title: § 602(q) — public buildings after closing
docs.text:
Section 602(q) expressly addresses a public building of a public agency, but its text is limited to hours when the building is regularly closed to the public. It also requires a request from a regularly employed guard, watchperson, or custodian and circumstances that would indicate to a reasonable person that the person has no apparent lawful business to pursue.

Published California authority confirms that those limitations matter. In Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968), the Court of Appeal considered the predecessor-lettered version of this same public-building closing-hours rule. A welfare-rights advocate remained in a county welfare building hours after its regular closing. The court treated regular closing, a qualifying request, and the apparent lawful business inquiry as substantive predicates and held that the latter uses an objective reasonable-person standard. The opinion also relied on In re Bacon for the proposition that expressive/grievance activity that may be lawful during open hours does not itself require a public building to remain open after its regular closing.

Doctrine-reviewed field rule: § 602(q) is a closing-hours statute, not a general daytime removal provision. The apparent lawful business component is objective rather than whatever the person personally believes.

Case source:

  • Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (Cal. Ct. App. 1968): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2d/258/497.html

docs.title: § 602(y) — security screening is its own rule
docs.text: Section 602(y) concerns intentionally avoiding submission to the screening and inspection of one's person and accessible property when entering or reentering a courthouse or city/county/state building, where the entrances carry the required notice. It is not a generic prohibition on recording or peaceful presence after successfully passing security.

docs.title: Screening is not the same thing as a visitor sign-in or ID requirement
docs.text:
A visitor log, badge procedure, appointment check, request to state a destination, or demand to show identification is a separate access-policy question. Section 602(y)'s text does not itself say that refusal to write one's name in a binder, state a purpose, or produce identification is criminal trespass.

A government office may still be able to impose reasonable, viewpoint-neutral visitor conditions under other lawful authority, especially in a nonpublic or limited-purpose forum. The legal analysis therefore has two steps:

  1. Is the visitor condition itself lawful for this particular area and purpose?
  2. If a person refuses it, what statute or other authority actually supports exclusion, detention, or arrest?

Do not collapse the facility has a sign-in policy into § 602(y) makes refusal a crime.

docs.title: Penal Code § 602.1 — interference with business/public-agency operations
docs.text: Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1

docs.title: § 602.1(b) — public agency open to the public
docs.text:
For a public agency open to the public, § 602.1(b) requires:

  1. intentional interference with lawful public-agency business;
  2. accomplished by obstructing or intimidating employees carrying on the business or people there to transact business; and
  3. refusal to leave after a qualifying request from the office manager/supervisor or a peace officer acting at that person's request.

The statute does not say employee asks + refusal = offense.

Under this project's standing scenario, the auditor is not blocking access, physically interfering, threatening, creating unreasonable noise, or invading personal space. That makes the statute's actual intentional interference / obstruction / intimidation language especially important.

docs.title: Published appellate guideposts — policy violation is not automatically the crime
docs.text:
In Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001), a photographer/legal observer was arrested near the Moscone Center under § 602.1. The Ninth Circuit described § 602.1 as requiring both intentional interference and refusal to leave and expressly rejected the argument that the intent-to-interfere element could simply be inferred from refusal. The record showed no deliberate obstruction or intimidation: Dubner was photographing, conversing, and positioned away from the doors.

The precise statutory wording quoted in Dubner concerned the business-establishment version of § 602.1 rather than today's public-agency subdivision (b), so the case should not be overstated as a published construction of every detail of current § 602.1(b). But the same intentional-interference/obstruction-or-intimidation structure appears in current subdivision (b), and Dubner is binding Ninth Circuit authority on the Fourth Amendment probable-cause consequences of treating refusal alone as sufficient under § 602.1.

California's published Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (2004) reaches a closely related point under § 602.1(a): violating or refusing to accept otherwise enforceable time/place/manner rules does not necessarily constitute the misdemeanor. The criminal § 602.1 question remains whether the statutory obstruction/intimidation/interference elements occurred. Hamburg involved private retail property, not a public-agency interior, so it does not decide the forum or policy authority of a government facility. It does strongly support keeping was the rule enforceable? separate from were the elements of § 602.1 committed?

A later unpublished Ninth Circuit decision, Mackey v. Meyer, 675 F. App'x 705 (9th Cir. 2017), applied Dubner specifically to § 602.1(b) at a California DMV and found no probable cause where video contradicted assertions of obstruction/intimidation. Because that disposition is unpublished, this guide retains it only as a research cross-check, not binding precedent.

Field rule: Do not concede that I refused to leave or I violated policy supplies the missing obstruction/intimidation facts. Ask what conduct is alleged to constitute intentional interference and separately identify the authority for the underlying policy/exclusion.

Case sources:

  • Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001): https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2004/03/17/9917319.pdf
  • Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (Cal. Ct. App. 2004): https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2004/a101829.html

docs.title: § 602.1(c) — knowingly material misrepresentation of law
docs.text:
This separate public-agency provision is easy to overlook. It applies where a person intentionally interferes with public-agency business by knowingly making a material misrepresentation of the law to people there to transact business with the agency, followed by refusal to leave after the qualifying request.

The 2017 legislative materials describe the amendment as aimed at a then-perceived gap involving illegitimate solicitors who made material misrepresentations of law to people transacting business with public agencies. The statute still must be applied according to its enacted elements.

Field implication: The project should be meticulous about stating law accurately. A good-faith disagreement over legal interpretation is not textually identical to knowingly making a material misrepresentation, but controlling judicial construction of subdivision (c) remains to be researched.

docs.title: § 602.1(d)(2) — constitutional-activity exception
docs.text:
Section 602.1 expressly states that it does not apply to a person on the premises engaging in activities protected by the California Constitution or United States Constitution.

This is significant, but it does not mean camera = automatic exemption. Whether the underlying conduct is constitutionally protected in that particular place remains a forum/doctrine question.

docs.title: § 602.1(e) — other law still matters
docs.text:
Section 602.1 does not supersede other law. Therefore:

I do not satisfy § 602.1(b) is not the same proposition as no other lawful authority can require me to leave.

That distinction is central to the Field Guide.

docs.title: Adjacent trespass/property provisions reviewed
docs.text:
The complete currently numbered § 602.x family and immediate surrounding trespass provisions were reviewed so that specialized statutes are not mistaken for general rules.

Authority Subject Classification § 601 Trespass following a credible threat with intent to execute the threat N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.2 Limits certain county written-permission ordinances for vacant/unimproved private land N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.3 Remaining lodger in specified owner-occupied dwelling after termination N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.4 Unauthorized selling/peddling on specified airport property SPECIALIZED § 602.5 Unauthorized entry/remain in noncommercial dwelling/residential place N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.6 Closed state/county/district/citrus-fair buildings or grounds; qualifying order plus failure to identify/account for presence SPECIALIZED; important ID-demand contrast § 602.7 Unauthorized selling/peddling on specified transit property SPECIALIZED § 602.8 Entry onto cultivated/fenced/posted land; includes express constitutional-activity exception SPECIALIZED; can independently matter even when § 602(m) does not § 602.9 Taking/claiming residential dwelling for unauthorized rental N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.10 Physical-force obstruction of students/teachers at UC/CSU/community-college facilities SPECIALIZED school/campus rule § 602.11 Physical detention/obstruction preventing entry/exit of health-care facility, place of worship, or school; statute expressly says physically does not include speech SPECIALIZED § 602.12 Entry onto residential property of academic researcher for purpose of chilling/interfering with academic freedom N/A-STANDING-SCOPE § 602.13 Unauthorized entry into posted animal enclosure at zoo/circus/traveling exhibit SPECIALIZED § 603 Forcible entry into occupied/occupiable building plus property damage N/A-STANDING-SCOPE

docs.title: § 602.6 — why it matters even though it is specialized
docs.text:
Section 602.6 is a useful antidote to vague claims that California always requires a person in a government facility to identify themselves. It is a specific statute for specified fair buildings/grounds when they are not open to the general public, after a qualifying direction to leave and determination that the person lacks apparent lawful business or another legitimate reason for remaining; the statute then expressly includes failure to identify and account for one's presence.

That specialized text should not be generalized into a statewide public employee asks for ID → ID is mandatory rule.

docs.title: Live removal / trespass decision tree
docs.text: This is a factual and legal sorting tool, not a set of magic words.

docs.title: 1. Establish the status of the specific area
docs.text:
Do not classify the entire building with one label if the encounter occurs in only part of it. Ask/document:

  • Is this government property?
  • What specific area am I in: exterior sidewalk/plaza, vestibule, public lobby, service counter area, meeting room, secured hallway, staff-only area, courtroom, records room, etc.?
  • Is this particular area presently open to the general public?
  • Is the building within normal public hours?
  • Is this area restricted/secured/staff-only even though another part of the building is public-facing?
  • Is there a posted closure, screening requirement, visitor sign-in rule, badge rule, appointment rule, or other access condition?

This immediately separates provisions such as § 602(o), § 602(q), and § 602(y).

Do not equate public access with public-forum status. A lobby can be open for agency business while remaining a nonpublic or limited-purpose forum. Forum classification is a separate constitutional inquiry and may differ from one area of the same facility to another.

docs.title: 2. Identify the rule being invoked
docs.text:
If an employee says policy says no filming, you must sign in, or you must show ID, distinguish:

  • the written facility policy;
  • whether the rule is a screening rule, visitor-management condition, or identification demand;
  • any statute/regulation/order authorizing the restriction;
  • the forum/access classification of the specific area;
  • any applicable constitutional limitation; and
  • the criminal statute, if police are threatening arrest.

A policy can be legally valid without itself being the criminal offense. Conversely, calling something policy does not immunize it from constitutional review. Hamburg is a useful statutory reminder that enforceability of a rule and commission of a § 602.1 crime are separate questions.

For planned facility investigations, Facility Research and Field Verification provides the project workflow for tracing the authority chain from controlling law to written policy, signage, prior enforcement, exclusion/removal authority, and any separate detention/citation/arrest authority invoked.

docs.title: 3. Identify the alleged conduct
docs.text:
Useful questions include:

  • What specific conduct are you saying violates the rule?
  • Is the asserted violation simply that I am recording?
  • Is the asserted violation that I declined to sign a visitor log or show identification?
  • Is this a security-screening requirement, or a separate visitor-access policy?
  • Who am I allegedly obstructing or intimidating?
  • What agency business am I intentionally interfering with?
  • Are you saying this particular area is not open to the general public?
  • Are you saying the building is currently closed?

If § 602.1 is asserted, Dubner makes the distinction between refusal and intentional interference especially important.

docs.title: 4. If police arrive, separate removal authority from detention authority
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Am I being detained?
  • What offense do you reasonably suspect?
  • Which Penal Code section/subdivision are you relying on?
  • What facts satisfy its elements?

A facility employee's desire that someone leave and a peace officer's authority to detain/arrest are analytically distinct questions.

Edgerly is also a useful reminder that probable cause must ultimately connect to a particular statutory offense. An officer can rely on a different offense from the one first announced if the known facts objectively establish it, so the correct field question is not merely Did you cite the wrong subsection? but What actual offense do the known facts establish?

docs.title: 5. Treat ID as a separate legal question
docs.text:
Do not provide false identifying information. Penal Code § 148.9 is separately queued for the police-encounters/identification chapter.

If an officer or employee asserts that identification is mandatory, identify the legal basis rather than assuming a universal California stop-and-identify or government-building sign-in rule. The existence of specialized statutes such as § 602.6 and § 602(y) reinforces why the precise legal setting matters.

docs.title: 6. If the encounter reaches a final arrest threat
docs.text:
A useful evidentiary question is:

Are you ordering me to leave under threat of arrest, and what law are you relying on?

If the person chooses to comply, they can make clear that compliance is under protest and not consent to the asserted legal basis. If the person chooses to remain, the risk changes substantially because an officer may arrest first and the legal merits may be litigated later.

The Field Guide's purpose is to help a person understand that choice and preserve the factual/legal record, not to pretend a correct legal argument guarantees that an arrest will not occur.

docs.title: What this review does not yet establish
docs.text:
This chapter does not yet establish final doctrine on:

  • application of § 602(m) specifically to ordinary government-property interiors open to the public, beyond the established nontransient/continuous-occupation requirement;
  • the full California appellate construction of § 602(o)'s not open to the general public limitation or the scope of its constitutional-savings language;
  • constitutional limits on removing a peaceful recorder from government-building interiors;
  • forum classification of libraries, police lobbies, DA/reception lobbies, agency counters, DMV lobbies, courthouses, and similar facilities;
  • whether and when visitor sign-in, badge, appointment, or ID conditions are lawful for a particular government-office area;
  • whether and when violation of a government-facility policy supplies lawful grounds for exclusion;
  • due-process issues surrounding longer-term bans/exclusions;
  • First Amendment retaliation where protected recording or criticism motivates removal;
  • the full current construction of § 602.1(b)'s obstruction/intimidation element in public-agency interiors;
  • § 602.1(c)'s material-misrepresentation provision;
  • identification duties during lawful detention;
  • local ordinances or agency regulations that independently govern a facility.

docs.title: Remaining case-law research queue
docs.text:
The next doctrinal pass should prioritize:

  • California appellate cases applying § 602(o) to public/government property;
  • § 602.1(b) public-agency obstruction/intimidation cases;
  • § 602.1(d)(2) constitutional-activity exception;
  • application of the now-reviewed core forum doctrine to specific government facilities;
  • area-specific forum classification rather than facility-wide labels;
  • visitor sign-in, badge, appointment, and identification conditions in public-facing government offices;
  • libraries and other limited/nonpublic forums;
  • retaliation for protected speech/recording;
  • reasonable suspicion based on a facility's request for removal;
  • whether an invalid policy/order can supply criminal trespass probable cause;
  • notice, authority of the person requesting departure, and lawful-business/public-hours issues.

docs.title: California Public Facility 1A Registry
docs.text: Working methodology v0.4 Status: Working project methodology; initial pilot validation complete Last revised: September 21, 2026

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
The California Public Facility 1A Registry is a research and accountability index for publicly accessible government facilities in California.

Its purpose is to document and organize:

  • publicly available facility information;
  • official agency policies, regulations, rules, and posted notices;
  • applicable constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, and case law;
  • documented field observations made during peaceful First Amendment activity;
  • public-records responses and other official follow-up materials;
  • later corrections, policy changes, or agency responses.

The Registry is intended to help readers understand how government facilities state and apply rules affecting peaceful observation, photography, recording, speech, petitioning, access, and related First Amendment activity.

The Registry is not a target list and must not be used to direct, organize, or encourage harassment, confrontation, disruption, or coordinated pressure against a facility, public employee, or private person.

A facility listing is not an instruction or request for anyone to visit, contact, confront, or audit that facility.

docs.title: Relationship to the Field Guide and facility methodology
docs.text:
The project now separates three functions:

  1. Field Guide — researches and explains generally applicable constitutional provisions, statutes, regulations, cases, and field rules.
  2. Facility Research and Field Verification — defines the investigation workflow, authority chain, source collection, field verification, police-policy transition, and post-visit records process.
  3. Registry — stores and publishes facility-specific facts, area-by-area access conditions, policies, signage, evidence history, research flags, and later corrections.

The canonical factual baseline is Standing Scenario. The canonical facility-research workflow is Facility Research and Field Verification.

Registry entries should consume those two documents rather than recreate them. A facility page should link to applicable Field Guide authorities and record only the facility-specific facts and analysis needed to apply those authorities.

docs.title: 2. Standing scenario
docs.text:
The Registry uses the project's canonical Standing Scenario.

Do not maintain a second, shorter list of baseline assumptions here. If the standing scenario changes, the Registry inherits that change through the canonical document.

A facility entry may document an incident that materially departs from the standing scenario, but it must identify the changed fact rather than silently treating the incident as equivalent to the baseline.

The Registry also does not assume that an entire building, floor, or agency office has one access or forum status. Entries should identify the specific area and activity being analyzed.

docs.title: 3. Unit of evaluation
docs.text:
The Registry evaluates government institutions, facilities, published rules, and documented government conduct.

The Registry does not grade individual employees.

Individual public employees may be identified in factual source material when relevant to an official action, report, policy, or public proceeding, but the Registry should avoid unnecessary personal profiling and should not publish private contact information, home information, personal schedules, family information, or other nonpublic personal details.

The objective is institutional accountability, not personal humiliation.

docs.title: 4. Facility universe and inclusion
docs.text:
The long-term goal is to identify the broad population of California government facilities to which this work may apply, using public and official sources where practical.

The Registry should not be built only from controversial encounters, viral videos, or facilities thought likely to produce conflict. A statewide or category-based facility directory may include facilities before any policy research or field observation has occurred.

Potential directory sources may include:

  • state-agency facility lists;
  • county and municipal directories;
  • court directories;
  • public-school, college, and university directories;
  • special-district directories;
  • transit and airport authority directories;
  • federal agency and USPS facility locators;
  • official GIS and open-data sources.

A federal facility physically located in California may be catalogued in the statewide directory for location and cross-reference purposes, but its substantive legal analysis belongs in the project's federal-premises track. California statutes, CPRA, and California facility rules must not be assumed to govern merely because the property is geographically in California.

A neutral facility directory may therefore contain many Gray entries awaiting research alongside Green, Yellow, and Red entries. Inclusion in the directory does not imply concern, suspicion, or a recommendation that anyone visit the facility.

The project should document how facility populations were assembled so claims of directory completeness can be audited and improved over time.

docs.title: 5. Source-first research
docs.text:
Each facility page should begin with documentary research before any field observation is evaluated.

Relevant public information may include:

  • official facility name and agency;
  • official address and public hours;
  • official facility or agency webpage;
  • published visitor and security rules;
  • published photography or recording policies;
  • posted notices and signs visible to the public;
  • public-meeting rules;
  • agency administrative manuals or directives;
  • applicable local ordinances;
  • California statutes and regulations;
  • federal statutes and regulations where applicable;
  • controlling and relevant persuasive case law;
  • public parcel, right-of-way, GIS, mapping, or other official geographic information when relevant to determining public property boundaries or access;
  • CPRA, FOIA, or other official records obtained after research or a field observation.

Every substantive legal authority or facility policy relied on by the Registry should have a direct source link when a stable public source is available and a last_verified date.

Primary sources are preferred. Secondary sources may be used for explanation or research leads but should not replace primary authority when primary authority is available.

A statement such as no supporting authority located as of [date] means only that the project's documented research did not locate supporting authority by that date. Failure to locate supporting authority is not, by itself, proof that no such authority exists.

docs.title: Source preservation and link rot
docs.text:
Important facility-specific source material should be preserved well enough that later readers can determine what the project actually reviewed, even if an agency later changes or removes the online material.

Where practical and legally appropriate, an entry should record:

  • source URL;
  • retrieval or observation date;
  • document title, version, revision date, or other identifying metadata;
  • a preserved copy or archived reference when appropriate;
  • a photograph of physical signage when signage is material;
  • an optional SHA-256 hash for a preserved file when useful for later comparison.

The project should distinguish a preserved historical source from the agency's current policy. A later policy change should update the current record without erasing the historical evidence.

docs.title: 6. Registry status system
docs.text: Color/status labels describe the state of the evidence. They are not judicial determinations. Public presentation must always display the text label and scope; color alone must never carry the status meaning.

docs.title: Status scope rule
docs.text:
A status is assigned to a defined area, policy, activity, or incident, not automatically to an entire street address, building, agency, or institution.

A single facility page may therefore contain multiple concurrent statuses. For example, one public lobby may have an unresolved recording-policy question while a separately controlled classroom, sidewalk, or meeting room has a different status.

Every non-Gray status should identify its scope clearly enough that a reader can tell what was actually researched or tested. A successful encounter in one area does not clear every policy or space at the facility, and an adverse encounter in one area does not establish that every operation at the facility is problematic.

docs.title: Gray — unresearched, incomplete, stale, or unresolved
docs.text:
Use Gray when:

  • facility research has not yet been completed;
  • available information is insufficient to evaluate a concern;
  • a prior entry has become stale and requires reverification;
  • material facts or governing law remain genuinely unresolved.

Gray does not imply either compliance or noncompliance.

docs.title: Green — no material concern identified or satisfactory documented response
docs.text:
Use Green when, based on the evidence reviewed:

  • no material conflict between published policy and governing authority has been identified; or
  • a field observation in the identified area and activity occurred without material adverse government action affecting the protected activity; or
  • a previously identified concern was satisfactorily clarified or corrected.

Green does not mean a facility has been comprehensively tested for every possible constitutional issue, area, or activity.

Positive outcomes should receive meaningful visibility. The Registry may highlight facilities with clear policies, accurate legal guidance, professional handling of peaceful protected activity, transparent records practices, constructive corrections, or other exemplary performance under a future published rubric.

docs.title: Yellow — pre-field policy or legal concern
docs.text:
Use Yellow when public research identifies a specific, documented question that merits clarification or further verification.

Examples may include:

  • an official rule or sign that appears broader than governing authority may permit;
  • conflicting agency policies;
  • a public-facing rule for which no supporting authority has yet been located;
  • an unresolved distinction between statewide law and local/facility practice.

A Yellow status must identify:

  1. the exact policy, sign, rule, or public information creating the concern;
  2. the source for that material;
  3. the legal authorities relevant to the concern;
  4. the precise unresolved question.

Yellow must not be described as proof that a facility is violating the Constitution or law.

Yellow means: a documented question exists.

It does not mean: go confront this facility.

docs.title: Red — documented adverse government action
docs.text:
Use Red only when reliable evidence documents a material adverse government action materially connected to the peaceful constitutional activity or facility-access issue being evaluated.

Examples may include:

  • removal from a public area;
  • detention;
  • arrest;
  • search;
  • seizure of a recording device or other property;
  • an order to cease protected activity;
  • a formal exclusion or trespass action;
  • other official coercive action materially affecting the activity.

An unrelated event, such as a general evacuation that affects everyone equally and is not connected to the protected activity, should not create Red status merely because it interrupted an audit.

A Red status describes what the government did. It does not, by itself, declare that a court has determined the action unconstitutional or unlawful.

The legal-analysis section should use appropriately precise language such as:

  • appears inconsistent with [authority];
  • raises a substantial First Amendment question;
  • raises a Fourth Amendment detention issue;
  • agency has not identified supporting authority;
  • legal status remains disputed;
  • court later held the conduct unconstitutional, when a court actually did so.

The Registry should reserve categorical statements such as unconstitutional, unlawful, or violated the First Amendment for situations where the underlying authority and procedural posture support that characterization.

docs.title: Current status and status history
docs.text:
Current status should not erase significant historical events.

A scoped issue may improve from Yellow or Red to Green after clarification or corrective action while retaining a visible status history, for example:

  • 2026-09-16 — RED: documented removal during peaceful recording.
  • 2026-10-12 — agency reports outdated sign removed and policy corrected.
  • 2026-10-15 — GREEN: correction independently verified.

Similarly, a currently stale issue may be Gray while retaining a historical Red or Yellow event. The project should distinguish each issue's current scoped status from its status history.

docs.title: 7. Status is evidence-based, not emotion-based
docs.text:
An area, policy, activity, or incident must not receive a Yellow or Red status because an encounter was unpleasant, rude, embarrassing, or unpopular.

The status should be traceable to source material and the published methodology.

Similarly, a scoped issue should not receive Green merely because an auditor personally liked the employees.

The Registry evaluates documented rules and conduct, not personalities.

docs.title: 8. No future-audit scheduling or targeting
docs.text:
The public Registry should not publish:

  • planned audit dates or times;
  • instructions to converge on a facility;
  • calls for followers to contact or confront employees;
  • predictions about which location is likely to generate conflict;
  • rankings such as best place to get arrested, easy target, or similar language;
  • employee work schedules for the purpose of timing an encounter;
  • nonpublic security vulnerabilities or access-control information.

Follow-up needed should mean that additional documentary research, policy clarification, records responses, or independently obtained observations would improve the record.

It should not mean that people are being asked to descend on the facility.

docs.title: 9. Pre-field research and intent
docs.text:
Facility research follows Facility Research and Field Verification.

A Registry entry may begin and remain desk-research only. Active field verification is not required merely because a policy question exists.

Pre-field work may establish:

  • the agency and property-control structure;
  • exact public-facing areas and ordinary access conditions;
  • published hours and visitor procedures;
  • written policies and posted signs;
  • the authority the agency claims supports a restriction;
  • relevant constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and case-law questions;
  • prior enforcement history;
  • CPRA/FOIA research targets;
  • unresolved questions that require records or later verification.

The entry should distinguish a documented question from a legal conclusion. If a field visit would create an avoidable conflict of interest, safety problem, privacy concern, employment complication, or other methodological problem, the Registry may expressly omit active testing and continue with documentary research.

docs.title: Researcher relationship or conflict
docs.text:
When a researcher has an employment, tenancy, contractual, family, or other relationship that could materially affect the investigation, the project should record that limitation internally.

The public entry should not rely on confidential, privileged, or nonpublic information available only because of that relationship. Firsthand observations may be used as evidence, but material public claims should be corroborated with public or official sources where practical.

The existence of a relationship does not automatically disqualify desk research. It may, however, make active field testing inappropriate. Public disclosure of the relationship should be made when it is materially necessary to understand the evidence or potential bias, rather than as an automatic requirement for every entry.

If field verification later occurs, it should test a defined question under the standing scenario rather than manufacture misconduct or confrontation.

docs.title: 10. Evidence standard for field observations
docs.text:
A Red or other adverse field status should not be based solely on a contributor's characterization of events.

Where reasonably available, the Registry should seek to preserve or link:

  • original video or audio recorded by the auditor;
  • an unedited or substantially complete version sufficient to evaluate context;
  • photographs of relevant signs or barriers;
  • date, approximate time, and exact public location;
  • police body-worn camera footage;
  • dispatch/CAD records;
  • 911 or nonemergency call recordings;
  • incident or arrest reports;
  • written exclusion or trespass notices;
  • facility surveillance footage when lawfully obtainable;
  • agency emails, messages, directives, or reports obtained through CPRA/FOIA;
  • applicable policies and training materials;
  • later agency correspondence.

Edited videos may be used for public presentation, but material legal conclusions should not depend on edits that omit context needed to evaluate the incident.

docs.title: Third-party submissions and incomplete recordings
docs.text:
Before assigning Red status based on a third-party audit or submission, a reviewer should determine whether the available evidence reasonably establishes the relevant facts from the canonical Standing Scenario during the material portion of the encounter.

A recording that begins only after the confrontation or omits material preceding events may still be useful evidence, but the project should not assume missing facts in either direction. When the available evidence is insufficient to apply the standard Registry methodology, the entry should remain Gray, pending, or otherwise expressly qualified rather than receiving an unsupported Red status.

docs.title: 11. Evidence integrity
docs.text:
When practical, significant original media should be preserved exactly as captured.

The project may record a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 for an original file so a later copy can be compared against the preserved original.

A Registry entry may distinguish:

  • Original media preserved;
  • Original-media hash;
  • Public/edited version;
  • Government-source media;
  • Other supporting records.

A hash verifies file identity. It does not independently prove that the recording is complete or that every factual interpretation of the recording is correct.

docs.title: 12. Separate fact, policy, and legal analysis
docs.text: Each facility entry should clearly separate at least three layers.

docs.title: A. Official sources
docs.text:
What the government has published or officially produced.

Examples:

  • rules;
  • policies;
  • official webpages;
  • regulations;
  • posted signs;
  • CPRA/FOIA responses.

docs.title: B. Field observations
docs.text:
What was actually documented.

Use neutral chronological descriptions where possible.

Example:

At 2:14 p.m., an employee approached the auditor and stated that recording was not allowed in the lobby. At 2:18 p.m., the employee contacted law enforcement. At 2:31 p.m., an officer stated that the auditor would be arrested for trespass if the auditor did not leave.

Avoid converting observation into legal conclusion inside the factual chronology.

docs.title: C. Legal analysis
docs.text:
What statutes, regulations, cases, or constitutional provisions may mean for the documented conduct.

Legal analysis should identify uncertainty, contrary authority, forum-specific limitations, and procedural posture where relevant.

docs.title: 13. Terminology standards
docs.text:
Preferred language includes:

  • documented adverse action;
  • policy concern;
  • unresolved legal question;
  • appears inconsistent with;
  • no supporting authority located as of [date];
  • binding authority;
  • persuasive authority;
  • field observation;
  • agency response;
  • corrected after notice.

Avoid unsupported or inflammatory labels such as:

  • tyrant;
  • criminal agency;
  • corrupt facility;
  • constitutional violator;
  • target;
  • hit list;
  • go audit these people.

Quoting another person who used such language is different from adopting the language as the Registry's own characterization, but quotes should be included only when materially relevant.

docs.title: 14. Future rubric or report-card scores
docs.text:
Numerical scores and report-card grades are not part of the current Registry methodology.

The Registry may eventually use a published 1A Audit Rubric or report-card system if the scoring criteria are developed in a separate proposal, adopted before they are applied to facilities, and remain transparent and reproducible.

Any score or grade should be described as:

the project's evaluation under its published rubric

and not as:

a judicial determination of legal liability.

Potential rubric categories may include:

  • clarity of public-access rules;
  • published recording/photography policy;
  • consistency between facility rules and higher authority;
  • response to peaceful protected activity;
  • de-escalation and professional handling;
  • law-enforcement response, if applicable;
  • accuracy of legal articulation;
  • records transparency;
  • willingness to correct erroneous policy or signage.

A category that was not actually tested should be marked NOT TESTED or otherwise excluded from the denominator rather than scored as zero.

High scores, exemplary practices, constructive corrections, and meaningful improvements should be eligible for the same public visibility as adverse findings. The Registry should not be designed so that only poor outcomes are noteworthy.

The final scoring rubric should be developed in a separate proposal before facility grades are published.

docs.title: 15. Public-information and privacy rule
docs.text:
The Registry may use pertinent information that a government agency has publicly posted or officially released.

However, the project should collect and publish only information reasonably relevant to the public-access, recording, speech, transparency, or accountability question being documented.

The fact that information is technically obtainable does not automatically make republishing it necessary.

The Registry should avoid unnecessary publication of:

  • private citizens' personal information;
  • private phone numbers or addresses;
  • personal schedules unrelated to official public duties;
  • children's identifying information;
  • medical or similarly sensitive personal information;
  • detailed nonpublic security information.

If private information is incidentally visible in footage, the public-facing version should ordinarily redact or blur it when the information does not advance the accountability purpose.

docs.title: 16. Maps, GIS, and property-boundary research
docs.text:
Official GIS, parcel, right-of-way, map, easement, and property records may be used when they materially help establish:

  • whether a location is publicly owned;
  • whether a sidewalk or plaza is within public right-of-way;
  • facility boundaries;
  • public entrances and ordinary public-access routes.

The Registry should cite the government source and date consulted.

Mapping evidence should not be overstated. A GIS layer may be strong evidence of a boundary without necessarily resolving every legal question concerning access, easements, forum classification, or temporary restrictions.

docs.title: 17. Agency response and correction process
docs.text:
The Registry should maintain a clear way for an agency to provide:

  • updated policies;
  • corrections to factual statements;
  • explanations of a rule;
  • evidence that signage or policy has changed;
  • relevant legal authority the project overlooked.

When practical, before publishing a materially adverse facility-specific factual claim or disputed legal characterization that depends on unresolved facts, the project should seek the agency's position. That is a source-quality practice, not an entitlement to prepublication review.

No separate contact is required merely to reproduce or analyze an agency's own published policy, public record, sign, court filing, or other sufficiently authenticated source.

An agency response should be evaluated under the same source standards as any other submission. The agency does not receive editorial control over the entry.

Valid corrections should be incorporated promptly and transparently through Git history.

The project should not erase prior history merely because a rule changed.

Example:

  • 2026-09-10 — No-recording sign documented.
  • 2026-10-12 — Agency states sign was obsolete and has been removed.
  • 2026-10-15 — Removal independently verified.

A scoped issue's current status or any future rubric treatment may improve when an agency corrects a problem, while the historical record remains visible.

docs.title: 18. Corrections when the project is wrong
docs.text:
The same standard applies to the project itself.

If later research shows that a status assignment or accompanying legal analysis was mistaken, incomplete, or overstated, the Registry should:

  1. correct the entry;
  2. cite the newly discovered authority or evidence;
  3. explain the material change when appropriate;
  4. preserve the correction history in Git;
  5. change the affected scoped status if warranted.

The Registry's credibility depends on being willing to document when the government's interpretation was correct and the project's earlier interpretation was not.

docs.title: 19. Facility-entry schema
docs.text:
The detailed investigation worksheet is maintained in docs/templates/facility-investigation-template.md. The Registry should not maintain a competing investigative template.

A mature public Registry entry should contain, at minimum:

Facility:
Agency:
Jurisdiction:
Facility type:
Official address:
Official website:
Last verified:
Research stage:
Current Registry status(es):
Status scope(s):
Status history:
Research flags:

AREA-BY-AREA ACCESS
- Area:
- Controlling/occupying entity:
- Public hours:
- Ordinary public-access condition:
- Access source / confidence:
- Check-in / badge / ID condition:
- Restricted boundary:
- Activity analyzed:
- Forum classification:
- Classification status / uncertainty:

POLICY AND IMPLEMENTATION
- Current written policy:
- Policy source / version:
- Posted signage:
- Exact wording:
- Sign location / scope:
- Claimed authority:
- Exclusion / removal authority:
- Separate police / criminal authority:

OFFICIAL SOURCES
- Agency/facility pages:
- Lease/property/control sources:
- Maps/GIS/floor plans:
- Policy/adoption sources:
- Retrieval dates:
- Preserved/archive references:

EVIDENCE HISTORY
- Passive observations:
- Field verification, if any:
- Prior incidents:
- Police/security involvement:
- Post-visit records:
- Agency response:
- Corrections / policy changes:

LEGAL ANALYSIS
- Applicable Field Guide chapters:
- Controlling authority:
- Material factual predicates:
- Application:
- Limits / contrary authority:

EVIDENCE INTEGRITY

- Hash, if used:

A single street address may require several area records. Public ownership, leasehold control, ordinary public access, purpose-limited access, forum classification, and criminal trespass authority are separate fields and should not be collapsed into one label.

docs.title: 20. Proposed public Registry notice
docs.text:
A public Registry index may display concise language substantially similar to the following:

The public Registry should also make favorable findings, high scores, verified improvements, and exemplary practices reasonably discoverable rather than presenting only adverse findings.

docs.title: About the Registry
docs.text: The California Public Facility 1A Registry documents how public facilities publish and apply rules affecting peaceful First Amendment activity. Statuses are scoped to identified areas, policies, activities, or incidents; they reflect documented evidence under a published methodology and are not judicial findings. Facility listings are not requests or instructions for anyone to visit, contact, confront, or audit a particular agency or employee.

docs.title: 21. Working status
docs.text:
An initial mixed-use, leased-facility pilot has been used internally to test this methodology. The pilot demonstrated that the Registry needs:

  • area-by-area rather than address-wide classification;
  • separate treatment of common areas, public service areas, purpose-limited rooms, and restricted workspaces;
  • separate property/control, public-access, forum, removal, and criminal-authority fields;
  • a way to record posted restrictions whose source authority remains unresolved;
  • a desk-research-only path when active field testing would be methodologically inappropriate;
  • scoped statuses rather than one blanket color for an entire facility.

The pilot record itself is not required to preserve those methodological lessons and may be discarded after review.

The methodology is now suitable for controlled Registry population, but it remains a working project standard. Real entries may expose additional schema problems, which should be corrected transparently before large-scale population.

The project may publish evidence-status labels and research flags before a numerical rubric exists, but it should not publish report-card grades or numeric scores until a separate scoring methodology has been adopted and tested.

docs.title: USPS Facilities in California
docs.text: A California post office is federal property. Do not assume that California public-agency trespass rules are the operative conduct rules simply because the building is physically located in California.

docs.title: Primary conduct regulation — 39 C.F.R. § 232.1
docs.text:
Primary source: 39 C.F.R. § 232.1

The regulation applies broadly to real property under Postal Service charge and control, subject to stated exceptions.

docs.title: Photography — § 232.1(i)
docs.text:
The regulation states that, except when prohibited by official signs, directions of security force personnel or other authorized personnel, or a federal court order/rule, photographs for news purposes may be taken in entrances, lobbies, foyers, corridors, or auditoriums when used for public meetings.

It further states that other photographs may be taken only with permission of the local postmaster or installation head.

docs.title: Field rule
docs.text:
Do not reduce § 232.1(i) to either of these slogans:

"Photography is prohibited in post offices."

or

"Poster 7 gives an absolute right to film anything in the lobby."

The actual regulation contains both an affirmative photography provision and express qualifications. The meaning/application of "news purposes," official signs/directions, and constitutional limits on enforcement require separate legal analysis.

docs.title: Disturbances — § 232.1(e)
docs.text:
The regulation prohibits disorderly conduct, loud/unusual noise, obstruction of ingress/egress and conduct that impedes or disturbs employees performing duties or the public transacting business.

Under the standing eight-condition scenario, an auditor is intentionally avoiding the clearest obstruction/noise/interference conduct. If § 232.1(e) is invoked, document the specific behavior the government claims satisfies it.

docs.title: Signs and directions — § 232.1(d)
docs.text:
The regulation requires compliance with official prohibitory/directory signs and directions of security-force personnel or other authorized individuals.

This provision must be read together with § 232.1(i), constitutional law, and any applicable agency interpretation. The mere existence of a sign should be documented, but a handbook entry should not assume that a sign answers every constitutional question.

docs.title: Closed property — § 232.1(b)(3)
docs.text:
Postal property generally may be closed to the public after normal business hours and may be closed in emergency situations or when necessary for orderly business. Admission during closed periods may be limited to authorized individuals.

This is one reason the standing field rules assume an auditor is present during lawful public access.

docs.title: Enforcement and penalties
docs.text: Section 232.1 contains its own enforcement and penalty provisions. Federal-property encounters should therefore be researched as federal-property encounters rather than treated as ordinary California public-agency lobby scenarios.

docs.title: Research still required
docs.text:
• current USPS Poster 7 text and its relationship to the CFR;
  • federal cases applying § 232.1(i) to independent journalists/auditors;
  • constitutional challenges to photography restrictions on postal property;
  • authority of local postmasters and security personnel;
  • federal trespass/removal authority;
  • records requests and preservation under federal FOIA/records law.

docs.title: California Authority Sweep Ledger
docs.text:
Purpose: Make the California Field Guide's completeness work reproducible and auditable.

This ledger records source ranges that have actually been reviewed, what was retained, what was treated as specialized or outside the standing scenario, and what still remains unswept. A completed slice does not mean the entire California code has been completed.

docs.title: Classification labels
docs.text:
• RETAINED — materially relevant to the standing peaceful/public-property audit scenario or to a recurring facility chapter.
  • CONTEXT — does not independently create the principal field rule but materially explains authority, definitions, procedure, or limits.
  • SPECIALIZED — relevant only to a distinct facility/event type and should be handled in that chapter.
  • N/A-STANDING-SCOPE — reviewed but ordinarily requires conduct excluded by the project's standing assumptions or concerns a setting outside the project's ordinary public-facility scope.
  • REVIEW-LATER — text identified, but case law or related provisions must be reviewed before final classification.

For handbook/index status terminology, PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED means current primary text was checked and an initial entry exists. It does not mean the controlling case-law layer is complete. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED is reserved for narrow propositions whose controlling doctrine/material case law have also been reviewed. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART means a narrow part of a broader statutory family has reached that stage while other applications remain unresolved.

The canonical factual baseline for N/A-STANDING-SCOPE and related classifications is maintained in ../california/standing-scenario.md. It expressly excludes unstated fighting, unreasonable noise, obstruction/intimidation, independent § 148 conduct, unlawful-assembly predicates, restricted-area entry, and other unrelated offenses so a sweep does not smuggle hypothetical misconduct into the issue under review.

Every retained authority should ultimately have a direct primary-source link, narrow proposition, important limitations, binding level where applicable, and last_verified date.

docs.title: Jurisdiction boundary — federal premises located in California
docs.text:
Federal premises are tracked separately under docs/federal/ and are not treated as another California-code sweep merely because the property is geographically located in California.

Federal-premises research begins with federal constitutional law, federal statutes/regulations, agency/facility rules, and federal case law. California law is checked only when a specific doctrine makes it relevant, such as concurrent/proprietary jurisdiction, incorporation of state law, or the Assimilative Crimes Act.

Federal FOIA belongs to the federal-agency records track and does not govern California state or local agencies.

docs.title: Review discoveries from Sweep 001
