docs.title: Sweep 002 — Trespass and property-access family
docs.text:
Review date: September 17, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-002-TRESPASS-PROPERTY.md

Primary-text scope completed: Penal Code §§ 601-603, including all subdivisions of § 602 and every current § 602.1-602.13 provision.

The sweep produced the complete § 602 matrix and a practical removal decision tree in docs/california/trespass-removal.md.

docs.title: Final controlling-case review incorporated before merge
docs.text:
The final PR #6 review promoted narrow propositions—not entire statutes—to doctrine-reviewed status:

  • In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (1981) and Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010) — § 602(m) occupation requires nontransient, continuous possession; transient/minutes-long presence did not establish that element in Edgerly.
  • Parrish v. Municipal Court, 258 Cal.App.2d 497 (1968) — predecessor of § 602(q) is a public-building closing-hours rule; apparent-lawful-business inquiry is objective.
  • Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001) — refusal alone does not supply § 602.1 intentional interference/obstruction facts.
  • Hamburg v. Wal-Mart Stores, Inc., 116 Cal.App.4th 497 (2004) — rule/policy enforcement and satisfaction of § 602.1 criminal elements remain separate; private-property facts limit its government-facility use.
  • People v. Hsiung (2026) — § 602(o) First Amendment discussion is in an expressly unpublished portion and is not relied on as precedent.

The final refinement also distinguishes specific-area public access, forum classification, security screening, visitor sign-in/ID policy, and criminal trespass authority. Section 602(y) is not treated as a generic visitor-log/ID statute.

Housekeeping correction recorded in Sweep 003: an earlier umbrella-ledger sentence saying no Sweep 002 proposition had reached doctrine review was stale after the final PR #6 case-law review. The detailed Sweep 002 ledger and merged chapter control; this umbrella ledger now matches them.

docs.title: Sweep 003 — California Public Records Act / evidence preservation
docs.text:
Review date: September 17, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-003-CPRA-EVIDENCE-PRESERVATION.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-records-evidence-preservation.md

Scope: targeted operational/preservation review. This is not yet a complete exemption-by-exemption sweep of all Government Code Division 10.

docs.title: Core statutory layer reviewed
docs.text:
• Gov. Code §§ 7920.530 and 7920.545 — public-record and writing definitions;
  • §§ 7921.000, 7921.010, 7921.300 — access, anti-evasion/lawful-destruction context, and purpose-neutral access;
  • § 7922.000 — justification for withholding;
  • §§ 7922.500-7922.605 — core request, inspection, copying, determination, denial, electronic-record, and duty-to-assist provisions;
  • §§ 7922.630-7922.640 — agency regulations/guidelines context;
  • §§ 7922.680, 7922.700-7922.725 — internet/enterprise-system provisions identified as contextual and queued for deeper relevance review;
  • § 7923.000 — enforcement/declaratory relief;
  • representative retention/destruction frameworks: Gov. Code §§ 12270-12279, 12275, 34090, 34090.6, 26202, 6200-6201.

docs.title: City of San Jose v. Superior Court, 2 Cal.5th 608 (2017)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • public-business writings do not cease being CPRA records merely because they are sent, received, or stored using personal accounts/devices;
  • public-record status depends on substantive relationship to public business, with content/context/purpose/audience/scope-of-employment factors;
  • primarily personal material with only incidental public-business references generally is not transformed into a public record;
  • agencies must make reasonable efforts to locate responsive material;
  • for likely personal-account/device records, agencies should communicate the request to employees and may reasonably rely on them to search their personal files/accounts/devices for responsive public-business records.

Auditor consequence: a personal-phone recording deliberately made on duty to document an official encounter is a strong public-record candidate, but the guide does not use the word always without the substantive-public-business analysis.

docs.title: City of Gilroy v. Superior Court, 19 Cal.5th 38 (2026)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the CPRA itself does not impose a three-year preservation duty on all responsive records withheld as exempt;
  • the CPRA is not a general retention statute;
  • other retention/preservation law can independently apply;
  • declaratory relief can remain available for an ongoing rights/obligations dispute likely to affect future requests/conduct;
  • footnote 20 limits the no-CPRA-preservation holding to normal implementation/operation of routine retention practices and expressly leaves intentional destruction reflecting possible deliberate misconduct unresolved.

Auditor consequence: a preservation notice is useful evidence, but a pending CPRA request or statement of intent to request a record is not represented as an automatic CPRA litigation hold.

docs.title: Key Sweep 003 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Public record ≠ automatically disclosable. Exemptions/redactions remain separate.
  2. Personal device ≠ private-record safe harbor. City of San Jose controls the categorical question.
  3. Search ≠ disclosure. An agency may need to search a personal device/account for qualifying records even if some responsive material is ultimately withheld.
  4. Disclosure ≠ retention. Gilroy separates CPRA access from retention law.
  5. Preservation notice ≠ magic legal hold. It still documents existence, knowledge, notice, and potentially intent.
  6. Routine lawful disposition ≠ deliberate destruction. The latter is expressly outside Gilroy footnote 20's resolved scenario.
  7. No universal retention period. State executive agencies, cities, counties, special districts, law enforcement, courts, and other bodies can have different statutes/schedules.
  8. Request the schedule. If evidence disappears, the governing retention/destruction policy becomes part of the factual/legal record.
  9. Do not declare a felony on scene. Government Code §§ 6200-6201 have their own record/custody/willfulness scope and must not be equated automatically with the CPRA definition.

docs.title: Practical output
docs.text:
The new chapter includes an auditor workflow for employee records me back:

  • establish on camera that a recording exists and its work-related context;
  • give a narrow preservation notice;
  • promptly submit a CPRA request including qualifying personal-device/account records;
  • invoke the City of San Jose search principle without demanding access to unrelated private content;
  • if withheld, demand the statutory withholding basis and segregable portions;
  • if missing/deleted, request retention schedules/policies, disposition/deletion records, metadata/audit logs if maintained, and communications about preservation/deletion;
  • analyze any destruction under the actual retention, litigation-preservation, and destruction law rather than asserting an automatic CPRA violation.

docs.title: Sweep 004 — Police Encounters: Fourth Amendment + Self-Incrimination
docs.text:
Review date: September 21, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-004-POLICE-ENCOUNTERS.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/police-encounters.md

Scope: targeted operational/doctrinal review of the encounter sequence that commonly follows protected recording or other First Amendment activity. This is not a complete Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, criminal-procedure, or remedies sweep.

docs.title: Core encounter layer reviewed
docs.text:
• consensual police contact versus Fourth Amendment seizure;
  • Terry investigative detention and reasonable suspicion;
  • the requirement that the stop be justified at inception;
  • detention scope/duration baseline under Sharpe and traffic-specific Rodriguez;
  • protective frisk as a separate armed-and-dangerous inquiry;
  • probable-cause arrest and Devenpeck's objective-offense rule;
  • California identification distinctions: carry-ID versus request versus statutory/case-law duty versus false identification;
  • California Vehicle Code § 2806.5 pedestrian-stop notice relevant to facility audits, distinct from full reasonable-suspicion disclosure; the statute's traffic-stop branch is not developed in the current project scope;
  • Fourth Amendment detention versus Fifth Amendment/Miranda custody;
  • clear invocation of the privilege/right to remain silent under Berghuis and the plurality-limited Salinas discussion;
  • physical device seizure versus digital-content search; Riley warrant baseline;
  • explicit unresolved treatment of compelled unlocking/passcodes/biometrics.

docs.title: Principal authorities incorporated
docs.text:
Federal controlling authorities include Terry v. Ohio, Berkemer v. McCarty, United States v. Sharpe, Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court, Devenpeck v. Alford, Berghuis v. Thompkins, Salinas v. Texas (plurality-limited proposition), Riley v. California, and traffic-specific Rodriguez v. United States.

California/Ninth Circuit anchors include:

  • People v. Tacardon, 14 Cal.5th 235 (2022) — totality-of-circumstances consensual-contact/seizure analysis; directed police attention does not itself establish a detention;
  • People v. Flores, 15 Cal.5th 1032 (2024) — particularized/objective reasonable suspicion required; high-crime-area context and the conduct there were insufficient in totality;
  • United States v. Landeros, 913 F.3d 862 (9th Cir. 2019) — passenger refusal to identify, without reasonable suspicion of an offense, did not supply reasonable suspicion and did not justify prolonging the traffic stop;
  • People v. Valle, A169080 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 18, 2024) — published California authority recognizing Vehicle Code § 2806.5's stop-reason notice requirement while keeping the federal objective Fourth Amendment justification inquiry separate.

docs.title: California identification findings
docs.text:
Primary text reviewed:

  • Penal Code § 148.9 — false/fictitious identity during qualifying lawful detention/arrest;
  • Penal Code § 853.5 — identity/thumbprint procedures in specified infraction-arrest citation context;
  • Vehicle Code § 2806.5 — for current project purposes, a pedestrian stop requires the reason to be stated before covered questioning, subject to the statute's imminent-threat exception;
  • Vehicle Code § 12951 — driver-specific license possession/presentation rule;
  • Vehicle Code § 40302 — specified custody/magistrate rules following nonfelony Vehicle Code arrest.

Bounded research conclusion: this targeted sweep has not identified a current general California pedestrian carry-ID statute or general statutory stop-and-identify law equivalent to the Nevada statute upheld in Hiibel. That does not mean identification or production of possessed identification can never be required. Older published California identification-production/search cases, including People v. Long, People v. Loudermilk, and People v. Garcia, still require a dedicated reconciliation, and specialized statutory contexts remain independently controlling.

Historical context: Kolender v. Lawson, 461 U.S. 352 (1983), invalidated California's former requirement that a detained person provide credible and reliable identification because the scheme was unconstitutionally vague. The history is useful, but the guide does not turn Kolender into a blanket rule against all modern California identification requirements.

docs.title: Key Sweep 004 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Police contact ≠ detention. A consensual encounter requires no reasonable suspicion.
  2. Detention ≠ arrest. Terry permits a limited seizure based on reasonable suspicion.
  3. Detention ≠ frisk. A frisk requires its own armed-and-dangerous safety justification.
  4. Detention ≠ Miranda custody. A person can be seized for Fourth Amendment purposes without yet being in Miranda custody.
  5. Reasonable suspicion ≠ probable cause. Arrest ordinarily requires the higher threshold.
  6. Recording alone ≠ obstruction/RS/PC. Penal Code § 148(g) expressly supplies this bridge within its scope.
  7. Asking for ID ≠ proof of a general carry-ID or stop-and-identify law. Identify the actual California statute, context, and applicable case law before treating the request as compulsory.
  8. No general duty found ≠ permission to lie. Penal Code § 148.9 separately prohibits qualifying false/fictitious identification.
  9. Hiibel ≠ national stop-and-ID mandate. It upheld Nevada's statute during a valid Terry stop.
  10. Reason for stop ≠ full RAS recital. For pedestrian stops within this project's current scope, Vehicle Code § 2806.5 requires the reason for the stop before covered questioning, subject to its exception; reasonable suspicion itself must still exist when the seizure begins.
  11. Officer's announced offense ≠ entire arrest analysis. Devenpeck makes probable cause objective.
  12. Phone seizure ≠ digital search. Riley protects digital contents beyond ordinary search-incident-to-arrest authority.
  13. No Miranda warning ≠ illegal arrest. Arrest/seizure legality and custodial-interrogation safeguards are separate questions.
  14. Silence is not the safest invocation method. The guide recommends clear invocation rather than relying on an inference from silence.

docs.title: Remaining Sweep 004 research
docs.text:
Important unresolved areas include:

  • handcuffs, drawn weapons, prone positioning, transport, and when a Terry stop becomes an arrest;
  • anonymous/911/security/employee reports and informant reliability;
  • collective knowledge and mistakes of law/fact;
  • older California identification-production/search cases, including Long, Loudermilk, Garcia, and later applications;
  • plain-feel/container doctrine and consent searches;
  • full Miranda custody/interrogation/public-safety/waiver/reinitiation doctrine;
  • physical seizure/retention of phones and cameras;
  • warrant scope/particularity for devices;
  • compelled unlocking/passcodes/biometrics;
  • independent California Constitution article I §§ 13 and 15 doctrine;
  • excessive force, suppression, § 1983, qualified immunity, Bane Act, and municipal liability.

Those issues remain explicitly queued rather than converted into field slogans.

docs.title: Sweep 005 — Public-forum doctrine
docs.text:
Review date: September 17, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-005-PUBLIC-FORUM-DOCTRINE.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-forum-doctrine.md

Scope: core federal forum architecture, Ninth Circuit government-building/application doctrine, California Speech Clause overlay, and an area-level registry methodology. This is not a facility-by-facility classification sweep.

docs.title: Core federal layer reviewed
docs.text:
• Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators' Association — traditional/designated/nonpublic architecture;
  • Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense & Educational Fund — define the forum by the access sought; intentional opening; nonpublic reasonableness/viewpoint neutrality;
  • United States v. Grace and United States v. Kokinda — ordinary perimeter sidewalk versus special-purpose walkway distinctions;
  • Ward v. Rock Against Racism — public-forum content-neutral time/place/manner test;
  • International Society for Krishna Consciousness v. Lee — airport-terminal/separated-area context;
  • Rosenberger — viewpoint-discrimination principle;
  • Christian Legal Society / Wright / Hopper — limited-forum doctrine and terminology;
  • Minnesota Voters Alliance v. Mansky — a nonpublic forum still requires a reasonable, workable speech rule.

docs.title: Sammartano v. First Judicial District Court, 303 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2002)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the judicial/municipal complex before the court was a nonpublic forum even though people entered it to conduct public business;
  • location, purpose, and governmental intent matter;
  • nonpublic-forum restrictions still must be reasonable in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutral;
  • the government did not obtain a free pass merely from the nonpublic classification: the evidentiary connection between the restriction and asserted safety/order needs still mattered.

docs.title: Norse v. City of Santa Cruz, 629 F.3d 966 (9th Cir. 2010) (en banc)
docs.text:
Retained propositions for the meeting crossover:

  • a city-council meeting opened to public participation is a limited public forum;
  • reasonable content/topic and time rules may apply, but viewpoint discrimination is not permitted;
  • the Ninth Circuit rejected a theory that First Amendment protection disappears after the public-comment period;
  • meeting removal doctrine remains tied to actual disruption rather than merely disfavored expression.

The Brown Act statutory layer remains separately governed by public-meetings.md.

docs.title: Camenzind v. California Exposition & State Fair, 84 F.4th 1102 (9th Cir. 2023)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • analyze physically/policy-distinct areas separately;
  • the enclosed/ticketed private-event portion was nonpublic on the facts;
  • the exterior area was a public forum under the California Speech Clause;
  • California's forum analysis differs from the federal one;
  • the panel acknowledged it was predicting unresolved California law for the precise state-constitutional issue, and a partial dissent disagreed with the majority's state-law analysis for the interior.

docs.title: California Speech Clause
docs.text:
• California Constitution art. I, § 2(a) is separately analyzed.
  • San Leandro Teachers Association v. Governing Board, 46 Cal.4th 822 (2009), classified internal school mailboxes as nonpublic under federal doctrine and separately rejected a broader California Speech Clause claim on the narrow facts. It also supplies an important warning against treating the older basic incompatibility formulation as the current California forum-classification rule.
  • International Society for Krishna Consciousness of California, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles, 48 Cal.4th 446 (2010), expressly declined to decide whether LAX was a public forum under the California Speech Clause; the challenged immediate-funds solicitation rule was valid even on an assumed-public-forum analysis.
  • Pruneyard, Ralphs Grocery, and Park Management are retained as context showing that California's Speech Clause can extend beyond federal public-forum doctrine and that location/access analysis is fact-sensitive. They are not converted into a universal rule that every public-facing property is a public forum.
  • Camenzind confirms that the old basic incompatibility classification approach used by some older Ninth Circuit cases rests on a doubtful foundation after San Leandro; the guide therefore does not use it as the current state-law classification test.

docs.title: Key Sweep 005 field distinctions
docs.text:
1. Public ownership ≠ public forum.
  2. Open to the public ≠ public forum.
  3. Classify the specific area/channel, not merely the building.
  4. Traditional/designated public forum ≠ limited/nonpublic forum. The governing restriction standard changes.
  5. Nonpublic ≠ no First Amendment rights. Reasonableness and viewpoint neutrality remain.
  6. Limited forum ≠ unrestricted forum. Government can confine speech to the forum's lawful purpose but cannot use the limit as a pretext for viewpoint discrimination.
  7. Federal classification ≠ automatic California classification.
  8. Forum status ≠ recording permission/prohibition. Separate recording, privacy, security, statutory, and facility rules may matter.
  9. Forum status ≠ criminal trespass. Constitutional restriction, exclusion authority, detention, and Penal Code elements remain separate questions.
  10. Unresolved is a legitimate registry result. Do not infer forum status from ownership, a public counter, or a sign.

docs.title: Registry consequence
docs.text:
Future facility records should contain, at minimum: facility, specific area, access status, federal forum classification, California Speech Clause classification, expressive activity analyzed, governing rule/policy, authority, confidence, and last-verified date.

The registry should use UNRESOLVED whenever authority is inadequate.

docs.title: Remaining facility work
docs.text: Still separately queued: administrative lobbies, police/sheriff lobbies, DMV offices, public-library branches and systems beyond the initial Contra Costa Sweep 006, courthouses and courtrooms, colleges/universities, K-12, transit property, public health facilities, digital forums, employee workspaces, and long-term exclusion orders.

docs.title: Sweep 006 — Contra Costa County Public Libraries
docs.text:
Review date: September 21, 2026 Detailed ledger: SWEEP-006-CONTRA-COSTA-LIBRARIES.md Handbook chapter: docs/california/public-libraries.md

Scope: targeted system-level facility-category sweep of the Contra Costa County Library. This is not a statewide survey of every California library system and does not assign a Registry status to the system or any branch.

docs.title: Prigmore v. City of Redding, 211 Cal.App.4th 1322 (2012)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • published California Court of Appeal authority involving the outdoor grounds of a municipal public library;
  • forum defined by the access sought rather than the whole library campus;
  • on the record, the public open space at the entry, entry/exit-door area, and adjacent parking lot were a traditional public forum;
  • classification depended on actual use, unrestricted access, physical/congregation characteristics, surrounding public spaces, and library function;
  • interior and exterior were expressly distinguished;
  • the older California "basic incompatibility" formulation was not used as the forum-classification test;
  • most challenged outdoor speech-zone/reservation restrictions were likely invalid at the preliminary-injunction stage, while the parking-lot vehicle-leafleting ban was upheld on its safety rationale.

Scope limit: do not convert the Redding property-specific holding into a universal rule that every library plaza, approach, or parking lot is automatically a traditional public forum. Footnote 11's broad interior observation is not treated as a categorical interior holding because the cited Faith Center forum was specifically the Antioch meeting room.

docs.title: Faith Center Church Evangelistic Ministries v. Glover, 480 F.3d 891 (9th Cir. 2007)
docs.text:
Retained propositions:

  • the forum before the Ninth Circuit was the Antioch Library meeting room, not the entire library system or building;
  • the Antioch meeting room was a limited public forum on the policy/practice record before the court;
  • restrictions in a limited public forum are analyzed for reasonableness in light of forum purpose and viewpoint neutrality;
  • the decision strongly reinforces the project's rule that forum analysis follows the specific access sought.

The current Contra Costa meeting-room policy shows the historical religious-services restriction involved in that litigation struck through effective July 6, 2009. The old restriction is not treated as current County policy.

The 2009 district-court Establishment Clause ruling on remand is retained only as historical litigation context because it relied on the then-prevailing Lemon framework. Modern Establishment Clause doctrine, including Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, must be used for current analysis.

docs.title: Current Contra Costa policy layer reviewed
docs.text:
Official sources reviewed include:

  • Board-approved 2026 Patron Conduct Policy;
  • Board-approved 2026 Suspension Policy;
  • Children/Teen Areas policy;
  • meeting-room policy/rules and branch room directory;
  • rules for displays/distribution of non-library materials;
  • privacy materials;
  • special Self-Service Sundays access information.

The February 10, 2026 Board record confirms formal approval of the amended Patron Conduct and Suspension policies.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
1. Library building ≠ one forum. Main floors, children/teen areas, study rooms, meeting rooms, display channels, staff areas, restrooms, and exterior areas must be separately analyzed.
  2. System rule ≠ branch implementation. Some community rooms associated with branches are booked or controlled by cities/towns rather than solely by the County Library.
  3. Current library-activity predicate. The Patron Conduct Policy requires patrons to be engaged in activities associated with public-library use. Whether peaceful government observation/recording qualifies or can be excluded under that rule is unresolved.
  4. No dedicated public-facing camera rule located. The reviewed current policy portal and core policies did not reveal a dedicated ordinary-patron photography/videography policy. This is a research finding, not proof that no branch/internal/newer rule exists.
  5. Children/teen areas have purpose/age access conditions. This supplies a concrete example of lawful-presence analysis being area-specific.
  6. Patron-record privacy ≠ visitor-camera prohibition. Government Code § 7927.105 concerns qualifying library-maintained patron records; it is not treated as a categorical camera statute.
  7. Suspension and removal are separate from criminal trespass. The Suspension Policy cites Penal Code § 602 generically for return/refusal after suspension, but does not identify a subdivision or statutory element chain.
  8. Policy-to-criminal bridge remains open. The generic § 602 statement is flagged POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP without presuming an arrest would be lawful or unlawful.
  9. Due process remains duration/context sensitive. Published controlling Ninth Circuit/California library-specific authority for short versus long systemwide exclusions was not located; persuasive cases are retained with their limits.
  10. Display/distribution channels require separate review. Current subject restrictions, including political/candidate and religious-use rules, are recorded as AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED pending channel-specific forum analysis.

docs.title: Persuasive library cases retained with limits
docs.text:
• Kreimer v. Bureau of Police, 958 F.2d 1242 (3d Cir. 1992) — persuasive library-purpose/compatible-use analysis and close analogue to a library-activity requirement.
  • Neinast v. Board of Trustees, 346 F.3d 585 (6th Cir. 2003) — persuasive short-eviction due-process analysis on its facts.
  • Doe v. City of Albuquerque, 667 F.3d 1111 (10th Cir. 2012) — persuasive right-to-receive-information/access analysis; different forum terminology cautions against importing categorical labels.
  • Spiehs v. Morgan, No. 25-3174 (10th Cir. Sept. 8, 2026) — persuasive sign-restriction/library-purpose analysis; not a filming case and not controlling in California.
  • Van Den Heuvel v. Dorothy, No. 2:21-cv-02176 (E.D. Cal. 2022) — nonbinding screening-stage context for longer countywide library exclusions.

docs.title: Practical output
docs.text:
Sweep 006 establishes a system → branch → area/activity research model.

A branch file should separately establish property/control, exterior boundaries, ordinary/special hours, entrance conditions, main-floor use, designated children/teen/computer areas, study/meeting rooms, display channels, restrooms, restricted areas, recording signs/rules, removal authority, and any criminal-law bridge.

docs.title: Remaining library work
docs.text:
Still queued:

  • controlling law for peaceful photography/videography in ordinary California public-library interiors;
  • treatment of peaceful government observation/information gathering under library-purpose rules;
  • California Speech Clause application to library interiors/opened channels;
  • retaliation doctrine in library-recording disputes;
  • exact process required for different suspension lengths/scopes;
  • exact California trespass subsection after a valid or disputed suspension;
  • constitutional review of Contra Costa display/distribution restrictions;
  • branch-specific property and room-control research;
  • privacy/minor/program-specific restrictions;
  • physical seizure/search of cameras or phones if an encounter escalates.

docs.title: Remaining planned slices
docs.text:
• Penal Code Title 15 provisions touching privacy/recording, schools, loitering, and public access.
  • complete Brown Act and Bagley-Keene range sweeps.
  • complete CPRA exemption/law-enforcement records sweep, including Penal Code § 832.7/body-camera rules.
  • controlling case-law sweep for remaining constitutional/public-peace/trespass authorities.

docs.title: Legal Source and Verification Standard
docs.text: Every substantive rule in this project should be traceable to authority that a reader can independently verify.

docs.title: Tier 1 — Primary controlling authority
docs.text:
Preferred whenever available:

  • U.S. Constitution;
  • California Constitution;
  • United States Code;
  • California Codes;
  • Code of Federal Regulations;
  • California Code of Regulations;
  • California Rules of Court;
  • U.S. Supreme Court opinions;
  • Ninth Circuit opinions;
  • California Supreme Court opinions;
  • published California Courts of Appeal opinions.

docs.title: Tier 2 — Primary persuasive authority
docs.text:
Examples:

  • federal appellate cases outside the Ninth Circuit;
  • federal district-court decisions;
  • unpublished dispositions where citation is lawful and useful;
  • attorney-general opinions;
  • official administrative decisions.

These sources may be informative but must not be described as binding California authority when they are not.

docs.title: Tier 3 — Official policy and guidance
docs.text:
Examples:

  • agency photography policies;
  • courthouse general orders;
  • departmental manuals;
  • official FAQs;
  • DOJ, POST, DMV, USPS, GSA, or other government guidance.

These can establish what an agency says its rule is. They do not override constitutions, statutes, regulations, or controlling cases.

docs.title: Tier 4 — Secondary material
docs.text:
Examples:

  • treatises;
  • law-review articles;
  • legal journalism;
  • nonprofit legal guides;
  • attorney commentary.

Use these for context and research leads. Whenever practical, follow the citation back to primary authority.

docs.title: Tier 5 — Incident evidence
docs.text:
Examples:

  • audit videos;
  • body-camera recordings;
  • dispatch audio;
  • public-record responses;
  • photographs of signs;
  • public employee statements;
  • news reports about an incident.

These may establish facts or demonstrate how a policy was applied. They are not authority for the meaning of the law.

docs.title: Facility and incident evidence workflow
docs.text:
Facility research should preserve the chain between law, policy, implementation, and enforcement rather than treating them as interchangeable.

For a facility-specific investigation, record whenever available:

  • the specific area and access status;
  • the current written policy and its exact version/effective date;
  • the authority the agency claims supports that policy;
  • posted signs and where they appeared;
  • policy adoption/revision records;
  • training or staff instructions;
  • prior incidents and original source material;
  • police/security involvement, the exclusion/removal authority invoked, and any separate offense/detention/arrest authority invoked;
  • later CPRA/FOIA records;
  • field-verification results;
  • later corrections, policy revisions, or adjudicated outcomes.

Chronology matters. A policy adopted after an incident is not evidence that the same policy governed the earlier event.

Incident evidence should preserve provenance: original source, date, whether the material is edited, how it was obtained, and whether a later official record confirms or contradicts it.

Use the facility investigation template in docs/templates/facility-investigation-template.md.

docs.title: Facility-policy research flags
docs.text:
These flags describe the state of the project's research; they are not adjudications:

  • SUPPORTED-BY-IDENTIFIED-AUTHORITY
  • AUTHORITY-UNRESOLVED
  • POTENTIAL-FACIAL-CONFLICT
  • POTENTIAL-AS-APPLIED-CONFLICT
  • POTENTIAL-VIEWPOINT-COMPARATOR
  • POLICY-TO-CRIMINAL-AUTHORITY-GAP
  • SUPERSEDED-OR-REVISED

A sign, employee statement, agency policy, or police practice may provide evidence that a restriction exists or was enforced. It does not by itself prove that the restriction is constitutional, statutorily authorized, or criminally enforceable.

docs.title: Binding-authority labels
docs.text:
Case entries should use one of these labels:

  • binding-us-supreme-court
  • binding-ninth-circuit
  • binding-california-supreme-court
  • binding-california-court-of-appeal — identify district when relevant
  • persuasive-federal-district
  • persuasive-other-circuit
  • persuasive-other-state
  • nonprecedential

Do not reduce this to a generic "case law" label.

docs.title: Verification metadata
docs.text:
Every substantive chapter should contain or link to entries with:

authority: "California Penal Code § 602.1(b)"
jurisdiction: "California"
source_type: "statute"
binding_level: "statewide-statute"
source_url: "https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/..."
last_verified: "2026-09-16"
status: "verified"

For cases add:

court: "U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit"
decision_date: "YYYY-MM-DD"
precedential: true

docs.title: Status values
docs.text:
• verified — current text/opinion checked against a primary or authoritative source.
  • needs-review — plausible but not adequately verified.
  • disputed — authorities or interpretations materially conflict.
  • superseded — no longer current but retained for history.
  • facility-specific — applies only to a particular agency/building/category.

Methodology documents may use project-methodology in front matter. That label describes the project's research/field procedure; it is not a legal-verification status and should not be applied to a substantive rule of law.

docs.title: Quoting law
docs.text:
Short operative language may be quoted when wording matters, but the guide should usually summarize the rule and link the full text.

Do not quote only the favorable half of a provision while omitting an adjacent exception that changes the rule.

docs.title: Date discipline
docs.text:
Law changes. Every entry should be checked again when:

  • the Legislature amends the statute;
  • a new controlling case is decided;
  • an agency revises its policy;
  • a facility changes rules;
  • a contributor flags contrary authority.

A reader should always be able to tell when a proposition was last checked.

docs.title: Legal-rule format
docs.text:
Whenever practical, write entries in this order:

  1. Field rule — short, memorable proposition.
  2. Authority — precise source.
  3. What the authority actually says.
  4. Why it matters during an audit.
  5. Limits/exceptions.
  6. Cases interpreting it.
  7. Last verified.

The purpose of the field rule is recall, not simplification at the expense of accuracy.

docs.title: Sweep 002 — California Trespass and Property-Access Family
docs.text: Date reviewed: September 17, 2026 Status: Primary-text sweep complete for the defined slice; first controlling-case pass completed for selected core propositions.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This sweep reviewed the California Penal Code trespass/property-access family from § 601 through § 603, with complete accounting for:

  • every subdivision of current Penal Code § 602, subdivisions (a) through (y);
  • §§ 602.1 through 602.13;
  • immediately surrounding §§ 601 and 603.

This is a slice-level completeness claim only. It is not a completed sweep of all Penal Code Title 14, school/campus statutes in §§ 626 et seq., local ordinances, agency regulations, or all controlling case law.

docs.title: Primary sources
docs.text:
• § 601: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=601.
  • § 602: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.
  • § 602.1: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=602.1
  • §§ 602.2-602.13: individual California Legislative Information section pages, linked from docs/california/trespass-removal.md
  • § 603: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=603.

docs.title: Retained core authorities
docs.text: Authority Classification Reason § 602(m) RETAINED / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART Occupying requires nontransient, continuous possession; broader public-property application remains unresolved. § 602(o) RETAINED Refusal-to-leave provision expressly limited to property not open to the general public; public-agency case layer remains incomplete. § 602(q) RETAINED Express public-building rule, but only during hours when building is regularly closed to the public and with additional predicates. § 602(y) RETAINED / SPECIALIZED Government-building/courthouse screening-evasion rule; distinct from ordinary recording/presence and from visitor sign-in or ID policies. § 602.1(b) RETAINED Public agency open to public: intentional interference by obstruction/intimidation plus refusal after qualifying request. § 602.1(c) RETAINED Public-agency interference by knowingly making a material misrepresentation of law to people there to transact business, plus qualifying refusal. § 602.1(d)(2) RETAINED Express constitutional-activity exception to § 602.1. § 602.1(e) CONTEXT § 602.1 does not supersede other law.

docs.title: Specialized authorities retained for facility chapters
docs.text: Authority Classification Reason § 602(h) SPECIALIZED Posted animal-raising land/buildings. § 602(l) SPECIALIZED Cultivated/fenced/posted land plus specified conduct. § 602(n) SPECIALIZED Vehicle on property known not open to general public. § 602(p) SPECIALIZED Public Resources Code land closure. § 602(u) SPECIALIZED Restricted airport/passenger-vessel/public-transit areas. § 602(v) SPECIALIZED Avoiding screening into sterile airport/vessel/transit areas. § 602(w) SPECIALIZED Domestic-violence shelter. § 602(x) SPECIALIZED Neonatal/maternity/birthing areas. § 602.4 SPECIALIZED Selling/peddling on specified airport property. § 602.6 SPECIALIZED Closed fair property; qualifying order plus failure to identify/account for presence. Useful contrast to generic ID demands. § 602.7 SPECIALIZED Selling/peddling on specified transit property. § 602.8 SPECIALIZED Cultivated/fenced/posted land; constitutional-activity exception; Edgerly shows it can independently support probable cause even when § 602(m) does not. § 602.10 SPECIALIZED Physical-force obstruction of students/teachers at specified public higher-ed facilities. § 602.11 SPECIALIZED Physical obstruction of entry/exit at health-care facility, place of worship, or school; physically excludes speech. § 602.13 SPECIALIZED Posted animal enclosure at zoo/circus/exhibit.

docs.title: Reviewed but outside standing scope
docs.text: Authority Classification Reason § 601 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Requires credible threat and intent to execute threat. § 602(a)-(g), (i)-(j) N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Timber/resource/property-damage/fire/fence/sign offenses outside standing peaceful-audit assumptions. § 602(r) N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Closed ski area/trail. § 602(s) N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Hotel/motel nonpayment. § 602(t) N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Specified private-property exclusion following prior conviction. § 602.2 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE County ordinance rule for vacant/unimproved private land. § 602.3 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Specified owner-occupied dwelling/lodger removal. § 602.5 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Noncommercial dwelling/residential entry/remain. § 602.9 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Unauthorized residential rental/possession scheme. § 602.12 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Residential property of academic researcher with chilling/interference purpose. § 603 N/A-STANDING-SCOPE Forcible building entry plus property damage.

docs.title: Key primary-text discoveries
docs.text:
1. Within the defined §§ 601-603 slice, there is no generic asked to leave = trespass provision for an ordinary public-agency interior open to the public. Potentially relevant provisions contain additional predicates, and other laws/regulations/local rules may still independently apply.
  2. § 602(o) says not open to the general public. This matters when refusal-to-leave language is invoked while the person is in an area currently open to everyone.
  3. § 602(q) expressly addresses public buildings but only when regularly closed to the public. Public hours are therefore a potentially dispositive statutory fact for that subsection.
  4. § 602(m) says entering and occupying. The case-law review confirms that occupying is a substantial additional element rather than surplusage.
  5. § 602(y) is a screening-evasion provision. It concerns screening/inspection of the person and accessible property and should not be conflated with ordinary filming after lawful entry through security.
  6. Visitor sign-in, badge, appointment, purpose-of-visit, and ID requirements are separate access-policy questions. § 602(y) does not itself convert refusal to sign a visitor log or produce identification into criminal trespass.
  7. § 602.1(c) is auditor-relevant and was missing from the earlier chapter. It specifically requires a knowing material misrepresentation of law to people there to transact business plus refusal after the qualifying request.
  8. § 602.6 contains a specialized identification/account-for-presence element in a narrow closed-fair setting. Its existence reinforces the need to identify a specific California legal basis before treating every public-building encounter as carrying a universal identification requirement.
  9. § 602.11 expressly says physically does not include speech. This is a useful facility/protest distinction for later chapters.
  10. Public access and forum classification are separate. A specific area may be open to members of the public for agency business without being a traditional or designated public forum for general expressive activity.

docs.title: § 602(m) — occupation is nontransient and continuous
docs.text:
• In re Catalano, 29 Cal.3d 1 (1981) — binding California Supreme Court authority. The court states that the entering-and-occupying subdivision requires occupation of the property, a nontransient, continuous type of possession, citing People v. Wilkinson. The subdivision was later renumbered to current § 602(m) without substantive change to this language.
  • Edgerly v. City & County of San Francisco, 599 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2010) — published/binding Ninth Circuit authority for federal probable-cause analysis. A matter of minutes on the property did not supply probable cause for the entering-and-occupying subdivision. The court nevertheless found probable cause under § 602.8(a), illustrating why each potentially applicable subsection must be checked independently.
  • CALCRIM No. 2931 — the Judicial Council instruction requires proof that the defendant occupied some part of the property continuously until removed.

Narrow doctrine-reviewed proposition: transient or momentary presence does not satisfy § 602(m)'s occupation requirement.

docs.title: § 602.1 — refusal and intentional interference are distinct
docs.text:
• Dubner v. City & County of San Francisco, 266 F.3d 959 (9th Cir. 2001) — published Ninth Circuit decision. The court treated § 602.1 as requiring intentional interference plus refusal to leave and rejected the contention that intent to interfere could be inferred merely from refusal. The photographer/legal observer's documented conduct did not supply facts of deliberate obstruction or intimidation.
  • The wording quoted in Dubner was the business-establishment version of § 602.1, not today's public-agency subdivision (b). The case is therefore used as a binding probable-cause guidepost on the common § 602.1 structure, not as a complete published construction of every element of current subdivision (b).
  • Mackey v. Meyer, 675 F. App'x 705 (9th Cir. 2017) applied Dubner specifically to § 602.1(b) at a DMV and found no probable cause on the video-supported facts, but it is unpublished and is not treated as binding precedent.

docs.title: § 602(o) — publication-status caution
docs.text: The 2026 Court of Appeal opinion People v. Hsiung discusses § 602(o)'s constitutional savings language, but that analysis appears in Part III, which the court expressly excluded from publication. The California Supreme Court later denied review and a depublication request, but that does not convert the excluded Part III analysis into published precedential authority. The Field Guide therefore does not rely on that discussion as controlling law.

docs.title: Sweep 003 — California Public Records Act / Evidence Preservation
docs.text: Date reviewed: September 17, 2026 Status: Core operational CPRA and preservation doctrine reviewed; complete exemption and agency-retention families remain pending.

docs.title: Defined scope
docs.text:
Sweep 003 is a targeted doctrinal and operational sweep, not yet a section-by-section completeness claim for all of Government Code Division 10.

The completed scope covers:

  1. the CPRA definition of public record and writing;
  2. core access/withholding principles;
  3. the request, inspection, copying, electronic-record, timeline, denial, and assistance provisions needed for an auditor to obtain incident evidence;
  4. personal-account/device doctrine under City of San Jose v. Superior Court, 2 Cal.5th 608 (2017);
  5. preservation/retention doctrine under City of Gilroy v. Superior Court, 19 Cal.5th 38 (2026);
  6. representative state/city/county retention frameworks needed to establish that retention is agency- and record-specific;
  7. Government Code §§ 6200-6201 as potential destruction authorities, with their applicability deliberately kept separate from the CPRA's broader disclosure definition;
  8. a practical workflow for work-related recordings made by public employees on personal devices.

This sweep does not yet claim complete review of:

  • every exemption in Division 10 Parts 5 and 6;
  • every law-enforcement records rule;
  • every retention statute for every type of state/local agency;
  • all spoliation/discovery sanctions;
  • all CPRA fee/attorney-fee litigation doctrine.

docs.title: Definitions and access
docs.text: Authority Classification Initial proposition Gov. Code § 7920.530 RETAINED / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED Public record = writing substantively relating to public business prepared, owned, used, or retained by state/local agency; City of San Jose supplies controlling personal-account doctrine. Gov. Code § 7920.545 RETAINED Writing includes photographs, pictures, sounds, electronic transmissions, and other recorded information regardless of storage method. Gov. Code § 7921.000 RETAINED Legislative declaration that access to information concerning the people's business is a fundamental and necessary right, balanced with privacy. Gov. Code § 7921.010 RETAINED / CONTEXT Restricts transfer to private entities to evade access; subdivision (c) recognizes destruction of a public record pursuant to law; central to Gilroy. Gov. Code § 7921.300 RETAINED Access to otherwise disclosable records generally may not be limited based on requester's purpose. Gov. Code § 7922.000 RETAINED Agency bears burden to justify withholding by express exemption or balancing facts under the statutory catchall.

docs.title: Request procedure and electronic records
docs.text: Authority Classification Initial proposition § 7922.500 RETAINED No delay or obstruction of inspection/copying. § 7922.505 CONTEXT Agency may adopt requirements providing faster, more efficient, or greater access than statutory minimum. § 7922.525 RETAINED Inspection during office hours; reasonably segregable nonexempt portions available after exempt portions removed. § 7922.530 RETAINED Copies of reasonably described identifiable records; personal copying equipment for on-premises inspection subject to statutory conditions/reasonable limits. § 7922.535 RETAINED Ordinarily 10-day determination; specified unusual circumstances permit written extension of no more than 14 additional days; 2026 text checked. § 7922.540 RETAINED Written denial requirements and identification of responsible person(s). § 7922.545 CONTEXT Agency website availability rules and copy obligation when requester cannot access/reproduce online record. §§ 7922.570-7922.585 RETAINED / CONTEXT Electronic-format availability, direct costs/extraction, limits on reconstruction, system-security limits, software/information distinction. §§ 7922.600-7922.605 RETAINED Duty to reasonably assist requester formulate focused/effective request, subject to listed exceptions. §§ 7922.630-7922.640 CONTEXT Agency regulations/guidelines; specified bodies must maintain written access guidelines; rules must remain consistent with public-access purpose. §§ 7922.680, 7922.700-7922.725 CONTEXT / REVIEW-LATER Internet resources and enterprise-system catalog provisions identified; not material to the personal-device preservation field rule in this pass.

docs.title: Enforcement
docs.text: Authority Classification Initial proposition § 7923.000 RETAINED / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART Injunctive/declaratory relief and mandate; City of Gilroy confirms declaratory relief can remain available for recurring disputed practices even after existing records have been produced/destroyed.

docs.title: City of San Jose v. Superior Court, 2 Cal.5th 608 (2017)
docs.text: Binding level: California Supreme Court.

docs.title: Holdings/propositions retained
docs.text:
1. A public employee's writings about public business do not fall outside CPRA merely because they are sent, received, or stored in a personal account.
  2. Storage location/device ownership is not dispositive of public-record status.
  3. At minimum, the writing must relate in some substantive way to the conduct of the public's business.
  4. Relevant factors include content, context/purpose, audience, and whether the employee acted or purported to act within the scope of employment.
  5. Primarily personal communications with only incidental public-business references generally are not public records.
  6. Agencies must make reasonable efforts to locate responsive records; searches need only be reasonably calculated to locate responsive documents and need not be extraordinarily intrusive.
  7. When responsive public records may be held in employee personal accounts/devices, an agency should communicate the request to the employees and may reasonably rely on them to search their personal files/accounts/devices for responsive public-business material.

docs.title: Auditor-specific consequence
docs.text: An employee-created personal-phone recording made on duty specifically to document an official encounter is a strong public-record candidate, because the medium is a CPRA writing and the content/context/purpose/scope factors point toward public business. The guide does not state that every recording by every public employee is automatically a public record.

docs.title: City of Gilroy v. Superior Court, 19 Cal.5th 38 (2026)
docs.text: Binding level: California Supreme Court. Filed: January 15, 2026.

docs.title: Holdings/propositions retained
docs.text:
1. The CPRA itself does not impose a duty to preserve for three years all responsive records withheld as exempt.
  2. CPRA contains no general records-retention requirement; retention/preservation duties arise from other law where applicable.
  3. Government Code § 7921.010(c)'s recognition of destruction pursuant to law reinforces the distinction between disclosure and retention.
  4. Declaratory relief under § 7923.000 remains available at least where it would resolve an ongoing rights/obligations dispute likely to affect future requests or future conduct.
  5. The Court recognized separate litigation-preservation/spoliation law when litigation is reasonably foreseeable rather than inferring that duty from CPRA.

docs.title: Footnote 20 limitation
docs.text: The Court expressly limited its no-CPRA-preservation holding to destruction connected with the normal adoption, implementation, and operation of routine records-retention practices/policies. It stated that it had no occasion to address intentional destruction in other contexts that may reflect deliberate misconduct.

docs.title: Auditor-specific consequence
docs.text: A requester must not claim that saying I will request that video or filing a CPRA request automatically freezes the record under CPRA. A preservation notice is still valuable evidence of existence, knowledge, notice, and intent, but the legal preservation duty must be located in the applicable retention law, schedule, litigation-preservation doctrine, or another statute.

docs.title: State executive agencies
docs.text:
The California State Archives identifies the State Records Management Act, Government Code §§ 12270-12279, and approved records-retention schedules as the state executive-agency framework. State Administrative Manual Chapter 1600 requires agency retention-schedule programs. State guidance notes that an unscheduled state record is not simply disposable at will and quotes § 12275's disposition restriction.

Classification: RETAINED / CONTEXT.

docs.title: Gov. Code § 34090
docs.text:
City-record destruction mechanism subject to legislative-body resolution, city-attorney consent, and statutory limitations/exceptions.

Classification: RETAINED / SPECIALIZED BY AGENCY TYPE.

docs.title: Gov. Code § 34090.6
docs.text:
Specialized rules for specified routine video monitoring and telephone/radio communications, with stated periods and conditions. It is not treated as a universal retention rule for ad hoc employee phone video.

Classification: SPECIALIZED.

docs.title: Counties — Gov. Code § 26202
docs.text:
County record-destruction authority under specified conditions; must be read with more specific law and the county's adopted schedule.

Classification: RETAINED / SPECIALIZED BY AGENCY TYPE.

docs.title: Gov. Code §§ 6200-6201
docs.text:
Criminal provisions concerning specified records/documents and willful removal, destruction, alteration, etc.

Classification: RETAINED / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART.

Published California authority includes People v. Sperl, 54 Cal.App.3d 640 (1976), which applied § 6200 to official county radio logs and rejected the claim that such a record was freely disposable merely because no statute expressly required its creation or retention. Related published authority includes People v. Pearson and Loder v. Municipal Court.

Important limitation: The guide does not equate the CPRA's broad public-record definition with the elements/scope of §§ 6200-6201. Those criminal provisions still have their own covered-record, custody, authorization, willfulness, and—under § 6200—officer having custody requirements. Their application to ad hoc personal-device recordings remains unresolved.

docs.title: Key Sweep 003 discoveries
docs.text:
1. Personal device is not a safe harbor. City of San Jose rejects categorical exclusion based on a personal account/device.
  2. Content/context control public-record status. Employment alone does not make every private item public.
  3. Search and disclosure are different. The agency may have a duty to search for a personal-device public record even though an exemption may ultimately permit withholding/redaction.
  4. Disclosure and retention are different. The CPRA is not a universal retention statute.
  5. A pending request is not an automatic CPRA litigation hold. Gilroy squarely rejects the proposed three-year CPRA preservation rule.
  6. Gilroy does not bless deliberate destruction. Its express footnote 20 limitation leaves intentional/destructive-misconduct contexts unresolved by that holding.
  7. Retention periods are not universal. State executive, city, county, special-district, law-enforcement, court, school, and other records can fall under different statutes and schedules.
  8. Request the retention schedule. If a record disappears, the applicable schedule/policy becomes evidence and part of the legal analysis.
  9. A preservation notice remains useful even without automatic legal effect. It identifies the record and can establish knowledge/notice before later disposition.
  10. The safest field statement is narrow: I intend to request that work-related recording; please preserve the original. Do not announce a felony or automatic CPRA violation based solely on later deletion.

docs.title: Sweep 004 — Police Encounters: Fourth Amendment + Self-Incrimination
docs.text: Date reviewed: September 21, 2026 Status: Core encounter doctrine reviewed in part; substantial edge-case/remedies work remains pending.

docs.title: Defined scope
docs.text:
Sweep 004 builds the encounter spine that commonly follows peaceful First Amendment activity:

  1. consensual police contact;
  2. Fourth Amendment seizure/detention;
  3. Terry reasonable suspicion;
  4. scope and duration;
  5. identification requests and California-specific identification law, including the distinction between carrying ID, stating identity, and producing possessed identification;
  6. protective frisks;
  7. probable-cause arrest;
  8. Fifth Amendment / Miranda questioning;
  9. physical seizure versus digital search of phones/cameras;
  10. field language that preserves facts without treating slogans as law.

This is a targeted operational/doctrinal sweep, not a complete Fourth Amendment, Fifth Amendment, California criminal-procedure, device-search, or remedies sweep.

docs.title: Constitutional architecture
docs.text:
Authority Status Narrow proposition U.S. Const. amend. IV DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART Seizure/detention, arrest, frisk, property/device search and seizure. U.S. Const. amend. V DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART Compelled testimonial self-incrimination; Miranda layer. U.S. Const. amend. XIV DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART Incorporation against California state/local actors; independent 14A doctrine remains broader. Cal. Const. art. I, § 13 PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED State search/seizure protection; independent state doctrine pending. Cal. Const. art. I, § 15 PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED State self-incrimination/due-process text; independent state doctrine pending.

docs.title: Mapp v. Ohio, 367 U.S. 643 (1961)
docs.text:
Binding: U.S. Supreme Court. Retained: Fourth Amendment protection/exclusionary layer applies against the States through the Fourteenth Amendment. The full exclusionary-rule doctrine is outside this sweep.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-367_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: Malloy v. Hogan, 378 U.S. 1 (1964)
docs.text:
Binding: U.S. Supreme Court. Retained: the Fourteenth Amendment secures the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination against state infringement.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-378_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: Terry v. Ohio, 392 U.S. 1 (1968)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: investigative detention may rest on reasonable suspicion supported by specific/articulable facts; stop and protective frisk are distinct; frisk requires an armed-and-dangerous safety basis; stop must be justified at inception and appropriately limited in scope.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-392_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: United States v. Sharpe, 470 U.S. 675 (1985)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART: no rigid universal stopwatch; duration analysis includes police diligence and circumstances.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-470_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: Devenpeck v. Alford, 543 U.S. 146 (2004)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: warrantless-arrest probable cause is objective; the offense supported by known facts need not be the offense announced by the arresting officer.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/543bv.pdf

docs.title: Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015)
docs.text:
SPECIALIZED / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART: traffic stop may not be prolonged beyond its traffic mission to pursue unrelated investigation without an independent legal basis.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/575bv.pdf

docs.title: People v. Tacardon, 14 Cal.5th 235 (2022)
docs.text:
Binding: California Supreme Court. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: consensual encounter versus detention uses totality of circumstances; directed police attention/spotlight did not automatically create a seizure on the facts there.

Official sources: - https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s264219-people-v-tacardon - https://www.courts.ca.gov/opinions/archive/S264219.PDF

docs.title: People v. Flores, 15 Cal.5th 1032 (2024)
docs.text:
Binding: California Supreme Court. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: reasonable suspicion requires particularized/objective grounds under the totality; high-crime-area context is not by itself individualized suspicion; facts there were insufficient. Evasive/nervous conduct remains potentially relevant in context rather than categorically irrelevant.

Official sources: - https://supreme.courts.ca.gov/case/s267522-people-v-flores - https://courts.ca.gov/opinion/citings-archive/2024-05-02/s267522

docs.title: Penal Code § 148(g)
docs.text:
Recording a public/peace officer in a public place or from a place the recorder has a right to be does not in and of itself establish §148 obstruction, reasonable suspicion, or probable cause.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148

Status: PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED.

docs.title: Vehicle Code § 2806.5 — pedestrian-stop notice relevant to this project
docs.text:
Effective January 1, 2024, a peace officer making a traffic or pedestrian stop must, before questioning related to a criminal investigation or traffic violation, state the reason for the stop. The officer must document the reason on any resulting citation or police report. The statute contains an exception when the officer reasonably believes withholding the reason is necessary to protect life or property from an imminent threat.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=2806.5

Status: PRIMARY-TEXT-VERIFIED.

docs.title: People v. Valle, A169080 (Cal. Ct. App. Sept. 18, 2024)
docs.text:
Binding level: published California Court of Appeal, First District, Division One. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART: the opinion recognizes § 2806.5's California stop-notice requirement and treats it as distinct from the federal Fourth Amendment question whether the stop was objectively justified. Valle itself arose from a traffic stop; the project retains it only for interpretation of a statute that also expressly covers pedestrian stops. The statute requires notice of the reason for the stop before the covered questioning; it does not convert the on-scene encounter into a requirement that the officer recite every fact later relied upon to establish reasonable suspicion. Valle also notes that proposed suppression language was removed before enactment and rejects treating the statute as altering federal Fourth Amendment admissibility analysis.

Official California Judicial Branch source: https://courts.ca.gov/opinion/published-extended-post/2024-09-18/a169080

Operational distinction: reasonable suspicion must actually exist when the seizure begins. Section 2806.5 may require the officer to state the reason for the stop before covered questioning, but later facts and later explanations cannot retroactively create reasonable suspicion for an earlier seizure.

docs.title: Penal Code § 148.9
docs.text:
False representation/identification as another or fictitious person to specified officers upon qualifying lawful detention/arrest, with the statutory evasive purpose.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=148.9

Retained distinction: false identity is an independent offense question; §148.9 does not itself state a universal affirmative duty for every detained pedestrian to identify.

docs.title: Penal Code § 853.5
docs.text:
Specified infraction-arrest/citation process addressing satisfactory identification and fingerprint/thumbprint procedure.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=853.5

docs.title: Vehicle Code § 12951
docs.text:
Driver-specific license possession/presentation requirement.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=12951

docs.title: Vehicle Code § 40302
docs.text:
Specified custody/magistrate rules after arrest for nonfelony Vehicle Code violations, including identity circumstances.

Primary source: https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=VEH&sectionNum=40302

docs.title: Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial District Court, 542 U.S. 177 (2004)
docs.text:
Binding: U.S. Supreme Court. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: Nevada enacted a specific stop-and-identify statute; the Court upheld its name requirement during a valid Terry stop on the facts there. Hiibel does not itself create a California identification duty. Its Fifth Amendment holding was also fact-specific: stating Hiibel's name did not present a reasonable danger of incrimination there.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/542bv.pdf

docs.title: Kolender v. Lawson, 461 U.S. 352 (1983)
docs.text:
Binding: U.S. Supreme Court. CONTEXT / DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: California's former credible and reliable identification scheme was invalidated as unconstitutionally vague. This history does not invalidate all modern California context-specific identification requirements.

Official discussion/source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/542bv.pdf (Hiibel's discussion of Kolender); official U.S. Reports citation 461 U.S. 352.

docs.title: United States v. Landeros, 913 F.3d 862 (9th Cir. 2019)
docs.text:
Binding: published Ninth Circuit federal authority in California. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: where officers lacked reasonable suspicion that a passenger had committed an offense, refusal to identify did not itself furnish reasonable suspicion and did not justify prolonging the traffic stop.

Official source: https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2019/01/11/17-10217.pdf

docs.title: People v. Quiroga, 16 Cal.App.4th 961 (1993)
docs.text:
Binding level: published California Court of Appeal. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART:

  • slow compliance/verbal argument did not automatically constitute Penal Code §148 obstruction;
  • refusal to state a name after arrest while being transported did not itself violate §148 because arrest had already been effected and booking had not begun;
  • refusal to disclose identity during a felony booking interview could violate §148 by obstructing/delaying booking;
  • the opinion distinguished misdemeanor/infraction contexts governed by other identification/release statutes.

The Judicial Council's current CALCRIM authority notes cite Quiroga under Verbal Resistance or Obstruction and describe the nondisclosure proposition as following arrest for a felony, not misdemeanor.

Official Judicial Council CALCRIM source: https://courts.ca.gov/advisory-body/criminal-jury-instructions-advisory-committee Published opinion reproduction: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/4th/16/961.html

docs.title: In re Chase C., 243 Cal.App.4th 107 (2015)
docs.text:
Binding level: published California Court of Appeal. DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART: on the facts there, refusal to identify while detained/postarrest but before booking did not constitute §148 obstruction; the court characterized that refusal as protected Fifth Amendment silence and distinguished booking-stage refusal and false identification. The opinion also emphasized that refusal to cooperate becomes criminal under §148 only when it actually obstructs lawful police activity.

Published opinion reproduction: https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2015/d067787.html

docs.title: Bounded California conclusion
docs.text:
This targeted sweep has not identified a current general California pedestrian carry-ID statute or a general statutory stop-and-identify law comparable to Nevada's statute in Hiibel.

Do not inflate that into either of these claims:

  • I can never be required to identify or produce possessed identification in California.
  • If I am lawfully detained, refusing my name automatically violates §148.

The first proposition is too broad because older published California cases, including People v. Long and People v. Loudermilk, address production/search for identification during otherwise lawful detentions under fact-specific Fourth Amendment reasoning. Loudermilk itself emphasized the limits of its holding, and later cases including People v. Garcia address limits on identification searches. That line requires a dedicated reconciliation before the Field Guide states a categorical rule about compelled production of possessed identification during a lawful detention.

The better current rule is:

No general carry-ID or statutory pedestrian stop-and-identify law has been identified. Separately analyze whether a specific context or case-law rule permits an officer to require particular identifying information or possessed proof of identity. Silence/refusal is not automatically §148 obstruction; booking and specialized statutory contexts can be different; false identity is separately regulated by §148.9.

docs.title: Berkemer v. McCarty, 468 U.S. 420 (1984)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: a person can be seized/not free to leave under the Fourth Amendment without automatically being in Miranda custody; ordinary traffic/Terry-type stops generally are not custodial solely because freedom of movement is curtailed.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/pdfs/USReports/USREPORTS-468_PDFA.pdf

docs.title: Berghuis v. Thompkins, 560 U.S. 370 (2010)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: in Miranda custody, invocation of the right to remain silent must be unambiguous; prolonged silence did not constitute invocation on the facts there.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/560bv.pdf

docs.title: Salinas v. Texas, 570 U.S. 178 (2013)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED-IN-PART / plurality-limited: in a voluntary noncustodial interview, the plurality rejected the Fifth Amendment claim where Salinas became silent but did not expressly invoke. Do not state a categorical majority rule that silence never invokes the privilege in any setting.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/570bv.pdf

Operational consequence: if intending to invoke, clear words are safer than relying on silence alone:

I invoke my right to remain silent. I do not want to answer investigative questions.

This is not magic phrasing.

docs.title: Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014)
docs.text:
DOCTRINE-REVIEWED: search incident to arrest does not ordinarily authorize a warrantless search of digital information on a seized cellphone; police generally need a warrant for digital contents subject to recognized exceptions. Physical seizure/retention and digital-content search remain analytically distinct.

Official source: https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/boundvolumes/573BV.pdf

Still RESEARCH: physical seizure/retention short of arrest; device warrant particularity; exigency details; compelled passcodes/biometrics/encryption; testimonial-act/foregone-conclusion doctrine; deletion/interference with recordings.

docs.title: Practical distinctions established by Sweep 004
docs.text:
1. Police contact ≠ detention. Mere approach/questioning can remain consensual.
  2. Detention ≠ arrest. Terry permits a limited seizure on reasonable suspicion.
  3. Detention ≠ frisk. A frisk needs its own armed-and-dangerous basis.
  4. Detention ≠ Miranda custody. Fourth and Fifth Amendment thresholds differ.
  5. Reasonable suspicion ≠ probable cause. Arrest ordinarily requires the higher threshold.
  6. Recording alone ≠ obstruction/RS/PC. Penal Code §148(g) says so expressly within its scope.
  7. Requesting ID ≠ proof of a general carry-ID or stop-and-identify law. Identify the actual statute, context, and applicable case law before treating the request as compulsory.
  8. Refusal/silence ≠ automatic §148 obstruction. Quiroga and Chase C. add California-specific limits; booking can be different.
  9. Refusing ID ≠ license to give false ID. §148.9 is separate.
  10. Hiibel ≠ nationwide ID mandate. It upheld Nevada's statute during a valid Terry stop.
  11. Reason for stop ≠ full RAS recital. For the pedestrian-stop setting relevant to this project, Vehicle Code §2806.5 requires the reason for the stop before covered questioning, subject to its exception; that is distinct from disclosing every fact underlying reasonable suspicion.
  12. Officer's announced offense ≠ entire arrest analysis. Devenpeck makes probable cause objective.
  13. Device seizure ≠ digital search. Riley sharply distinguishes digital contents.
  14. No Miranda warning ≠ illegal arrest. Arrest legality and interrogation safeguards are separate.
  15. Silence ≠ safest invocation strategy. Clear invocation avoids relying on inference.

docs.title: Sweep 005 — Public-Forum Doctrine
docs.text: Review date: September 17, 2026 Status: Core federal forum architecture and California overlay reviewed; facility-specific classifications remain open.

docs.title: Defined scope
docs.text:
Sweep 005 closes the structural gap identified in the trespass/property work: the Field Guide must distinguish public access from forum status and must classify the specific area/channel at issue, not treat an entire government building as one constitutional unit.

This is a targeted doctrine sweep covering:

  1. forum identification/perimeter;
  2. traditional public forums;
  3. designated public forums;
  4. limited public forums;
  5. nonpublic forums;
  6. viewpoint discrimination;
  7. public-forum time/place/manner restrictions;
  8. government-building interiors;
  9. California Constitution article I, section 2(a);
  10. the relationship among forum status, recording, removal, trespass, meetings, and the facility registry.

This is not a complete facility-by-facility forum survey.
